<note>original: "Pasquillorum" — A pasquil (or pasquinade) is a form of anonymous satire, usually a short poem or lampoon, named after "Pasquino," a statue in Rome where such critiques were historically posted.</note>

## TO THE READER.

<image-desc>Decorative historiated drop cap 'V' featuring an ornate frame with scrollwork, foliage, and a central human face or mask at the top.</image-desc>

It is an old habit among men, and implanted in most by nature, that they delight in ridiculous and fabled stories, while they turn away from things said seriously and gravely. Indeed, certain signs of this tendency shine forth even in children; for this reason, parents and teachers provide them with apologues <note>original: "apologos." These are moral fables, such as those of Aesop, which use storytelling to teach a lesson.</note> and fables from the very beginning. Since children do not easily accept serious and weighty instructions, they are meanwhile instructed toward virtue <note>original: "uirtutem." In this context, it refers to both moral character and civic duty.</note> through those humorous examples, as if through play. Therefore, those who have been educated in this fashion, and have become accustomed to and charmed by those empty but plausible tales, usually tend to retain that same habit even when they are adults and established in age. They often prefer, even in more serious matters, to be led along by feigned and veiled words, rather than to be warned about affairs through open speech in a grave and serious manner. Accordingly, even Demosthenes <note>The most famous orator of ancient Athens, known for his persuasive and powerful political speeches.</note>—when he once had judges who were less than attentive while he was delivering his closing plea <note>original: "peroranda." A technical term for the final part of an orator's speech.</note> in a capital case—cast aside the severity of his oration and turned to certain trifles—

<meta>catchword: turned</meta>

<summary>In this preface, the author argues that humans are naturally drawn to humor and fables rather than dry, serious instruction. He justifies the use of satire (pasquils) by noting that even great orators like Demosthenes used lighthearted stories to recapture the attention of an audience when discussing life-and-death matters.</summary>
<keywords>human nature, fables, education, virtue, satire, Demosthenes, rhetoric, pedagogy</keywords>

### PREFACE.

turned aside, and recited the fable of the donkey's shadow <note>original: "fabulam de asini umbra." This is a famous Greek anecdote where Demosthenes tells a story about a man who hired a donkey and then argued with the owner over who had the right to sit in the animal's shadow. When the audience leaned in to hear the ending, he scolded them for caring more about a donkey's shadow than the life of a man on trial.</note> to them while they were sitting and listening. By this means, he not only woke them as if from a deep sleep, but also, having soon rebuked them because they were more attentive to little stories than to the matter at hand, he found them somewhat more fair and diligent in understanding the legal case. 

Especially if you offer any warning regarding morals or duties, most people turn away their ears and minds; they would allow you to do anything rather than—as a certain poet says—"scrape those tender ears with the biting truth." <note>original: "radere uero." This is a reference to the Roman satirist Persius, who used the metaphor of a doctor or a sharp instrument scraping away falsehoods to describe the painful but necessary effect of satire.</note> Therefore, it is just as doctors sometimes do, who:

> when healers attempt to give bitter wormwood <term>wormwood: a proverbially bitter herb (absinthium) used in ancient medicine to treat intestinal worms and fever.</term>, 
> they first touch the rims around the cups 
> with the sweet, golden liquid of honey. <note>These lines are a famous passage from the Roman poet Lucretius's *On the Nature of Things*. He used this metaphor to explain why he wrote his difficult philosophy in beautiful verse.</note>

In the same way here, it is necessary to enter the minds of men through certain charms and allurements of words, as it were, and to occupy their turned and alienated minds as if by doing something else. Seeing this very thing long ago, those most ancient and wisest of the Greeks permitted this license and power to the youth, so that, carried around in wagons and [having smeared] their faces with dregs <note>The author is describing the legendary origins of Greek comedy and satire, where performers in the "Dionysia" would ride in wagons and mock citizens, often using wine dregs to disguise their faces.</note>...

### PREFACE.

...having been smeared <note>original: "perūcti." Likely completing the phrase *faecibus peruncti*, referring to the tradition of early Greek actors smearing their faces with wine dregs to disguise themselves.</note> with wine dregs, they would sing out publicly through the streets and crossroads those things which others had done shamefully or foully. From this origin, it is said that the beginning of what is called **Old Comedy** <note>original: "ueteris comoediae." This refers to the early style of Greek theater, most famous through the works of Aristophanes, known for its bold, direct, and often biting political satire.</note> soon began. In this form of theater, not only were the **morals of men** <note>original: "mores hominum."</note> censured publicly and openly, but even the characters and way of life of those who were secretly suffering from vices were depicted through gesture and imitation.

Because this custom and method then seemed useful to the public—and therefore honorable and worthy of being promoted—the same practice passed from the Greeks to others in succession. Just as the possession of empire passed from them to the Romans, so too was this **freedom of criticism** <note>original: "carpendi libertas." Literally the "freedom of plucking," referring to the right to pick apart or find fault with someone's behavior.</note> transferred in the same way. 

For what the choruses of plays had once performed in Athens, the **Satires** <note>original: "Satyrorum poëmata." While the word looks like "Satyrs," the author is referring to the Roman literary genre of Satire (*Satura*), which used verse to critique social and moral failings.</note> of the poets later represented in Rome. These works were so far from being hated or forbidden in those times that their authors and poets would prefix them with their own names and titles. 

Although this freedom of speech was interrupted several times afterwards, or even lay suppressed for a while by the tyranny of certain people, it was nevertheless restored from time to time, and like l...

# PREFACE.

->P R A E F A T I O .<-

...restored to its own place <note>original: "loco suo." Completing the thought from the previous page that satire was restored to its proper function.</note>, nor was it ever entirely or deeply extinguished. For in nearly every age there have been wise and good men, one after another, who, seeing the same thing as those ancients, understood that the lives and **morals of men** <note>original: "mores hominum."</note> could not be corrected in any better or more effective way than if a person saw in someone else that which he might judge to be a credit or a vice to himself at some point in the future. 

These same men judged that in a **free state** <note>original: "in ciuitate libera."</note>, just as the bodies of men are free, so also ought their **tongues to be free** <note>original: "linguas liberas." An early expression of the necessity of free speech in a healthy society.</note>. And for this reason, I believe, even one of the **Supreme Pontiffs** <note>original: "summorū Pontificum." A title for the Pope.</note>—whoever he may have been in a former age—acting on counsel that was neither bad nor useless (as far as can be seen from the matter itself), either established or permitted at Rome that, following that same **ancient example** <note>original: "ueterū exemplo." Referring back to the Greek and Roman traditions of public satire.</note> and custom, people might publish at specific times those things they had seen or known about others at a certain statue dedicated under the name of **Pasquillus** <term>Pasquillus: Latin for Pasquino, a famous "talking statue" in Rome. Starting in the 16th century, citizens would anonymously post satirical verses, or "pasquinades," on this statue to criticize the authorities.</term>, marked with the same license as in the past. 

For since it is entirely necessary that the morals of men be corrected, but no one easily dares to challenge the vices of the powerful with plain and open speech, that supreme and most prudent...

# PREFACE

->P R A E F A T I O<-

...he <note>Referring to the Pope or authority mentioned on the previous page who permitted the statue's use.</note> [judged] that this was the one remaining way by which men might know themselves, and understand how their own deeds were judged by others and from the outside. If there were things that others did not dare to say openly and face-to-face, this **Pasquillus** <term>Pasquillus: The Latin name for Pasquino, a "talking statue" in Rome where citizens posted anonymous satirical poems (pasquinades) to criticize the government or clergy.</term> would take the task of pointing them out upon himself, and bring them to the public in his own name. He would be, as it were, a certain **public censor of morals** <note>original: "publicus morum censor." In Roman history, the Censor was an official who overseen public morality; the author suggests Pasquino performs this role for the Renaissance.</note> and a teacher of life: an interpreter of all things serious as well as ridiculous. 

If anyone were to remove him from our midst, that same person would be removing a great and good part of **liberty** <note>original: "libertatis." This highlights the Renaissance value of "Pasquino's liberty"—the tradition of anonymous free speech.</note>, and no small part of utility as well. Therefore, since certain ingenious men have recently published examples and some brief **dialogues** <note>original: "dialogismos."</note> of this Pasquillus—in which they have not only noted the times and morals, but also touched upon certain other things not unpleasant to know within the same theme—it seemed that it would be worth the effort if we were to collect from all over those that were a little more festive and elegant, and, gathering them under a single bundle, as it were, present them to those who study such things. For that matter would provide not only delight, but also that advantage...

# PREFACE

->P R A E F A T I O<-

...it likewise happens that from this point it will be permitted to note down a certain concise and brief **history of this age** <note>original: "seculi huius historiam." The author suggests that these satirical verses serve as a historical record of contemporary life.</note>. Furthermore, if at any time it was necessary that men be invited in some way to hear what belongs to each person’s duty, it is certainly so necessary in these most miserable and ruined times that it seems never to have been equally so. For how few are there—not only among those powerful men, but even among private citizens—who allow themselves to be moved simply and plainly with a somewhat calm mind? Or who, again, is there who deigns at any time to **measure himself by his own foot** <note>original: "se ipse suo pede metiri." A Roman idiom (from Horace) meaning to judge oneself by one's own true measure or circumstances rather than by vanity.</note>, or to look upon that part of the **knapsack** <term>knapsack: A reference to the ancient fable (found in Aesop and the poet Persius) stating that Jupiter gave men two bags: one hanging in front for the faults of others, and one on the back for our own, which we never see.</term> which is on one's back, as the poet says?

Everything is corrupt and has collapsed into the very worst state; the ears and minds of all are obstructed and closed. As the proverb is commonly said: **The filth has defeated the washing** <note>original: "Vicit podex lotionem." A vulgar Roman proverb used when a situation is so corrupt or "messy" that no amount of cleaning or remedy can fix it.</note>. And so, you would find it much easier to find someone who allows himself to be petulantly torn apart by some buffoon or street-peddler, than one who can endure being seriously admonished about his own affairs by a prudent and grave man. For **truth** is considered foolish and hateful, and the more so, the more open and clear it is. Wherefore, even for that reason...

<sig>* 4</sig>
<meta>catchword: editio</meta>

<summary>The author laments the deep corruption of the current age, arguing that people are so resistant to honest correction that they prefer the insults of buffoons over the serious advice of the wise.</summary>

# PREFACE

->P R A E F A T I O<-

...this edition and work ought not to be considered entirely useless or poorly invested. But perhaps some will criticize this plan of ours, to whom some things in various places will seem somewhat harsh, and others treated with less modesty or reverence; and these same people will shout that those **Pasquinades** <note>original: "Pasquillos." These were satirical verses, often biting and anonymous, traditionally posted on the "Pasquino" statue in Rome.</note> differ very little from what others call **defamatory libels** <term>defamatory libels: Known in Latin as *libelli famosi*, these were anonymous writings intended to damage a person's reputation, an act that carried significant legal and social penalties in the Renaissance.</term>. 

To these people, although there are many things which might be answered quite fittingly, having set aside the rest, we wish first to testify to this: we have undertaken no part of this work for the sake of anyone's insult, nor were we driven by any private desire. Rather, because we had decided to present the writings of others to the public, we thought it dishonest and unworthy to publish them **truncated or mutilated** <note>The publisher is arguing for editorial integrity, claiming it is better to provide the full text than to censor or "mutilate" the original verses.</note>. 

Therefore, let the credibility of the sayings rest with the **authors** <note>original: "autores." The publisher is distancing himself from the content, placing the moral responsibility on the original anonymous writers.</note> everywhere; however, the nature of the subject matter itself ought to be judged such that we reflect that nothing can ever be established for the sake of **warning** <note>original: "monendi." This refers to the tradition of "corrective" satire, meant to warn the reader against vice.</note> so gently or calmly that it does not somewhere offend the ears of others and leave behind certain **barbs** <note>original: "aculeos." Literally "stings" or "thorns," a common metaphor for the sharp "point" of a satirical joke.</note> after it. Although if anyone [views] the matter correctly...

<summary>The publisher defends the publication of the Pasquinades against charges of libel, arguing that editorial honesty requires printing the full text and that satire naturally "stings" those it intends to correct.</summary>
<keywords>Pasquinades, libel, censorship, editorial integrity, satire, Roman law, Pasquillus</keywords>

# PREFACE

->P R A E F A T I O<-

...if one wishes to consider the matter fairly, the blame for whatever is found here should by no means be assigned to those who merely recount what was said or done. Rather, the blame belongs above all to those who, when they speak or act wrongly, cannot bear to be known or heard about. Just as their own minds are besieged and shut off by vices, they also contend that the speech and tongues of others should be held captive. 

And what resentment is this—to listen patiently and with a calm mind to some **buffoon** or **jester** <term>buffoon and jester: The Latin terms *scurra* and *balatro* refer to professional entertainers or social parasites in classical comedy who used sharp wit to mock others. The publisher is asking why people tolerate insults from common jokers but not from satires.</term>, as you might appear to the public; yet to shrink so violently from the same thing said by **Pasquill** <note>original: "Pasquillo." Referring to the persona of the "speaking statue" in Rome, a famous outlet for anonymous political and religious satire.</note>, as if it were an intolerable insult? As if indeed a deed once done could be undone, or an evil could become less of an evil just because it is reported by one person rather than another. 

Indeed, I am of the opinion that it is best for everyone to live well and honorably. However, the next best thing is that if you have stumbled anywhere, you acknowledge the error and—as the writer says—bear your misfortune with a calm and patient spirit. For as far as the **powerful** <term>powerful: *potentiores*, referring here to those in high ecclesiastical or secular office who are the frequent targets of these satires.</term> are concerned, it is by no means possible for the actions of **nobles** <note>original: "nobiles." Here referring to those of high social rank or public fame.</note> to remain hidden or obscure...

<sig>* 5</sig>
<meta>catchword: by no- [original Latin "qua-", likely for "quaque"]</meta>

<summary>The publisher argues that the targets of satire should blame their own shameful actions rather than the satirists who report them, emphasizing that the deeds of the powerful cannot remain hidden.</summary>

# PREFACE

->P R A E F A T I O<-

...by any means they can. For, as that poet <note>original: "ut ille dixit." Referring to the Roman satirist Juvenal, Satire 8, 140–141.</note> said:
*Every vice of the soul carries with it a blame that is all the more visible, the higher the rank of the one who commits the sin.*
Furthermore, those same people—as **Cicero** <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BCE), the Roman statesman and philosopher whose writings on ethics and oratory were foundational for Renaissance humanists.</note> remarks elsewhere—whether they begin to act rightly or wrongly, excel so greatly in either direction that no one born to a lower station could ever match them. 

Therefore, honest **Reader** <term>Reader: *Lector*. A standard direct address in early modern prefaces to establish a relationship between the publisher and the audience.</term>, if there should happen to be anything in this **medley** <note>original: "farragine." Literally a "farrago" or mixed fodder for cattle; a term frequently used to describe a satirical collection of various short works.</note> of **Pasquils** <term>Pasquils: *Pasquillorum*. Anonymous satirical verses or lampoons, named after the "Pasquino" statue in Rome where such critiques were often posted.</term> or **Dialogues** <term>Dialogues: *Dialogismorum*. Short literary works written as conversations, often used to debate religious or political ideas.</term> (for so I choose to call them now) that seems spoken somewhat too sharply or with too much malice, you ought to excuse it for the sake of the subject matter, out of your own kindness, and interpret everything in the best possible light. As for us, we stand beyond blame; it was never our intention through this work and our labor to serve the insult of any person, nor to promote ourselves. 

->We wish for this to be<-
->duly attested by<-
->this prologue.<-

<summary>The publisher concludes the preface by arguing that the flaws of powerful figures are naturally more conspicuous and justifies the sharp tone of the satirical works as a necessary reflection of the subject matter. He asks the reader for a charitable reading and distances himself from any personal malice.</summary>

# PASQUILLUS CONCERNING HIM-
## self and his origin.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'V' featuring a floral and foliage design within a square frame.</image-desc>

So that the venerable youth <note>original: "pubes incana." This phrase is a paradox, literally "gray-haired youth," likely referring to young scholars who have grown wise or "gray" through their studies.</note> may know my true form,
And so that no empty tale may be told of my fate,
I myself shall sing (recounting all things from their first beginning)
Of my destiny and my fortunes, by what name I am called,
Why, turned into hard stone, I sought the steep
Seas, and why, raised again into the upper air,
I am praised, and honors are preserved for this unmoving stone,
And why poets eagerly bring their sublime poems to me.
->I am Lichas, once the most sorrowful<-
->servant of Hylas of Oechalia,<-
<note>In Roman mythology, Lichas was the servant of Hercules (Alcides) who brought him the poisoned shirt of Nessus. Oechalia was the city Hercules had recently conquered.</note>
A guide whose like never wandered the earth.
Unfortunate, desiring to deliver my commands swiftly,
While Alcides <note>A title for Hercules, derived from the name of his grandfather, Alcaeus.</note> wished to prepare sacred offerings
To Cenaean Jupiter <note>original: "Cænæo... Ioui." Referring to a temple of Jupiter on the promontory of Cenaeum in Euboea.</note>, I delivered the robe soaked
In the blood of Nessus <note>Nessus was a centaur; his blood, poisoned by the Hydra, was used by Hercules's wife Deianira in a mistaken attempt to regain her husband's love.</note>, which his wife sent. The unwitting Hero took it
And put it on: the power of the evil spread through the limbs
Of Hercules, and the poison sank deep into his bones.
When he could not tear away the lethal garment,
Burning with rage, he cried out these words to me with a troubled face:
"O crime! You, the most certain cause of my death,
You shall not escape unpunished for acting against my fate."

<summary>This page introduces the persona of Pasquillus through a mythological lens, identifying the Roman statue with Lichas, the servant of Hercules who unwittingly delivered the poisoned shirt that killed the hero.</summary>
<keywords>Pasquillus, Lichas, Hercules, mythology, Roman satire, origins, Nessus, Oechalia</keywords>

--- Page 28 ---
<meta>This page continues the mythological origin story of Pasquillus, identifying him as Lichas, the servant of Hercules. The previous page ended just as Hercules (Alcides) donned the poisoned robe sent by his wife. This page describes his transformation into a stone and his eventual "resurrection" in Rome as a site for poetry and satire.</meta>

"I myself burn, and now you shall die in the cold waves!" 
Without delay, as he spoke words of excuse, swift 
Alcides <note>A title for Hercules.</note> seized him and hurled him through the clear air. 
His body, suspended in the air, turned to stone, 
And bloodless with fear, it finally settled in the 
Euboean <note>original: "Euboicis." Referring to the sea around the Greek island of Euboea.</note> waves, preserving the likeness of its former shape. 
Alas, how often have I seen curved keels press upon my neck, 
And wretched sailors, driven by their wanderings, 
Dash against the rocks and pour out their frail lives. 
And so much did this reputation strike fear into all, 
That no one dared to brave the hidden places of Euboea 
With ships: until you, Neptune, with your great trident, 
Overturned the massive strength of the rigid rock. 
As soon as I felt myself uprooted, I strove 
Little by little to reach the land, and gliding from the middle of the sea, 
I was finally driven, fortunate, onto the dry sand. 
Now Rome holds me, and the crowd of scholars <note>original: "pædagogū" (pedagogues). This refers to the teachers and students who historically decorated the Pasquino statue on St. Mark's Day.</note>, 
Pitying my lot, renews my well-deserved honors every year.

### The same concerning himself.

If I am not as you are, my weight has a cause: 
Deucalion <note>In Greek myth, Deucalion and Pyrrha repopulated the earth by throwing stones that turned into people. The joke here is that Pasquillus was too heavy or stubborn to be transformed into a man.</note> could not roll this stone.

## Pasquillus.
<note>Pasquillus (or Pasquino) is a battered Hellenistic statue in Rome that became a "talking" monument where citizens posted anonymous satirical verses. For the feast of Saint Mark, the statue was often dressed in costume; in 1525, it was dressed as Fortune.</note>

I am a goddess, yet no goddess am I: now a man, now a woman I am called:
The wheel holds me, the stone holds me; yet no wheel, no stones hold me.
Unstable, yet stable: not firm, yet firm: to my friends 
I am dear, and not dear: I am a stone, and I am a goddess.
I am seen with a shining face, and worshiped as a deity:
But tomorrow, alas, I shall provide jokes for the boys without my clothing.
<note>original: "sine ueste iocos." This refers to the statue being stripped of its elaborate festival decorations and costumes once the holiday ended, returning to its weathered, "naked" marble state.</note>

## To Fortune.

You are too majestic <term>Augusta</term> <note>A title for an empress, here used as a pun on the Emperor's title "Augustus."</note>. Why was there no suitable little crack made for you, through which our member could be taken?
<note>This is a crude satirical couplet typical of Roman "pasquinades," mocking the physical weathered condition of the ancient statue while personified as a goddess.</note>

## Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor, Always August, addresses Fortune.
<note>Charles V (1500–1558) was the most powerful monarch in Europe. This poem presents an idealized, pious version of the Emperor responding to the idea of "Luck" or "Fortune" after his victory at the Battle of Pavia.</note>

Fortune shall not rule my flights,
Nor shall my own mind move the arms of men.
But He who, upon the starry axis,
Guides His chariots with eternal command,
He it is who tames fierce nations,
And casts down kings and lords to the depths.
Under whose name I, that Caesar, am called:
King of kings, and lord of the most severe.
<note>Charles V claims his authority comes from God's providence rather than the whims of Fortune. This reflects the "Imperial" ideology that the Emperor was God's vicegerent on earth.</note>

## Concerning the same.

When the virtue of Charles contends with the Fortune of the world,
So that the latter might take away, while the former might bestow empire:
Chance cries out, "I am conquered! O Gods above, look to yourselves!"
<note>This poem suggests that Charles V’s personal merit (virtue) is so great that it overcomes even the power of Fate (Fortune), scaring the gods themselves.</note>

So great a God is not contained by our world.
<note>original: "Non capitur nostro tantus ab orbe Deus." This line likely concludes a previous poem contrasting the divine with the earthly power of the Emperor.</note>

## On Pasquin.

The common saying of the crowd can now be spoken as truth:
Fortune protects the foolish. Behold, you can see it for yourself.
<note>This refers to the "luck of the fool," mocking the perceived incompetence of those currently in power or favor in Rome.</note>

## Pasquin when he represented
## Opportunity under Paul III.
## In the year 1535.
<note>Paul III (Alessandro Farnese) was Pope from 1534 to 1549. In 1535, for the annual feast of Saint Mark, the Pasquino statue was dressed as "Occasio" (Opportunity), typically depicted with a long forelock of hair but bald at the back, signifying that one must grab a moment as it approaches, for it cannot be caught once it has passed.</note>

Cease to wonder why my right hand holds a dagger,
For a form suitable to the times is given to me.
<note>While "Opportunity" usually carries a razor or shears, here she holds a dagger, reflecting the violent and precarious political climate of Rome in the 1530s.</note>

### A hidden interpretation 
### of Opportunity.
<note>The following poem is a "cabalistic" or numerical riddle based on the spelling of the Latin word for Opportunity: **O-C-C-A-S-I-O**.</note>

O is nothing; CC announces twice a hundred; A is nothing;
S is the fifth; I is one; and again O is nothing.
The beginning is nothing; twice a hundred is a great many; five
is not enough; one is enough; from there comes nothing.
And although these verses may seem obscure, they can—
if you look closely—speak clearly on each point.
<note>The poem breaks down the word OCCASIO: O (zero/nothing), C (100 in Roman numerals), C (100), A (nothing/zero), S (the 5th letter of the word), I (the numeral 1), O (nothing). It suggests that while there is much wealth (the 200), it starts and ends with "nothing" for the common people.</note>

### Another.

**O**mnes **C**æca **C**upiditas **A**uri **S**uffocat, **I**mplicat, **O**pprimit. <margin>(Smell this!</margin>
<note>This is an acrostic: the first letters of each word spell OCCASIO. Translation: "Blind Greed for Gold Suffocates, Entangles, and Oppresses Everyone." The marginal note "Smell this" is a sarcastic invitation to notice the "stench" of corruption.</note>
**O** Blind Cardinals, gain **W**isdom at last, **U**nderstand...
<note>original: "O Cæci Cardinales Aliquãdo Sapite, Intelligite." This is another acrostic (O-C-A-S-I) addressing the Church leadership. The transcription is cut off at the end of the line.</note>

Groan, weep together, mourn, O Saturnian land <term>Saturnia tellus</term>,
<note>A poetic name for Italy or the Roman territory, referencing the mythical Golden Age of the god Saturn.</note>
the malignant stars threaten you with destruction.
You shall be submerged in a deluge of water, and a sea of blood.

### Opportunity speaks to Caesar.
<note>Caesar refers to the Holy Roman Emperor, Charles V, who had a complex and often antagonistic relationship with the Papacy.</note>

### Pasquin, concerning a Jew baptized by Paul.
<note>This refers to the practice of providing financial or social incentives to Jewish people in Rome who converted to Christianity. "Paul" is Pope Paul III.</note>

*A portion of the riverbank and gold were given to you, the Jew,*
*So that you might be turned toward our faith here in the City.*
*But to me, a Christian, Rome gives nothing; the order of things is wandering,*

<note>The poet sarcastically asks if he should renounce his faith just so he can be "converted" and finally receive some of the Pope's money.</note>

### To Pasquin.

*Since, Pasquin, according to the times, you are accustomed every year*
*To take on a new form, a new title, and a new name.*
*The form of an assassin is fitting for you, but there is an error in the name:*
*For where the "alpha" is, you can put an "iota" in its place.*
<note>This is a clever linguistic joke. The statue was dressed as "Occasio" (Opportunity). By changing the letter 'a' (alpha) to 'i' (iota), the word becomes "Occisio," which means "Slaughter" or "Murder"—fitting for a statue holding a dagger.</note>

*The empire has fallen, as has the hope of Christ, and law, and piety:*

### Pasquin (when in the following year, 1536, he represented Religion, while Emperor Charles was in Rome after his African victory) to the Poets.
<note>In 1536, the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V visited Rome following his successful conquest of Tunis (the "African victory"). For the festivities, the Pasquino statue was dressed up in a costume representing "Religion."</note>

How well has Pasquin, the father of elegance,

the "venerable religion" of the great Christ?

<meta>This page continues the series of satirical "Pasquils"—anonymous poems posted on the Pasquino statue in Rome. ## Pasquin, when he was dressed as Perseus under Paul III. In the year 1539.

*I, who was once a deformed trunk of cheap marble,*
*do you wonder that I now have the face of Perseus?*
*Since Paul changes his mind ten times in an hour,*
*why am I not allowed to change my face just once?*
<note>original: "Qui deformis eram uili de marmore truncus..." The poet jokes that the Pope’s political vacillation is so frequent that the statue’s physical transformation into a costumed hero is modest by comparison.</note>

### To Paul.

*While you seek smoke, and while you desire fame from the great Caesar,*
*nothing remains among us, Paul, but hunger.*
<note>original: "fama... fames." A clever pun on the Latin words for "fame" and "hunger." The poet suggests that while the Pope chases diplomatic glory with Emperor Charles V (Caesar), the Roman people are left starving.</note>

### Pasquin.

*The Pope is the head of Medusa, and the crowd of Nephews is the hair:*
*Perseus, strike off the head, and the hair is destroyed.*
<note>original: "coma turba Nepotũ." This is a scathing attack on <term>Nepotism</term> (from the Italian 'nipote' for nephew/grandson). Pope Paul III was infamous for elevating his young grandsons to the cardinalate. Like Medusa's snake-hair, the poet argues the family's power depends entirely on the "head"—the Pope.</note>

### To Paul.

*Nothing has been done by you that is praiseworthy, except*
*when Camerino was made free through your wars.*
*If you perhaps turn this man into another Tyrant,*
*you yourself, Paul, will be the Tyrant of Tyrants.*
<note>original: "Camers." Refers to the city of Camerino. Paul III waged war to reclaim it for the Papal States, but the poet fears he is simply replacing one ruler with a worse one (specifically for his own son, Pier Luigi Farnese).</note>

### To the same.

*Cerberus had three throats, and with a triple mouth*
*he gave forth barks within black Tartarus.*
*And you have three or four mouths full of hunger,*
*which bark at no one, but rather devour everyone.*
<note>Cerberus was the three-headed hound of the underworld (Tartarus). The poet compares the Pope's greed to the monster's hunger, suggesting the Papacy swallows the wealth of the people.</note>

### To the same.

*If a prostitute cautiously plunders her greedy lovers,*

The prostitute, O Paul, pays her taxes to you. 
If a governor despoils the people, he too divides the spoils, 
and makes you a partner in his gain. 
Thus, any plundering pleases you at last, provided 
that no prey is taken without your consent.
<note>original: "Perſoluit meretrix Paule tributa tibi." This refers to the *tassa sulle meretrici*, a tax levied on prostitutes in Rome, which critics used to argue the Papacy was profiting from vice.</note>

### To the same.

To ensure they would sing, much coin was once given to the bards: 
To ensure I stay silent, how much will you give me, Paul?
<note>A classic satirical trope: the poet suggests his silence is more valuable (and more expensive) to the corrupt Pope than his praise would be.</note>

### To the same Paul.

I do not know if it is true, but since you have been active throughout the City, 
everyone says that salt is sold more dearly. 
O, well-considered! Nothing is more perfect than this one thing: 
you are already starting to rot, so it is only fair that you have a care for salt.
<note>original: "Iam fœtes, æquum est ſit tibi cura ſalis." This refers to the "Salt War" (1540), triggered when Paul III doubled the price of salt. The poet cruelly jokes that the Pope needs the salt to preserve his own "stinking" or morally decaying body.</note>

### To the Duchess of Florence, betrothed to Octavius, the grandson of Paul, a boy of 15 years.

O you, who are so poorly joined to a husband far too young, 
what do you do in your lonely bed in the silent night? 
As I myself believe, you grieve that your harvest is still in the blade, 
and a small penis tortures your mind.
<note>original: "meſſis in herba" (harvest in the blade/grain). This refers to Margaret of Austria, daughter of Charles V and widow of Alessandro de' Medici, who was married to the 14-year-old <term>Octavius Farnese</term> (Ottavio) to cement a political alliance. The poet mocks the age gap and the likely lack of consummation.</note>

### To Pasquin as Perseus.

To have lopped off the Gorgon's head is a small glory for you: 
to lop the tail off the priests, that would be a greater glory.
<note>original: "Preſbyteris caudam." A crude suggestion that the statue of Perseus, instead of fighting mythical monsters, should castrate the Roman clergy to curb their perceived lust and corruption.</note>

### Pasquin to Paul.

Why is there such hunger, why such a great scarcity of things...

Of the ox, the acorn, and the hair, do you see any

### Various epigrams of Pasquin follow, in no particular order.

## Pasquin to Rome.

Rome, once you had servants who were the Lords of Lords; 
now, the servants of servants are your Lords.
<note>A biting play on the Pope’s official title, *Servus servorum Dei* ("Servant of the servants of God"). The poet suggests that those who claim to be the lowest servants are actually acting as Rome's most oppressive masters.</note>

## Another.

Once, Rome, the Lords of Lords were subject to you; 
now, miserable one, you are subject to the servants of servants. 
You once heard the oracles of the divine Paul, 
but now you carry out the unspeakable commands of the wicked.
<note>The poet uses a Greek pun here. He contrasts the "divine Paul" (the Apostle) with "the wicked" (in Greek: *tōn phaulōn*), which sounds nearly identical to the name of the Pope, Paul (*Paulos*).</note>

## Pasquin on Caesar, when he had come to Rome from the African victory.

From Libya the victor has come into the Roman citadels, 
Caesar, and he went golden upon snowy horses. 
He triumphed, but you, Paul, triumph more:
<note>This refers to Emperor Charles V ("Caesar"), who visited Rome in 1536 after his successful campaign in Tunis (Libya). While the Emperor had a military triumph, the poet implies the Pope's "triumph" is one of greed or political manipulation.</note>

The body does not lie here, nor did the spirit seek the stars;

A favorable day dawned for those in Heaven

# Pasquin on Pope Alexander VI.

<meta>This page continues the "Pasquinades"—satirical verses named after the Roman "talking statue" Pasquin—which were used to mock the corruption of the Roman elite. ## Epitaph for Leo.
<note>Leo X (Giovanni de' Medici, reigned 1513–1521). He was famous for his patronage of the arts but also for exhausting the papal treasury.</note>

Overwhelmed in this tomb, along with his body, is the reputation of Leo,
  Who fed his sheep poorly; now he feeds the earth well.
<note>original: "Qui male pauit oues, nūc bene paſcit humū." This is a biting pun. As Pope, he was the "shepherd" of the Church who failed his "sheep," but as a corpse, he finally performs a "service" by fertilizing the soil.</note>

## Pasquin on the Emperor and Suleiman.
<note>Refers to the rivalry between the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V and the Ottoman Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent. The poem mocks their 1532 encounter near the Danube where both armies avoided a direct battle.</note>

The Commanders, Suleiman and the young Charles,
  One from the East, the other from the West,
Having devised a battle worthy of the <term>Theban riddle</term>,
  Deployed their battle lines on the banks of the <term>Ister</term>.
<note>Theban riddle: A reference to the Sphinx's riddle or the tragic, self-destructive wars of Thebes. Ister: The ancient Latin name for the Danube River.</note>
They never clashed, nor did they bear hostile standards;
  Neither was even within sight of the other.
Each conquered the other, yet neither was a victor in arms:
  For each provided for himself with a shameful flight.
Close <term>Helicon</term> now, O Goddesses, and let the Poets be silent:
  The Leaders themselves disgrace the weapons of <term>Pallas</term>.
<note>Helicon: The mountain of the Muses; the poet suggests art should cease because reality has become so shameful. Pallas: Athena, goddess of wise warfare; the poet argues these kings are not worthy of her protection.</note>

## Pasquin to Paul III.
<note>Pope Paul III (reigned 1534–1549). He was notable for being the first Pope in many years to wear a full beard, which he grew as a sign of mourning after the Sack of Rome.</note>

Why, Paul, does your divine face turn into a goat with those hairs?
  Woe is me, that sight does not hold a good omen.
When kings and fathers ruled the world clean-shaven...
<note>original: "capriſſat" (acts like a goat). The poet mocks the Pope's beard, suggesting that the change from the traditional clean-shaven look of the clergy signifies a decline in Roman authority.</note>

### To Pasquino, Transformed into Perseus.

<note>Pasquino is one of the "talking statues" of Rome where citizens posted anonymous satirical poems (pasquinades). Here, the statue is imagined as the hero Perseus.</note>

Oh, how well you appear, Pasquino, changed in form.
Oh, how timely it is that you have become Perseus.
See Rome full of impious Medusas, of Gorgons—
Gorgons who turn living souls into stone.
Holy peace is turned to stone; the holy council is stone; <note>A reference to the long-delayed Council of Trent, which was intended to reform the Church but faced constant political obstruction.</note>
Stone is the great undertaking that should have been done.
All the virtues that dwell in such a poisonous country
Turn into hard stone if they look upon it.

Their children have been made stone alongside their grieving mothers.
Therefore, raise the fierce heads, Perseus, while from above
The avenging sword and the strong hand are given to you.
Cut them off, for the world can no longer endure them,
And let the ugly Tiber run with their blood.
Free Rome first, before it becomes stone or marble;
Preserve for Christ what remains healthy among us.
Ah, what a difficult time; if you delay even a moment,
It may be that only a sea-god can ever defend us.

## To Pasquino.

Three or four miracles—saving the truth—
The Lutheran sect writes to Pasquino, <note>The "Lutheran sect" here is used as a rhetorical device; the poet attributes these criticisms to the Protestants to highlight the failings of the Catholic Church from an outside perspective.</note>
Which neither Christ nor Saint Peter can perform,
Nor can any son of a whore:
To diminish the Pope’s stinginess by a single zero, <note>original: "miseria." In this context, it refers to the Pope's legendary greed or miserly nature.</note>
To make the Lady Duchess a Christian, <note>Likely referring to Margaret of Austria, Duchess of Florence and later Parma, daughter of Emperor Charles V. Her political influence was often viewed with suspicion in Rome.</note>
To free Farnese from his "matter," <note>This refers to Cardinal Alessandro Farnese the Younger. "Matter" (*materia*) could be a pun on physical illness (phlegm/humors) or his preoccupation with worldly, material wealth over spiritual duties.</note>
And to make "Saint" Fiore speak, who is mute. <note>Guido Ascanio Sforza di Santa Fiora, a cardinal and grandson of Pope Paul III. He was often mocked for being young, silent, or intellectually vacuous in church matters.</note>

## Reply

That the Pope is a miser, I do not well agree,
For he seems quite generous to me—in his extortions! <term>angariare: To oppress, harass, or extort through heavy taxes or forced labor.</term>
That the Duchess is not a Christian? You are wrong;
Rather, she is so holy that she has herself worshipped.
You say Farnese is a fool; I find him shrewd,
Since he acquires so much with so little effort.
You say Santa Fiore is mute? God forbid!
At night, he talks plenty with the little Turkish girl. <note>A scandalous jab suggesting the Cardinal's "silence" in public covers for a private life of debauchery, specifically involving a "turchetta" (a common derogatory term for a dark-complexioned or foreign concubine).</note>

# Pasquino to Caesar returning from the African victory. <note>“Caesar” refers to the Holy Roman Emperor, Charles V. This poem commemorates his 1535 victory in Tunis against the Ottoman-backed corsair Barbarossa.</note>

*When the Senate proclaims your victorious standards,*
*And all the people, subject to the Latin Pontiff,*
*And so many triumphal arches, and the silent prophets* <note>“Silent prophets” likely refers to the statues or architectural allegories decorating the temporary triumphal arches built for Charles V’s entry into Italian cities.</note>

*Let these titles, which your Rome has prepared for you,*
*Truly be for the love of holy religion.*
*Do you wish to be considered a champion of the sincere faith,*
*While you cherish Turks and Barbary leaders?* <note>Pasquino mocks Charles V for his alliance with the deposed Sultan of Tunis, Muley Hassan, suggesting it is hypocritical for a Christian Emperor to lead "infidel" allies.</note>
*Look, the envoy of Muley Hassan* <note>original: "Muliaffæ". Muley Hassan was the Hafsid ruler Charles V restored to the throne in Tunis as a tributary vassal.</note> *adores you with gifts,*

*And he leads twin camels from the Libyan region,*
*Which they say have excelled in swift running.*
*He himself leads dogs, that impious dog: everything, Caesar,* <note>original: "canis impius". A common derogatory pun; Pasquino calls the Muslim ruler a dog while noting he brings actual hunting dogs as a gift.</note>
*Believe me, these rewards are signs of flight.* <note>Pasquino suggests the gifts—all animals known for speed—are not symbols of victory, but tools for a cowardly escape.</note>

## A response on behalf of Caesar to Pasquino.

*The King of Libya sends you due gifts, Caesar,*
*Signs foretelling the outcome of your war.*
*Falcones, and Libyan horses, and swift camels,*
*And dogs which are accustomed to outrun chariots.*
*Surely, so that you might more swiftly and strongly follow*
*The French—who are accustomed to trust in shameful flight.* <note>original: "Gallos". The response cleverly flips Pasquino’s insult. It claims the fast animals aren't for Charles V to flee, but for him to hunt down the French King Francis I, Charles's perennial rival who was often accused of retreating from the Emperor's forces.</note>

## Marforio to Pasquino. <note>Marforio and Pasquino are two of the famous "talking statues" of Rome. It was a common literary device to write satires as dialogues between these statues.</note>

If the Romans of old used to perform sacred rites to the heavenly dwellers,
So that bright peace might be made for all peoples,
Why now is incense not given to the blessed Pope, <note>Refers to Pope Paul III.</note>
Since under this leader, quiet has been restored to the whole world?
*Pas.* They do this late, because when he returns to the stars,
They will consecrate the divinity of Paul with sacred incense.
->Glory after the ashes.<- <note>original: "Gloria post cineres." A cynical suggestion that the Pope will only be honored once he is dead and gone.</note>

## Pasquino on Clement. <note>Refers to Pope Clement VII, who reigned from 1523 to 1534. His reign was viewed by many as a disaster, notably including the 1527 Sack of Rome.</note>

When the eldest of the Fates <note>The Parcae, the three goddesses who spin and cut the thread of life.</note> already wished
To break the life-threads of the long-lived Pope Clement:
A most bitter dispute suddenly arose among the Gods,
Started by Pluto <note>The Roman god of the underworld.</note> and Peter the key-bearer.
For when they saw his final destiny was pressing upon him,
Heaven did not want him, nor did the abyss.
Peter says, "I do not want this man, who is girded with sword and arms;
Impious and swollen with pride, he stirs up nothing but wars,
And he who strives to incite great Kings to battle,
Sows the frequent seeds of horrific Mars <note>The god of war; used here to mean warfare itself.</note>.
The commands of the highest Thunderer <note>A poetic title for God, borrowing from the Roman "Jupiter Tonans."</note> did not show these things.
This rule was not written for a Pope.
And although he boasts that he himself is my grandson, <note>A satirical jab at "nepotism." Popes often referred to their illegitimate children or favored relatives as "nephews" or "grandsons."</note>
Nevertheless, he has not earned his place in the choir of the heavenly ones."
Then Pluto: "Shall I allow this man to descend to our spirits of the dead?
Shall I even suffer this man to take over my kingdoms?"

P. Give me at least this before my death. M. You talk nonsense. P. Grant this one thing to one who begs. M. You are mad. P. This. M. Die sooner. P. This. M. I yield. P. Curtius killed Clement. Curtius should be rewarded with gold, for through him public safety has been secured.

Your committed sins were to be wiped away by your weeping,

## A Pasquil on the coat of arms
## of Cardinal Cesarini.

The Empire possesses the Eagle, the High Column holds its lords,

## On Clement.

After many were slain by the sword, and even more by poison,

## Pasquillus to the Guest
### by J. F. F. In the year 1537.

*Why do you laugh, impudent guest, at the face of old Pasquillus, as if these things were just now seen by you for the first time?*

<note>Pasquillus (or Pasquino) is a battered ancient statue near Piazza Navona in Rome. Since the early 16th century, it served as a "talking statue" where citizens posted anonymous satirical poems. Here, the poet personifies the broken marble fragment, explaining that its physical disfigurement is a symbol of how Rome treats those who speak the truth about corruption.</note>

# Dialogue between the Guest and Pasquillus, by Johann Fichard of Frankfurt <note>Johann Fichard (1512–1581) was a German jurist and humanist. This dialogue uses Pasquillus—the famous "talking statue" of Rome—to satirize the city's corruption.</note>

## The Guest.

While I wander as a stranger in foreign lands far from my fatherland,
And it is my great desire to see many things;
While I busy myself in learning the excellent harbors of the sea,
And seeing each of the famous bays in person;
While everywhere I seek out the ancient ruins of the City <note>original: "Vrbi" (the City). In this context, it always refers to Rome.</note>,
Yet you especially, and your friend Marforio <note>Marforio is another of the "talking statues" of Rome; traditionally, Pasquillus and Marforio would "speak" to each other via placards posted by citizens.</note>;
And from there I survey Parthenope <note>The ancient Greek name for Naples.</note>, the parent of poets,
And whatever noble sights the Campanian fields hold:
The hot springs of Baiae, the remains of ancient Cumae,
And those wondrous caves that lie in those mountains;
Then to where the abyss of black Avernus <note>A lake near Naples which the ancients believed was the entrance to the Underworld.</note> reveals itself nearby,
A place which holds that name even to this day;
Behold, at last I return here a wretch (of which I am ashamed),
With my pockets drained three and four times over.
Now, Father Pasquillus, because you were also a great 
Cause for why I am now so weighed down by these misfortunes;
And because you so readily give counsel now to these, now to those,
And no one in the whole City is now wiser than you:
Come, tell me, tell me some way I might sustain myself,
And how my wealth, once lost, might be restored.
Tell me by what pursuits I might be held dear here,
And how to win over the highest-ranking men.

So may your old age be perpetually light and joyful,

### Pasquillus.

<margin>For he stands in the open sun.</margin>
My friend Guest, is there truly no one known to you in the City who could have looked after your interests, that you are forced to be the first to disturb my peace—I, who for a long time now have certainly been loath to utter words? 

Wretch that I am, I have this misfortune besides all others: that everyone turns every single thing I say into a joke. Indeed, I seem like a senile old man because of my many years; that is the gratitude, of course, that returns for my services. 

So it is a wonder that you finally come as the first person who wishes to grow wise by my advice. However, lest I perhaps seem unlike my usual self now, take these few words of mine: 

First of all, what great madness <note>original: "uecordia" (senselessness or insanity).</note> vexes your mind? Do you expect to recover your lost wealth here? Do you really mean to grow rich in Rome as a stranger? And do you think that what you lost will be added back to your purses from this place? 

It is the lot of a guest to bring full purses to Rome; it is the lot of a guest to bring back empty pockets from there. It is the lot of a guest to go to Rome on noble horses; it is the lot of a guest to return soon after on bare feet. Rome takes everything, it snatches everything; even in the ancient times of old, it was never the custom to return much. 

Yet, you will say, we see many people here and there...

<meta>This page concludes the direct address to the "Etruscan" critic (an Italian skeptic or perhaps a follower of a different theological path) by the German humanist Joachim Camerarius. Every religious rite of all lands pleases everywhere.
"Indeed," you say, "the just and good man pleases God everywhere,

That whoever would approve of every religion and faith,
and who would say all rites are good,
This man for the most part lacks all faith and religion;
To him for whom everything is sacred, nothing is sacred.
Therefore, choose which religion is true, lest anyone
think that you believe nothing of the truth in this matter.
For since it is necessary that the truth be no more than one,
if anyone approves many things, then he approves nothing.

## To the Reader.

The various Epigrams <term>Epigrammata; short, witty poems often ending in a sharp point or sting</term> that follow we have collected from diverse writings, both Pasquillic <note>original: "Pasquillicis," referring to "Pasquino," a famous "talking statue" in Rome where people posted anonymous satirical poems or "pasquinades" attacking the papacy</note> and others by learned men, so that for you, a student of truth, whoever you are, Reader, the testimonies of so many good and erudite men might confirm your spirit more and more. Therefore, may it not weary you to read them through, since they are indeed most worthy of reading.

O Peter, a woman once dared to sit in your chair,

Having been impregnated <note>original: "compressa"</note>, she might have remained hidden for many years,

### On Paul II, Supreme Pontiff, by Janus Pannonius <note>Janus Pannonius (1434–1472) was a renowned Hungarian humanist and bishop, known for his biting satirical epigrams against the Roman curia.</note>

Since you have a daughter, Paul, and you possess

# On the Pope.

Who is that swollen man, bubbling <note>original: "bullat." The author plays on the word "bulla," which means a bubble, but also the lead seal on an official papal document (a "Papal Bull").</note> upon a high throne?
He is a God—and yet he would be nothing, if he were not a bubble.
What does he usually provide? He sells "bubbled" bulls. <note>original: "bullatas uendere bullas." He is selling sealed documents that are as empty and fleeting as bubbles.</note>
What good are these bulls? Only to make a man "bubbly" <note>term: "bulleus" (bubbly/empty). The implication is that the person who buys these documents becomes empty-headed or is being swindled.</note>.
What disease does he cure? The dropsy of a bubbling purse:
In this one disease, he surpasses even Hippocrates. <note>Hippocrates was the ancient Greek "Father of Medicine." The poem suggests the Pope is a master at "curing" people of their money (the "swelling" of their wallets).</note>
Is he so "bubbly"? Indeed, those whom he feeds and nourishes,
they all immediately turn into a "bubbly" crowd.

## On the Drunken Priest, by Johannes Stigelius <note>Johannes Stigelius (1515–1562) was a German humanist poet and professor at Jena, known for his witty Latin verse.</note>

### On Rome, by Conrad Celtis <note>Conrad Celtis (1459–1508) was a leading German humanist poet who often expressed early nationalist frustrations regarding the influence and greed of the Roman Church.</note>

O, what a face Rome shows, and what a transformation:
She once sold bodies <note>A reference to the slave trade of Ancient Rome.</note>, but now she sells souls.
Whatever wealth Germany held in her furthest lands,
And whatever she contains in her central regions,
Has been exhausted; it has all migrated into the Latin citadels,
So that impious Rome may satisfy your luxuries.
While those coins ought to be granted to the soldiers,
To make the homes in our part of the world safe,
The Roman "soldier" <note>A satirical reference to the Pope’s agents or the clergy.</note> now takes them for his own use,

Sixtus, you lie here at last; Rome rejoices—she who

Sixtus, you lie here at last, the discord of our age:

To the common crime, the Scot <note>original: *Scotus*. This likely refers to a specific military ally or mercenary leader of the time, or perhaps a reference to the theologian Duns Scotus used metaphorically to represent scholastic justification for war.</note> brought his weapons.

### On the same subject.
<margin>Delitiæ Poetarum Italorum III. 490</margin> <note>This margin note refers to a later 1608 anthology where these poems were preserved for scholars.</note>

"Give me the beard of Paul, the sword of Paul, everything of Paul!
That key-bearer Peter <note>St. Peter is traditionally depicted with the Keys to the Kingdom of Heaven, symbolizing spiritual authority.</note> is nothing to my desires."
As soon as he [Julius II] uttered this, we believed he intended

One whom it is fitting to kill with the sword, should not be killed with the sword of Paul;
rather, it is enough to be armed with the keys of Peter.

## On the Character of Julius.

*After Julius had taken up the keys of Peter and had*
*Begun to lead the flock,*
*Immediately a fierce wolf invaded the sheep, and a terrible*
*Destruction ensued.*
*That man, distrusting the keys given to Peter, left*
*The sheep he drove defenseless.*
*Without delay, oh Paul, he rushed toward your sword to protect himself,* <note>In Christian iconography, St. Peter carries keys representing spiritual authority ("the keys to the kingdom of heaven"), while St. Paul carries a sword, the instrument of his martyrdom. *But look! When the wolf sees him coming against his camp*

*He forced the leader—unskilled with the sword—to abandon*

*Peter, having been scorned, takes back his gift of the keys;*
*There will be another to carry them.*
*But Paul, unaware, lest anyone should misuse his weapons,*
*Also deprives the man of his sword.*
*What sheep will he lead now, and into what pastures, crippled*
*Without both the keys and the sword?*

### An allusion regarding the same man.

*Julius is in Rome; who is missing? O gods, grant us a Brutus.* <note>The poet refers to Marcus Junius Brutus, the most famous assassin of Julius Caesar. The implication is that Pope Julius II is a tyrant who, like Caesar, deserves a "Brutus" to stop him.</note>

### On the Indulgences of Julius. <note>Indulgences were payments made to the Church in exchange for the remission of temporal punishment for sins. During the reign of Julius II, these funds were often used to finance military campaigns and the rebuilding of St. Peter's Basilica.</note>

*The merchant Julius captures the whole world through fraud,*
*For he sells the heavens, yet he does not possess them himself.*
*Sell me what you have! For where is your shame, that you sell me*
*That which you yourself, Julius, are seen to lack?*
*Why does the wild earth not send forth the hundred-handed Giants,* <note>In Greek mythology, the Hecatoncheires (hundred-handed giants) fought against the gods. The poet suggests that if Julius can "sell" heaven, he must have overthrown God as the Giants attempted to do.</note>

*For as long as another rules the heavens and thunders from there,*
*I will not be a buyer of such a great gift.*

### To Julius, by V. H. <note>likely Ulrich von Hutten (1488–1523), a German knight, humanist, and fierce critic of the Roman Catholic Church.</note>

*Tell me, holy father, gatekeeper of the heavenly court,*
*You who bear the crown of the highest religion.*
*You who rule kings, and who place and replace tyrants,*
*Who loosen and bind all things with your nod.* <note>This refers to the "Power of the Keys" (Matthew 16:19), the spiritual authority the Pope claims to bind or loose sins on earth and in heaven.</note>
*You who make saints, and who happened to be blessed*
*Before death, and who blesses us before our death.*
*What need have you of cannons,* <note>original: "bombardis" - early heavy artillery. The poet contrasts the Pope's spiritual claims with his reliance on modern, destructive technology.</note> *or of horses and men,*
*Or of the armed hand that precedes and follows you,*
*And that crop of spears and bristling weapons?*
*What need have you for this belt and for your swords?*
*Why do you drag all these things along? Or why, most holy one, do you*
*Conquer towns, fortresses, and homes with such great military labor?*

Could you not, with a raised hand and a trembling mouth, 
  Suddenly give these things to the spirits of the dead, and these to the Gods? <note>original: "Dijs Manibus." In Roman religion, the Manes were the spirits of deceased loved ones; here, the poet uses classical terminology to ask why the Pope deals in death rather than life.</note>
Surely all Popes who are like Peter, or those of 
  Proven character, are capable of all these spiritual things.
What shall I say? Is it because you are wicked, and distrusting the spiritual arms 
  Of the Popes, you rush headlong into the arms of Mars? <note>original: "Martis." Mars was the Roman god of war. The poet contrasts the "weapons" of the papacy (excommunication/prayer) with the physical warfare favored by Julius II.</note>
O, how the world is mistaken about you! For while you do these things, 
  It does not see how far you have strayed from the path of Peter.

## On the Roman State, by the same Ulrich.
## Epigrams of Hutten to Crotus Rubianus, <note>Crotus Rubianus (c. 1480–1545) was a German humanist and a close friend of Hutten; they were both key figures in the production of the "Letters of Obscure Men."</note>
## sent from the City. <note>original: "ex Vrbe." In this period, "The City" (Urbs) always referred to Rome.</note>

We have seen the half-ruined walls of Ausonian Rome, <note>original: "Ausoniae." A poetic name for Italy.</note>
  Here, where God himself is sold along with sacred things.
We have seen the mighty Pope, Crotus, and the sacred Senate, 
  And the high-ranking Cardinals in a long procession.
So many scribes, and a crowd of men useless for any honest work, 
  Whom wandering purple robes clothe while their horses are draped.
So many, Crotus, who do these things, and so many who endure them; 
  Those who live in orgies, while they pretend to be men of ancient virtue. <note>original: "Curios." Refers to Manius Curius Dentatus, an ancient Roman hero famous for his austerity and incorruptibility. Hutten is calling the Roman clergy hypocrites who act like stoics but live in excess.</note>
Again, there are those who neither pretend to be good, nor live well, 
  Who laugh at and hiss at good morals.
Those whom it pleases to be wicked, and for whom it is permitted; to whose yoke 
  The German land has consented in wretched ways. <note>original: "Teutona terra." This reflects the growing "Gravamina" or grievances of the German nation regarding Roman financial exploitation and legal interference.</note>
Those who give and those who forbid, who reopen those whom they have shut out, 
  And distribute the heavens according to their own whim.

Cease wanting to visit "sacred" Rome above all else, Crotus;
You will find nothing Roman here, where Rome once was.

### On the Same Subject.

Rome sells God, sells sacred things, sells honors;
And Rome herself—as strange as it is to say—is for sale.
To such an extent there is nothing there that gold does not purchase,
Evidently so that Rome may become "Golden" once again. <note>A satirical play on words. While the "Golden Age" of mythology was a period of peace and virtue, Hutten suggests Rome is now "Golden" only because it is filled with bribes and literal gold.</note>

---

### On the Romans, as they are now.

The fathers speak holy words, but perform the worst deeds at Rome;
Some even speak poorly, and do no better.
Yet religion and Christ are boasted of by them,
While the image of the cross is held aloft and prostituted everywhere.
And the patrimony of Peter the fisherman grows fat, <note>original: "patrimonia Petri." The "Patrimony of St. Peter" refers to the land and wealth held by the Papacy.</note>
While the lightning bolts of the Great Pontiff are brandished. <note>The "lightning bolts" are a classical metaphor for the Pope's power of excommunication and spiritual censure, comparing him to a thundering Jupiter.</note>
The finest purple clothes them from head to toe, with a long train
Following behind; you might say they live simply.
But unless I am mistaken—and things are never entirely deceptive—
That image of sheep clothes remarkable wolves. <note>An allusion to the "wolves in sheep's clothing" from the Gospel of Matthew (7:15).</note>

### Everything at Rome is redeemed by money.

Go now, men, join hands, and live by plunder;
Kill, snatch from the sanctuary, and commit every wickedness.

Go forth, mix the profane with the sacred, grow accustomed to luxury;
  Go, you men, through every kind of pleasure.
Speak, and do all the worst things by your very word;
  Naturally, believe also that there are no Gods.
We have seen these things happen at Rome—and what is holier than she?
  And yet, the way to the heavens is no less open.
Let everyone bring gold to Rome, for there virtue is found in abundance.
  In short, he is a fool at Rome who does not know how to buy good things.
Moreover, so that you may act, you buy shameful things with gold at Rome.
  Since these things are so, I say what I said before: be wicked.

### On the Roman State.

Peter has left the Aventine heights, the Tarpeian rocks,
  And all the rest in the conquered City. <note>original: "Vrbe." Hutten refers to Rome as a "conquered" city, suggesting it has been taken over by vice rather than foreign enemies.</note>
And in place of Peter, that man Simon <term>Simon Magus: A biblical figure who tried to buy the power of the Holy Spirit (Acts 8); his name is the root of "simony," the sin of selling church offices.</term> enters, and reigns through the altars;
  And Simon reigns in the conquered city.
I know not to what place that captive ship—the Church—has
  Fled; nothing of the sort is to be seen at Rome.
Simon sells sacred things, and sells profane things just the same;
  And as Christ may love me, he sells everything.
It is not safe to buy those things, however, even if you buy with gold;
  A heavy <term>bulla: A lead seal used for papal documents. Hutten plays on the double meaning of "bulla" as both a weighty official document and a hollow, empty bubble.</term> is returned from the leaden lineage.
O the bulls, and O Rome, and King Simon!
  Is it lawful to buy sacred things, and to sell sacred things at Rome?

What limit is there, O citizens? To what end does this patience finally...

## On the Same State of Rome
## to the same people.

Is anyone’s mind more blind, or more in need of light,
  Than the man who believes that heaven is bought for him at Rome?
Or who thinks any man is blessed according to his gold?
  When, in that place, a "blessed life" is bought with gold.
Who would scorn the Stygian waters <note>The River Styx in the underworld; here meaning Hell.</note>, or fail to fear
  Grim punishment, because he trusts that heavenly things are bought at Rome?
Or would not Peter himself burn with the greatest anger,
  That there is someone—himself wicked—who "rents out" heaven?
Therefore, citizens, flee from this sin and seek what is right;
  By this commerce alone <note>meaning virtue/righteousness</note> will you be permitted to buy heaven.

## On a certain dead Bishop
## to the Germans.

The bishop has died; seek new <term>pallia: A circular band of white wool (a pallium) granted by the Pope to archbishops as a symbol of their authority. Hutten critiques the massive fees Germany paid to Rome every time a new bishop was appointed.</term>, citizens,

But you, Simon, as long as Germany has no brain
  And no eyes, continue to sell your pallia.

## A Satire on the Times of Julius. <note>Refers to Pope Julius II (reigned 1503–1513), known as the "Warrior Pope."</note>

In clouds, and changed by a pitiable stupor,

### Pasquil on Leo X. <note>A "Pasquillus" or Pasquinade was a form of anonymous satirical poetry, often posted on the "Pasquino" statue in Rome to criticize the authorities.</note>

Just as the shepherd Proteus <note>A shape-shifting sea god from Greek mythology, used here to represent the Pope's perceived fickleness and deceit.</note> is known by his shifting face,
And often wanders doubtfully through the flowing waters:
So, Leo, there is no faith in you, nor constancy in your affairs,
And your deeds are hateful in comparison to your promises.
Neither good nor bad things should be believed from the doubtful Leo;
Even when he speaks the truth, faith can scarcely be applied.
When imprudent nature made a belly for the greedy lion <note>A pun on the Pope's name, "Leo," which means "lion" in Latin.</note>,

will gape open, unable to bear such a great weight.
How much Julius himself differs from Leo the Tenth,
Rome is able to learn from the names of both. <note>Julius II was the "warrior Pope" (Caesar), while Leo X was the "beast" (Lion) of excess.</note>

## On a picture of Europe being subdued by Monks, by E.R. <note>Likely Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam, though many such satires were attributed to him to lend them authority.</note>

## Rome for sale, by Pictorius. <note>original: "Pictorij" — referring to Ludovico Pittorio (1454–1525), a Ferrarese poet and scholar.</note>

Until now, the city of the great Quirinus <note>original: "Quirini" — an ancient name for Romulus, the legendary founder of Rome; the name evokes Rome's ancient dignity.</note> was unable to find a buyer, so great was the sum of its price. Now, however, it is offered so cheaply that the mere sound of a voice <note>original: "sonus ipse" — perhaps implying that Rome is sold for empty promises or that its reputation has vanished.</note> buys it, let alone such a small amount of brass coin.

## Rome’s luxury, by L. Bigi. <note>original: "L. Bigi" — Ludovico Bigi Pittorio, who often wrote on the moral failings of his time.</note>

Where have we come, O gods above? How far has the power of Dione <note>original: "Diones" — a name for Venus, here used to represent lust and carnal desire.</note> progressed? Where has gluttony gone, where has luxury, where has every kind of evil gone? ### To the Reader.

It has pleased me to add here the **Complaint of Faith**, written by some pious and spiritual Parish Priest, as it seems, from before this our current age. It was recently discovered in Germany. I include it so that you may see, excellent Reader, that even before our time there were always some pious and holy men in the Church. Although they did not dare to publicly profess their spirit and convictions, they did so in their own private corners—for at that time the Church had been driven into the wilderness by the Dragon. <note>The "Dragon" is a biblical reference to Revelation 12, frequently used by Reformers to identify the Papacy as a satanic force that had forced the "true" believers into hiding for centuries.</note>

The clergy and all the people...

## Concerning the Prelates <note>A prelate is a high-ranking member of the clergy, such as a bishop or abbot.</note>.

The Prelates of the Churches

And exclude the poor.
To those who give back, it is given;
For the needy, no care is taken.

Alas, what are they if not swindlers? <note>original: *truffatores*; a term for tricksters or those who use deceits to profit.</note>
Whether they buy, or whether they sell,
They always intend to deceive:
They swear false oaths by God and the saints,
And care very little about lying.
When good coins pass through their hands,
They immediately consign them to the fire. <note>This refers to the illegal practice of debasing currency—melting down pure silver coins to mix them with cheaper metals, or "clipping" the edges to steal the precious metal.</note>
And so the payment remains
As dross, and not silver. <term>dross|Latin: *scoria*; the scum or impurities left on the surface of melting metal.</term>
Thus they throw the whole world into confusion;
This is known everywhere.
Weight, number, and measure,
Along with all commerce,
Are so corrupted by them,
That scarcely one man acts rightly.
Unless God provides assistance,
The world is left to perish.
So great and so many are the crimes,

## A Dialogue between the Church and Simony, recently in Swit-
## zerland from a very ancient manuscript
## transcribed.

*Church: Why do you rage, Simony, you who corrupts all law?* <note>original: *adultera iuris*; Simony is personified here as an "adulteress" or one who violates the purity of the law.</note>
*Why do you disturb my affairs, wicked woman, through greedy crowds?*
*You set up a marketplace everywhere; a crowd of evil men follows you.*
*You take away what is mine; you soften iron hearts,*
*Now by promising, now by giving or receiving.*
*You plunder, you spend, you stretch out your arms through the world,*
*Trying everything, gaping at all ranks of the clergy.* <note>original: *gradibus cunctis inhiando*; This refers to "gaping" after or hungrily seeking every level of the church hierarchy, from the lowest clerk to the highest office.</note>
*You do not make priests of the altar, but priests of the tithes.* <term>Tithes</term> (decimarum) were the mandatory tenth-part taxes paid to the church; the poet argues that Simony creates clergy motivated by money rather than the sacraments.
*You appoint vain provosts and deans.*
*You handle the business of Abbots, you rule and grant the Papacy,* <note>original: *Pontificatum*; While often referring specifically to the Pope, this term can also refer to the office of a Bishop.</note>

*Simony: I am clearly not the cause of such great evils,*
*But because it irks the superiors to cultivate their inferiors,*
*And they shrink from giving possessed things freely to good patrons:*
*Hence superiors do not grant honors for free.*
*They thrust out what is hidden; they unlock metals that were badly shut away;*
*They expose to use what any greedy men store up.*
*The stuffed purse now lacks a rich vein,*
*Within its safe wrappings, eaten away by tiny moths.* <note>Simony argues that by taking money for offices, she is actually "freeing" wealth that was previously hoarded and being eaten by moths in the purses of the greedy.</note>
*And what was denied before, behold, is now prepared for use.*
*I think such things are a divine matter, not Simony.*

*Church: How well protected are these righteous ones by their cloaks,* <note>original: *pallia*; The pallium is a specific ecclesiastical vestment, but here it suggests the outward appearance or "cover" of office.</note>

<note>Technical vocabulary from the bottom of the page: Church (*Ecclesia*), Simony (*Simonia*), a dialogue (*colloquium*), Switzerland (*Heluetia*), of tithes (*decimarum*), the Papacy or Episcopacy (*Pontificatum*).</note>

<summary>This page presents a personified debate where the Church accuses Simony of corrupting the clergy for profit, while Simony defensively argues that she is merely circulating wealth that would otherwise be hoarded.</summary>

--- Page 131 ---
<meta>This page continues the rhythmic dialogue from page 110 between the personified Church and Simony. On the previous page, Simony argued that her presence was caused by the failure of superiors to support their inferiors. Here, the Church counters that Simony is a deceiver, while Simony attempts to justify her trade by distinguishing between spiritual duties and earthly finances.</meta>

*Church:* You yourself, poisonous and treacherous one, deceive those whom you wickedly and flatteringly wish to call "good patrons," though they abuse the things of this world and are powerful only in their crimes. For the things they seize for themselves, or rather fit to their own use more licentiously, they call "good"; and those who are truly good, they sentence to ruin through unworthy judgment, alongside a malignant possessor.

Because of this, though you desire to cleverly excuse your father <note>original: *expurgaſſe per artem*; literally "to have purged through art," meaning to use trickery or sophisticated arguments to clear a reputation.</note>, you are instead more strongly accused. You appear even more harmful because you cause gifts to be driven out and shut up in [illegible]. <note>The transcription contains an asterisk, marking a word missing or illegible in the original manuscript.</note> Nor do you wish to give those divine things freely to the proven and worthy; instead, you sell them to the reprobate, and you extend your merchandise through all things.

*Simony:* If I sell what is mine, taking what is allowed to me—just as I take it upon myself to give, so I take back earthly gifts. I do not sell the glory of the altars, but I distribute the business of the <term>tithes</term>. <note>Simony argues that she is only dealing in the financial administration—the "tithes" or church taxes—and the physical land, not the spiritual grace of the sacraments themselves.</note> And I securely sell the <term>manors</term> <note>original: *manſus*; a "manse" or farmstead belonging to the church.</note> which are mine by right. Let the heavenly things be handled by the Bishops who moderate them, and let the order of the sacred rites be celebrated in the manner of the ancestors. Why, I ask, are you amazed? Or why are you burdened with envy? If we sow sacred things, is it so great a matter if we reap carnal rewards? <note>Simony is misquoting St. Paul (1 Corinthians 9:11) to justify taking money for spiritual services.</note> Paul expressly preaches that this is no great thing.

*Church:* Ah, by what trickery does a wicked mind lie to itself? You take care to wickedly pervert the Scriptures through your vice. Why do you draw to yourself the rights of the earthly churches? Paul certainly agrees openly with what I shall say: Who owes wages to himself, or who provides his own pay while performing the customs of military service and enduring hard labor? <note>The Church counters by using the same Pauline imagery (1 Corinthians 9:7) to argue that while a worker deserves pay, the pay is provided by the master, not seized by the worker through the sale of the master's goods.</note>

<summary>In this segment of the dialogue, Simony defends her actions by claiming she only sells the church's earthly property and tithes rather than spiritual grace, a distinction the Church rejects as a perversion of Scripture.</summary>
<keywords>Simony, ecclesiastical corruption, tithes, St. Paul, church property, canon law, personification allegory</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the rhythmic dialogue from page 111 between the personified Church (Ecclesia) and Simony. To the one striving below, the King gives rewards to the one who overcomes.
For the wages of my servants, I thus judge all my things.

Having been taken into the camp <note>original: *sumptus in castris*; a metaphor for entering spiritual service or the "army of Christ."</note>, Christ gives rewards among the stars.
