He sought food while he brought the words of life.
He asked these things for himself, but he provided for the needy;
This is evident everywhere in the order of their writings.

**SI.** You tell of clear wonders, by which it seems empty
That anyone should possess the rights of any churches.
If he gives unwillingly, by what right was he the possessor?
If he is forced to give, he is not even held to want his own property.
If he gives his own things for free, he will receive no benefit.
It is not I who seek to dominate these goods;
Such a possession is not worth three grains of salt. <note>original: *non tria grana salis*; a Latin idiom meaning something is completely worthless.</note>

**EC.** It is clearly evident that what you put forward is empty.
Let this appearance of religion not be a friend to good men,
In which it is as if I am allowed to use my own things as I please.

**SI.** I block my ears now, if you repeat such profane words!

**EC.** I do not deny you the right of your churches.
Take the just portions of all the <term>tithes</term>. <note>original: *decimarum*; the tenth part of agricultural produce or income paid as a tax to support the church.</note>
Let the debts for your services be paid.
But let one be sought from the flock who may be set over the little ones. <note>The Church argues that while the clergy have a right to financial support (tithes), their primary duty is the care of the "flock" (the congregation).</note>

Then, once all those groups were excluded, I changed the date again to be earlier than I had first said, and I held the council in Rome with only those I had personally prepared for the task.

Finally, Christ explains His own riches: in place of the pleasures you have left behind—which seemed honey-sweet but were actually steeped in bitter aloe <note>original: *aloe tinctis*; aloe was frequently used in ancient medicine and literature as the ultimate symbol of bitterness, contrasting with the sweetness of honey</note>—He imparts a taste of heavenly joys. ## PASQUIL IN EXILE

->INTERLOCUTORS,<-
->Cyrus. Pasquil.<-

**PASQUIL:** I will leave Rome myself, intending to seek out Saint James <note>Referring to the popular pilgrimage to the shrine of St. James in Santiago de Compostela, Spain</note>. **CYRUS:** What is your reason for leaving holy Rome? **PASQUIL:** Very pressing reasons, and many of them. **CYRUS:** And what are they? **PASQUIL:** First of all, although I have served many masters in Rome for many years now, hoping to gain something, I see that I am stripped of all hope. **CYRUS:** Why, I ask, is all hope taken from you? **PASQUIL:** Do you not see how great the number of Cardinals is? **CYRUS:** What of it? Why do you think it matters to you? **PASQUIL:** It matters a great deal. For they are so poor among themselves that if they needed another hat <term>galerum: the distinctive wide-brimmed red hat that serves as a symbol of a Cardinal's rank</term>, some would hardly have the means to buy one. They are so poor that their households (among whom I have lived for a long time) can hardly keep hunger away—I speak from experience.

<summary>This page concludes the satire of Pope Julius II and introduces a new dialogue where Pasquil, the personification of Roman satire, decides to flee a poverty-stricken and overcrowded Roman Curia.</summary>
<keywords>Pasquillus, Rome, Cardinals, corruption, Saint James, satire, poverty, ecclesiastical hierarchy</keywords>

<meta>Continuity with page 178: Pasquil and Cyrus continue their dialogue regarding the economic struggles of Rome's clerical class and the difficulty of securing patronage.</meta>

**CYRUS:** Why are you so inquisitive, my friend, as to track their poverty so relentlessly? **PASQUIL:** Because of it, all my hope is plucked away. For to address their own poverty, they snatch up, devour, and resell every single benefice <term>beneficia: church appointments or properties that provided a steady income to the holder</term>, even those of the smallest importance. What hope remains for me then? **CYRUS:** The Pope <term>Pontifex maximus: literally "Greatest Priest," the standard title for the Pope</term> will provide for you as well, among the rest of his household. **PASQUIL:** There are so many "nephews" <note>original: nepotes; a reference to nepotism, where Popes promoted their own relatives—often illegitimate sons styled as nephews—to high office</note>, such a huge troop of nephews, that even the Cardinals themselves who are not of that number suffer hardships because of it. For those nephews want riches, and massive ones at that, and for this a great heap of benefices is necessary. What hope is left for me? **CYRUS:** "Expectative graces" <term>Gratiae expectatiuae: legal promises of a church office or income granted before the current holder died or resigned</term> will be granted at this time. Stay your step here; wait a little while, and you will finally have what you desire. **PASQUIL:** For many years now I have "expected the expectatives," yet none of these things have been given. But even if they are given, what then? Do you think the Florentines <note>original: Florentinos; a reference to the Florentine associates of the Medici Popes, such as Leo X, who were often accused of monopolizing Roman wealth and influence</note> are forgetful of their own? ## THE SUBSTANCE OF THE PETITION
### of Pasquillus.

Most Blessed Father, in order that the salvation of souls, the Christian religion, and the common benefit of all might be more rightly served, may your Holiness deign to provide that those who—by a persuasion no less foolish than false—have taken the name of "learning" upon themselves and are accustomed to boast in the title of **Theologian**, may no longer lead the simple people astray. Nor should they dare henceforth to profane the majesty of most holy **Theology** so filthily and corruptly, or to brand it with marks of disgrace. For they not only live with perverse morals, but they are also utterly devoid of all scholarly disciplines. Therefore, first of all, let those who aspire to the highest **Theology** learn **Grammar**, lest they grow accustomed to speaking foolishly and corruptly (as they currently do) like manual laborers. Next, it seems especially necessary that they embrace **Rhetoric**...

# DECREE OF OUR HOLY LORD THE POPE
## regarding the petition of Pasquillus, read and published by the Lord Bishop of Sutri. <note>Pasquillus refers to "Pasquin," a famous talking statue in Rome upon which critics and satirists posted anonymous lampoons (pasquinades) against the Church and government. The "Bishop of Sutri" likely refers to a specific contemporary official involved in the humanist circles of the time.</note>

His Holiness our Lord the Pope, having held a mature council, has decreed to send legates <term>legatos</term> <note>Official messengers or representatives of the Pope.</note>—namely, the most learned men—to the entire Christian world. These men are to search out with diligent investigation and examine those who consider themselves worthy of the name of "theologian." 

If they find men who philosophize legitimately in both their words and their deeds, who adhere zealously to the truth of the Gospel, and who devote their labor to the doctrine of Paul and the <term>ancient theologians</term> <note>original: "priscorum theologorum"; referring to the early Church Fathers like Augustine, Jerome, and Chrysostom, whom the Humanists preferred over medieval writers.</note>, the legates shall extol them with proclamations and praises. They shall honor them with gifts and exhort them to continue their work happily, so that they may hand down to their successors a proper rule for living and teaching.

However, those whom the legates find to be clashing <note>original: "digladiari"; literally "to fence with swords," used here to describe aggressive, unproductive intellectual debating.</note> not with reality, but only with empty words—those who corrupt the Gospel and ancient theology with <term>sophistical garrulity</term> <note>Meaningless, over-complicated chatter used to win arguments rather than find truth.</note> and corrupted **logic** <note>original: "dialectica"; the formal system of logic that dominated medieval universities.</note>—the legates must take action. Especially against those who live most wickedly, in a manner contrary to what they themselves teach, and finally, those who are found to be completely ignorant of the Latin language. The legates should deter such men with appropriate threats, to prevent them from staining the most sacred name of **theology** with their wicked and shameful habits, along with their gross and lazy ignorance...

# MOMUS.
## THE SPEAKERS,
->Momus, Menippus, Pasquillus.<-

**Momus.** Go from here into France <note>original: "Gallias"</note>, Menippus; I myself shall wander through Germany. 

**Menippus.** I shall do so, and from there I will soon visit Spain <note>original: "Hispanias"</note>. But where shall I meet you again? 

**Momus.** In Germany; as soon as we have satisfied our duty here, we shall return to our homeland. 

**Menippus.** The way is dangerous and full of peril: I fear I may suffer some harm from the crafty and shifty French. 

**Momus.** Lay aside your fear; nothing will happen to you. But if you are altogether afraid to bring charges openly, mock them with secret hissing; or, taking up a writing tablet, record them in notes. But look, there is a traveler. Hey there, friend, where are you going?

## THE PLOT OF CHARLES

Charles, Emperor of the Romans <note>referring to Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor (reigned 1519–1556)</note>, having been advised to visit Maximilian <note>Maximilian I (1459–1519), the previous Emperor and Charles's grandfather</note>, is first led by his <term>spirit guide: "Genio," a personal tutelary spirit or guiding soul</term> to the Sibylline cave, where he learns many things concerning the Sibyl. Then, reaching Maximilian, he discusses many things with him concerning the future kingdom and the restoration of the Church. Finally, through the <term>Cave of Saint Patrick: "antrum Patritium," usually referring to the famous site of purgatory in Ireland, though the author here places it in a mythical "subterranean Spain"</term> in subterranean Spain, he returns to the living. Nor should this seem absurd to anyone, since even Homer, who was knowledgeable of that province, first depicted the Elysian field—the seat dedicated to the pious—in that same Spain. It was to this place that the prophesying Proteus sang that Menelaus would eventually depart. This follows the same manner in which Virgil imagines Aeneas visiting his father Anchises, and likewise how Lucian portrays his character Menippus.

<summary>The dialogue between Pasquillus and Momus concludes with a final jab at arrogant monks before introducing a new narrative: a visionary journey by Emperor Charles V to visit his predecessor in the underworld.</summary>
<keywords>Menippus, Momus, Pasquillus, Charles V, Maximilian I, Sibylline Cave, Saint Patrick's Purgatory, Elysium, Underworld journey, Church reform</keywords>

# THE BATTLE OF PIETY AND SUPERSTITION,
## A truly festive Dialogue, Concerning
### the corrupted Christian
### religion.

->INTERLOCUTORS.<-

->Piety. Superstition.<-

# Page 138

They say, "because we have been made rich: let us kill and slaughter; and let us not only shear the flock, but even butcher them, like wolves, like bears." It is enough for them that they possess all the revenues and goods, that they breed the most beautiful horses—and I wish that they would not act so wickedly even now, and most villainously squander the **patrimony of Christ** <term>patrimonium Christi: The wealth and property of the Church, which was traditionally intended for the relief of the poor and the upkeep of the faith.</term>. They make trappings <note>original: "Phaleras"; these were decorative metal disks or plates used on a horse's harness to show off wealth.</note> out of gold and silver, and the very iron shoes with which they protect the horses' feet are made of silver; meanwhile, the poor of Christ lack bread, and the beggar **Lazarus** <note>A reference to the parable in Luke 16, where a beggar named Lazarus lies at the gate of a rich man, hoping for crumbs from his table.</note> can hardly be satisfied by the crumbs that fall from their tables—tables more luxurious than those of **Croesus** <note>original: "Cresis"; referring to the King of Lydia, a legendary figure of antiquity famous for his immense wealth.</note>, more **Sybaritic** <note>original: "sybariticis"; an allusion to the ancient Greek city of Sybaris, whose inhabitants were notorious for their pursuit of luxury and pleasure.</note>, more profligate <term>asotijs: Derived from the Greek 'asotia,' meaning wasteful or reckless debauchery.</term>, and most sensual.

Of their mistresses I say nothing—though this is, after all, more human—yet they keep them not as the common people do, but only the most beautiful. And perhaps even this might be tolerated, if they did not also secretly ravish so many young girls, and commit so many adulteries, and incests, and sacrileges. Whatever is best in the market, or in the butcher's shop, they devour; they waste it all away <note>original: "abliguriunt"; a term for squandering money specifically on fine foods and delicacies.</note>, for they are creatures of the belly, and useful for nothing except for **gormandizing** <term>helluandum: The act of gluttonously devouring or squandering resources.</term>. ...by my oath, I have caused **your Masterships** <note>original: "Magistralitates uestras"; a mock-scholastic title used to lampoon the overly formal jargon of the Cologne theologians.</note> to be called together, to hold a council regarding these kinds of heretical, scandalous, blasphemous doctrines that are offensive to pious ears, to see what you, lords, think. **For although** in the previous year, according to our legal process, we condemned the propositions of a certain brother of the Order of Saint Augustine <note>A reference to Martin Luther, an Augustinian friar, whose works were formally burned and condemned by the universities of Cologne and Louvain in 1519 and 1520.</note>, so that they were worth nothing at all; nevertheless, because that same brother does not cease to seduce the people with his perverse doctrines, and calls us heretics and Pharisees, and ignorant men who do not know the Scriptures, I have deemed it necessary to once again sift through those same propositions along with many dialogues of others, so that we may burn the chaff with unquenchable fire. However, as is the custom, before I proceed to the act itself, I wish first to hear the sentiments of *our Masters*. And call the lord beadle <note>original: "pedellum"; the university official responsible for administrative duties and maintaining order during ceremonies.</note>, so that he may write everything down diligently.

**HOOGSTRATEN.** *Our Master Duplex*, as I said, what do you think of those "new poets" <note>original: "nouis poëtis"; the scholastics used "poet" as a derogatory term for Humanist scholars who focused on classical literature and Greek/Hebrew rather than traditional medieval logic.</note>, and of those novelties which are now being printed by the art of printing—or rather, the diabolical art? ## CONSTITUTION OF THE BEADLE

In the name of the Lord, Amen. By the authority of our most holy lord **Pope Leo X** <note>The Pope who presided over the beginning of the Reformation and excommunicated Martin Luther</note> and of other holy pontiffs who founded, established, and fortified with privileges our nourishing University of **Cologne** and of **Louvain**, we, the Masters of Cologne and of Louvain, do decree and ordain that in our nourishing University—which is the mother of the Universities of **Germany**—no one shall read, publicly or privately, in the schools of the theologians, anything of those **new doctrines** which have now emerged at the devil’s persuasion and are seducing so many people.

Furthermore, let them not speak of these doctrines, nor write of them in letters, or anywhere else. And let booksellers not import or sell anything [of this nature] to our scholars. And as for the **religious** <note>In this period, "the religious" specifically refers to members of monastic orders like monks or friars</note>, let them not store any of those works in their libraries, under a fine of 4 **marks of gold** <term>marcarum auri: a significant currency unit based on the weight of gold; 4 marks would be a very heavy fine</term>, for each and every time they are caught.

Those who act against this, as stubborn and rebellious people, we wish to be excluded here and everywhere, and from all honorable places by the Universities, and under penalty of disqualification from any degree in **Theology**, if the offender is already a Master:

<meta>This page marks a transition from the satirical "Constitution" of the conservative theologians in the previous section to a dialogue between two characters, Vadiscus and Pasquillus. These figures were popular tropes in Reformation literature—Vadiscus represents the critic of Roman corruption (often associated with the humanist Ulrich von Hutten), while Pasquillus represents the "talking statue" of Rome used to voice anonymous grievances against the papacy.</meta>

# THE WISE SAYINGS OF VADISCUS
## & Pasquillus, Concerning the Corrupted
## State of the Church.

**Vadiscus** said: The Romanist <term>Romanenses: a derogatory term used by Reformers for those who prioritized the authority of the Roman Curia over the broader Christian community</term> theologians distinguish between two types of Church. One is the general Church; the other is the "special" Church—that is, the Roman Church. This Roman Church consists of thieves and robbers, of a simoniacal <term>Simony: the corrupt practice of buying or selling church offices or spiritual favors</term> Pope, of impostors and the sacrilegious, of frauds and legal notaries, of bishops who flatter the Roman Pope, scribes, and similar types of deceivers.

**Pasquillus** <note>Pasquillus refers to "Pasquino," a statue in Rome where citizens would traditionally post satirical poems and criticisms of the government or the Church.</note> said: Today, that which the prophet **Malachi** wrote in chapter 2 is fulfilled in the high-ranking prelates, the priests, and the monks:
> "The lips of the priest preserve knowledge, and men seek the law from his mouth, because he is the messenger of the Lord of hosts. But you have turned aside from the way, and have caused many to stumble in the law; you have voided the covenant of Levi, says the Lord of hosts." <note>original Latin: "Labia sacerdotis custodiunt scientiam... irritum fecistis pactum Leui" — a quote from Malachi 2:7–8, used here to accuse the clergy of failing their divine duty.</note>

What then if these priests are now held in contempt? Their own sins have earned this. And if they are cast down, despised, plundered, or even sent back to work at the plows <note>A common suggestion in Reformation polemics—that corrupt clergy should be stripped of their wealth and forced to live as simple laborers</note>, this is for their own benefit, so that their souls may be saved on the day of judgment. For God does not judge twice for the same thing. <note>original: "non iudicat deus bis in idipsum" — a theological-legal principle suggesting that if a sin is punished on earth, the sinner might be spared eternal punishment.</note> And with the Lord also

It will never be inhabited to the end, nor will it be settled from generation to generation." <note>While the text cites Isaiah 14, the quote is from Isaiah 13:19–20. Likening Rome to Babylon was a central theme for those who saw the Papacy as an oppressive, "captive" power.</note>

But because very soon I must appear before the tribunal of Christ <note>original: "tribunal Christi" — refers to the Final Judgment.</note>, I shall bring these scars <note>original: "stigmata" — while often meaning the wounds of Christ, here it refers to the physical marks of Truth's persecution.</note> into the open; so that they may see what kind of goddess they have stabbed, and how they have done these things not to me, but to Christ himself, who is the Truth.

**HUTTEN.** Are you going to accuse them at the tribunal of Christ?

**TRUTH.** I will even condemn them to the underworld and to Pluto's torture-chamber. <note>original: "Plutonis carnificinam" — Hutten blends classical Greek/Roman mythology (Pluto, the god of the dead) with Christian concepts of hell.</note>

**HUTTEN.** Do you think they even believe there is a God, or an underworld?

**TRUTH.** They decreed thus in the Lateran Council <note>The Fifth Lateran Council (1512–1517) dogmatically defined the individuality and immortality of the soul, partly to counter certain philosophical challenges of the time.</note>, that the soul is immortal.

**HUTTEN.** As if we did not know this before! Blind one, do you not understand the fraud?

**TRUTH.** What fraud?

**HUTTEN.** That if they seem to believe it, we might more easily overlook their wickedness, assuming they will have a judge other than us. To ensure they cannot be judged by us here on earth, they established that law for themselves, which is otherwise beyond doubt.

**TRUTH.** You are suspicious of those men.

**HUTTEN.** Most unfavorably, as if of Turks and pagans <note>original: "Turcis & ethnicis" — a common 16th-century trope comparing the perceived corruption of the Roman Church to non-Christian "infidels."</note>. But come, teach me this art, so that I may be invulnerable <note>original: "insauciabilis" — literally "un-woundable."</note> from now on.

**TRUTH.** That is not right for me...

# THE ROMAN TRIAD
## A Dialogue.

->INTERLOCUTORS.<-

->Ernhold. Hutten.<-

**HUTTEN.** Have you not heard Vadiscus <note>The protagonist of this dialogue, whose name is likely a Latinized version of "The Wanderer," who returns from Rome to report on its vices.</note> wandering about here recently, publicly exposing what he saw in Rome with such great insult, and stirring up immense hatred against that nation? **ERNH.** I did not hear him myself, but Philip the consul <note>original: "Philippus consul" — likely referring to a contemporary magistrate or city official known to the authors.</note> told me how boldly he was accustomed to speak. I had decided to see him, but I do not know what obstacle occurred, and in the meantime, he departed. **HUTTEN.** You would have heard wonders! You would not only have approved of the subject matter, but you would have admired the man’s talent in the way he attacked those customs—for he did so in a completely new way. **ERNH.** How, I pray? **HUTTEN.** There are many things to tell, but time is short, and I am already summoned to courtly duties <note>original: "aulica" — refers to the duties Hutten performed at the court of the Archbishop of Mainz.</note>. **ERNH.** Explain this first. **HUTTEN.** I have no time. **ERNH.** No time? As if you serve the court so strictly that you must do it constantly, and cannot steal one or two hours a day for your studies and for friendship? Come, speak, why do you allow yourself to be pleaded with? **HUTTEN.** Then...

But truly, if the "privilege of Constantine" <note>The document detailing the forged "Donation of Constantine."</note> grants the Empire of the West, there is a danger for Charles <note>Charles V (1500–1558), who was at this time the King of Spain and the newly elected Holy Roman Emperor.</note> that he might possess nothing of those things which either came to him by inheritance, or to whose succession he has already been elected. 

**HVT.** If the matter were to be handled by the judgment of the "most reverend men" at Rome, he will possess nothing, for all things belong to the church. 

**ERNH.** Therefore, I believe the former popes were far too generous, since they did not claim everything that was given to them, but, content with a few things, they allowed other things to kings and permitted the emperor to remain in this portion, however small it may be. 

**HVT.** That was not generosity, but weakness; for they feared, when they first fabricated this donation, that if they gave up nothing of it, there would be a unanimous conspiracy of kings against them, which they could not resist. But what most proves that this fiction was created by the impulse of pontifical greed is this: if the morals of the priests then were what they are today, they would have allowed nothing to be dragged away from them; but if indeed—as I believe—the bishops <note>original: "antistites" — referring to high-ranking church officials or overseers</note> of that age were holy men, they would not have accepted it. And if those to whom Constantine gave these things did not admit him (viewing him as one offering useless things), by what right do their successors reclaim what their ancestors judged themselves unworthy to receive, and even persuaded the donors not to give? Certainly, in truth, no pope ever came into possession of those things which this fiction encompasses,

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Ernhold (ERNH.) and Hutten (HVT.) concerning the Donation of Constantine. On the previous page, Hutten argued that the papacy’s claims to worldly power are based on a fabricated document and that if the early bishops were truly holy, they would never have accepted such a gift. Ernhold now responds by detailing how he believes the forgery was actually constructed and the long gap between the historical Constantine and the papacy’s eventual seizure of Rome.</meta>

On the contrary, they finally dared to seize the city of Rome many centuries after Constantine, even though they had not held it before; thus, the possession of even a tiny part followed that so-called "ancient donation" only very late. Furthermore, if they had ever voluntarily given back anything granted to them, would they have done so without formal letters and seals? Or would those who guarded that "privilege" <note>Referring to the *Constitutum Constantini*, the document allegedly proving the Donation.</note> so anxiously have been so negligent with the evidence of their own generosity?

Trifles! On the contrary, to speak my mind: I believe the "privilege of Constantine" was born like this: when a certain greedy Pope (whoever he might have been) found an opportunity and snatched a portion of Italy, he was so delighted by the advantage that he could not stop there—for the pursuit of greed is insatiable. He resolved to push even further. Those were times when superstition flourished, offering hope that much could be easily obtained if one were willing to exploit the simple-mindedness of the common people and the laziness of princes. 

He began to expand his borders, and his successors, following his lead, turned this stolen license for plunder into a regular custom. Finally, some very "clever" <note>The Latin *prudentissimus* ("most prudent") is used ironically here to mean "cunning."</note> Pope, wishing to provide for the Church’s interests, wrote out this "divine edict" on a piece of old parchment—perhaps one previously dragged through the dust or covered in mold to make it look ancient—certainly many centuries after the time of Constantine.

**ERNH.**

<summary>Ernhold argues that the Donation of Constantine is a late forgery created to justify the Papacy's gradual and illegal seizure of Italian lands centuries after Constantine's death. He describes a process where opportunistic Popes exploited the superstition of the public and the negligence of rulers to expand their territory, eventually fabricating a "divine edict" on aged parchment to legitimize their claims.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Ernhold and Hutten. *ERNH.* Nevertheless, if Leo X <note>Pope Leo X (reigned 1513–1521), a member of the Medici family and the Pope during the early years of the Reformation.</note> should demand these things back from Charles, what do you think will happen? 

*HVT.* What else, indeed, but that he should in turn remember his own rights against Leo, and remember that he is both a King and a German. 

*ERNH.* And [what if the Pope] sets everything in motion, stirs things up, brings ruin, prostrates, and overturns all? 

*HVT.* May Christ grant better things; the matter will not go that far. 

*ERNH.* If those men know how to restrain themselves? Those who, while they would not dare to injure someone they feared, do not refrain from insulting even a Roman prince? To whom the Pope offers the crown with his feet <note>An allusion to the claim that certain Popes showed their superiority by kicking the imperial crown onto the Emperor's head or making him kiss their feet.</note> while the prince is cast down on his knees, and whom he forces to renounce the city of Rome and the rule of Italy. 

*HVT.* Indeed, Pope Urban <note>Urban V (reigned 1362–1370).</note> crowned Charles the Bohemian <note>Emperor Charles IV (reigned 1346–1378), whom Hutten and other German humanists viewed as a weak ruler for his submission to papal authority in the Golden Bull and other treaties.</note> only after receiving an oath that he would leave Italy within that same year. The Pope despised him so much that he did not even come to meet him for a conference, but sent one of the cardinals with the crown to meet him on the road; he forbade him from entering the city of Rome, and deprived him of several Italian cities. 

*ERNH.* Oh, a man least worthy of life, let alone the Roman Empire, to have endured such things! The Romanists <note>original: *Romanenses*. A derogatory term for the supporters and officials of the Papal court in Rome.</note> themselves do not believe, as it seems to me, that those three things <note>A reference to Hutten’s "Triads"—usually Truth, Piety, and Liberty—which he argues the Roman Church has "killed" through corruption.</note> they have so miserably killed will live again at the Last Judgment, or that they will have to give an account for having afflicted them so. 

*HVT.* Certainly, they mock that Last Judgment. 

*ERNH.* I believe they are slaughtering the Judgment itself along with the others. 

*HVT.* Not at all; they hold it so much for nothing...

For they have reached such a state that they do not seek to kill that which they believe does not exist; otherwise, there would be a conscience in Rome.

ERNH. And there would not be so many poisoners <note>original: *uenefici*. In the polemics of this period, Rome was frequently accused of being a center for political assassinations via poison.</note>.

HVT. And so Vadiscus <note>The central figure of Hutten’s "Triads," a character who reports on the corrupt "trinities" he observed in Rome.</note> says that the city of Rome abounds in three things especially: antiquities, poisons, and devastation. To this I added in turn that three things are likewise exiled from there: simplicity, self-restraint, and integrity.

ERNH. You are right, for the city's customs cannot endure simplicity, no one lives with restraint in Rome, and as for integrity—who is upright there?

HVT. In truth, no one; though in the popular opinion, it is whoever is most wealthy, and especially those with the most money.

ERNH. As you say—but that is a wretched opinion. How much more desirable is it to be far from Rome than to avoid the body-destroying venom of scorpions, serpents, and lizards? <meta>This page continues the dialogue between the characters Ernhold and Hutten, who are discussing the corruption of the Roman Curia and the hypocrisy of the Papal office compared to the life of Christ. ...the Pope himself <note>original: *pontificem*</note>, being held by a zeal for these [worldly] matters rather than for peace, religion, evangelical doctrine, and in short, for charity. Furthermore, when did Christ ever intend this: that He should leave behind someone after Him who—having set aside the instructions handed down by Him and having followed a life that is anything but Christian—would harass the whole world with pardons and **bulls**? <term>bullis: official papal decrees or charters, named after the lead seal (*bulla*) attached to them. Here, the author critiques their use in the sale of indulgences.</term> Or, since the Pope is a shepherd of souls, why is it necessary for him to seal a bull for one to whom he has given life, or for one to whom he has given heaven? In the business of souls, there is no need for letters, nor for testimony brought in from elsewhere, but rather each person’s own **conscience** <note>original: *conscientia*. This reflects the Reformation-era emphasis on the internal, direct relationship between the believer and God.</note>, which is known to God; nor does it require a judge before Him who explores all human thoughts.

What of the "vicars of Christ" and their magnificent horses, when He Himself once rode upon a lowly donkey? Is it because wars must be waged? But He detested these things; He embraced tranquility and urged peace, and passed that same devotion on to those who followed Him. How foreign it is to the institution of Christ to love women above all else and to satisfy lust with prostitutes—especially for those whom He wished to live by the spirit, and to whom He did not permit the pleasure of the flesh even within marriage! Or was it for this reason that **Callixtus** <note>Referring to Pope Callixtus I or the various medieval decrees attributed to the early popes regarding clerical celibacy. The author is sarcastically suggesting that forbidding marriage only served to encourage secret immorality.</note> forbade marriage to the **priestly order**: so that priests alone would be allowed to whore, and so that the spiritual state might return from holy marriage to the foulest debauchery...

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Ernhold and Hutten. ...restores in our age? <note>Referring to the pride and worldliness of the Papal court under Pope Leo X (r. 1513–1521).</note> Or what holy pontiff [has there been]? <meta>This page continues the dialogue between Ernhold and Hutten from page 206. They are discussing the reception of the Emperor Charles V and the corruption inherent in the Roman Curia, specifically focusing on the "Roman Triads"—groups of three things that characterize the state of Rome.</meta>

...thought [worthy of praise] by the most learned men?

HUTTEN: That those who are idle in Rome do three things: stroll about, consort with prostitutes, and hold banquets. 

ERNHOLD: They do nothing else; for those who have no leisure spend their time meditating, writing, appealing, canvassing, and petitioning—they defraud, deceive, commit perjury, betray, plunder, steal, corrupt, and cheat. 

HUTTEN: What about this? That there are three side-dishes for the poor there: cabbage, onions, and garlic; and on the contrary, three for the wealthy: the sweat of the poor, usury, and the spoils of the Christian people.

HUTTEN: In this matter they especially deserve hatred, because they think us so brainless <note>original: *sine cerebros* (without brains)</note> that when something is acquired with money, we can be persuaded it is not being bought and sold—even though they do this so openly that even to the Fuggers... <term>Fugger: A powerful German banking family who handled the transfer of funds for papal indulgences and ecclesiastical offices.</term>

Nor can any obstacle be so difficult to overcome that a legal trick cannot be found to resolve it there in Rome. 

Furthermore, the **Pope's right** <term>pontifici ius: the legal claim of the Pope to reassign a "benefice" (church office) if the holder dies while at the papal court</term> applies to the possessions of anyone who dies in Rome, or even within a two-day journey from the city. **ERNHOLD.** A great deal, I think. Indeed, we lived more safely in Rome for the very reason that, because we held no church offices, we did not fear such ambushes.

H V T . <note>HUTTEN; This refers to Ulrich von Hutten, the author of the dialogue, though here it likely marks the speaker Ernhold quoting Hutten’s character Vadiscus.</note> He spoke these things in almost these same words: "Where now," he asked, "is that **salt of the earth** <note>original: "sal terrae"; a reference to Matthew 5:13</note>, of which Christ spoke to the apostles: 'You are the salt of the earth; but if the salt loses its flavor, with what shall it be seasoned?' Has it not already lost its flavor, and in its place is this adulterated, worthless, and foolish salt scattered? Is it not time for it to be cast out and trampled underfoot by men?"

As for **faculties** <term>facultates; legal dispensations or licenses granted by the Church to do something otherwise forbidden by canon law</term>—even though they are, as I related a little while ago from Vadiscus, the granting of license to commit all manner of wicked deeds—they are nonetheless easily granted; they are granted often and repeatedly. Previously, these were contained within the walls of the city <note>Rome</note>, where those who wanted them had to seek them out. Recently, however, because it seemed not enough people were traveling to Rome to trade in such things, they began to send **legates** <term>legatos; official representatives of the Pope</term>. 

These men, if anything is prohibited by divine or human laws, grant an indulgence for it in exchange for money. These are called "faculties": for instance, if someone wishes to eat the flesh of animals on fast days, or milk, or eggs, or butter; or if someone knows of a debt for which he is repentant but wants to be able to not return it; or if someone has sworn an oath that is difficult to keep; or if he seeks a wife whom the laws forbid him to marry. Furthermore, it is bought from these legates so that one man can hold twenty **benefices with cure of souls** <term>sacerdotia curata; church offices that required the holder to provide spiritual care to a parish</term> without even being a **priest** <term>presbyter; a fully ordained minister</term> (for it bothers many and even shames them, especially in Germany, to actually perform sacred rites). When we receive such men here, what else are we doing but welcoming that fatal... <note>The text cuts off here; the catchword "equum" suggests a reference to the "fatal horse" of Troy, implying that these legates are a hidden enemy brought within the walls.</note>

<summary>Hutten critiques the Roman Church for selling "faculties" (dispensations) that allow people to break religious laws—such as dietary restrictions or marriage prohibitions—for money, while lamenting the corruption of the clergy who hold multiple offices without performing their duties.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Hutten and Ernhold. ...the horse, and the Greeks <note>original: "Danaos"</note> shut inside its belly, when the Trojans place them within their walls and in the citadel?

HUTTEN: We do the same, but to a greater extent: all the wicked are made clean <note>original: "mundi"</note> and innocent of their sins. This is true even if someone has killed a man, or killed his own father, or—what is considered worse than these—if someone, at the devil's persuasion, has struck a member of the clergy, or if someone has committed sexual assault against his mother, sister, or daughter, or even if someone happens to have been excommunicated from the highest level by the very **Vicar of Christ** <term>Vicar of Christ; a title for the Pope, indicating his role as Christ's representative on earth</term> himself. In short, whatever has been done is rendered "undone" through these **faculties** <term>facultates; legal dispensations or licenses granted by the Church that allowed individuals to bypass canon law for a fee</term>. 

And here we must call to mind those matters known as **papal cases** <term>casus papales; specific grave sins or legal disputes that were reserved for the Pope's personal judgment or that of his direct delegates</term>. For it is from these cases that the "faculties" are prepared. However, it is not only the **legates from the side** <term>legati de latere; the highest-ranking papal ambassadors, sent directly from the Pope’s "side" with full authority</term> who bring them here; there is also a retail market for them in that place as well. 

For the **mendicant brothers** <term>mendicantes; friars from orders like the Franciscans or Dominicans who originally took vows of poverty and survived on alms</term>, as well as other orders and colleges, buy these dispensations in Rome so that they may sell them here later. The mendicants especially do this because of their skill in salesmanship <note>original: "commendandi peritiam"</note>. They carry out the Pope's business faithfully, persuading the uneducated common folk and simple women of marvelous things regarding **indulgences** <term>indulgentiae; certificates sold by the church to reduce the temporal punishment required for sins</term>. They govern every nod and refusal of these women, whom they have entirely at their will by means of the help of **confession** <term>confessio; the practice of telling one's sins to a priest to receive absolution</term>.

ERNHOLD: I see no difference at all between regular merchants and these traders in "faculties."

HUTTEN: Nor is there any difference, except that giving silver for indulgences is not called "selling" them; otherwise...

They impatiently endure that legal disputes continue to be transferred to **Rome** at such great expense to **Germany**. They wretchedly desire that those heads of the church might at last cast off the vices they now possess—folly, sloth, luxury, greed, rapacity, treachery, drunkenness, cunning, lust, insolence, sedition, fraud, violence, crime, and cruelty—and instead put on these virtues: prudence, vigilance, diligence, parsimony, frugality, temperance, sincerity, sobriety, simplicity, continence,

**HUTTEN.** And in a city that is so hostile to its own citizens, how fittingly is the **head of the church** <note>The Pope.</note> housed there?

**ERNHOLD.** It seems to me most unfitting.

**HUTTEN.** And how is life lived in that city, where there are three things men will hardly do unless forced: keep their word, help others, and give way on the street?

**ERNHOLD.** What morals could be more opposed to **Christian innocence**? For while that innocence consists in this one thing—doing to others what one would want done to oneself—the Romans pursue the opposite to such a degree that they find it difficult even to step aside for someone on the path. Furthermore, faith and generosity are virtues far too divine for the city of Rome to contain.

**HUTTEN.** And what of a city that so overflows with three other things that they can hardly be counted: **prostitutes, priests, and scribes**? This is an idle flock, men of the least worth. **ERNHOLD.** By my faith, the cost is intolerable. For, to say nothing of others, we are finally feeling what **Germany** must pay <note>original: *quid Germania luat*. <summary>In this dialogue, Hutten and Ernhold describe Rome as a city ruled by vice and inhabited by an idle, exploitative population of clerics and usurers. <meta>This page serves as a poetic epilogue to Ulrich von Hutten’s "Vadiscus" (The Roman Triads). Following the dialogue of the previous pages, which detailed the triple-layered corruption of the Roman Curia, this epigram summarizes those grievances for the reader, focusing on the themes of simony, the exploitation of Germany, and the hypocrisy of the Papacy.</meta>

# TO THE READER REGARDING THE TRIAD
## *Hutten's Roman Epigram.*

You see, reader, how in Ausonian Rome <note>original: *Ausoniæ*; a poetic term for Italy</note> all things in threes
Infatuate men and defile God.
You see how, after many obstacles and having cast out Peter,
The impostor Simon <note>Simon Magus, the biblical figure who attempted to buy spiritual power. From his name comes "simony," the practice of selling church offices or "benefices," which Hutten is attacking here</note> reigns in the conquered city.
You see Christ mocked, and the mystical thefts
Of the Palatine Pope <note>original: *Palatini... pontificis*; referring to the Palatine Hill in Rome, equating the Pope’s power with that of the ancient Roman Emperors</note> called sacred.
You see how oracles, often founded by the new fraud
Of the Ausonian fathers <note>The Roman Catholic leadership</note>, blind the deceived world,
And the cunning which hauls away German gold <note>original: *Teutonicum... aurum*</note>,
The art by which Rome pursues foreign wealth.
You grieve for so many spoils and various things, and that a wondrous trap
For sacred things is covered with a veil of religion,
And that nowhere is there less faith than in that city
Which prescribes itself as the head of faith.
You see honored laws give way to fraud,
And the fabrications of "sacred law" take their place.
You see God being driven and carried off; you see all things done
For the hope of profit, and you see the joys of heaven being bought.
You see how wicked money profanes chaste morals;
You see it being bought so that you may live following depraved ways,
That pacts and given faith are corrupted, and treaties dissolved,
And how you are deceived by a God who has been sworn upon.
[You see] things done being undone, and sacred things mixed with the profane,

<sig>A</sig> <meta>catchword: THm (Likely for "Themata," the propositions often appended to this work)</meta>

It frames the Papacy not as the successor of St. Peter, but of Simon Magus, the biblical sorcerer who tried to buy the power of the Holy Spirit.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the Latin epigram concluding Ulrich von Hutten’s "Vadiscus" to a German-language summary of his famous "Roman Triads." These triads were a popular satirical device used to critique the perceived corruption and moral decay of the Roman Catholic Church in the early 16th century.</meta>

# The Roman Triad
## In German.

### Pasquill.
<note>Pasquill (or Pasquin) refers to a famous "talking statue" in Rome where anonymous satirists would post biting verses criticizing the Pope and the Roman court.</note>

Three things hold Rome in high regard: Relics, the Pope, and indulgences. <note>original: *Heyltū, Pabst, vnd ablaß*. Indulgences were payments made to the Church in exchange for the remission of temporal punishment for sins, a major grievance of the Reformation.</note>

Three things are considered costly <note>original: *Köstlich*; meaning both precious and expensive.</note> in Rome: Women, horses, and legal briefs.

Three things are cheap in Rome: Fever, pestilence, and poor people.

Three things one usually brings home from Rome: A bad conscience, a bad stomach, and an empty purse.

Three things are necessary for a petitioner <note>original: *solicitātī*; refers to someone seeking a legal favor or office from the Roman courts.</note> in Rome: Much money, many written decrees, and many lies.

Three things one finds in Rome in every alleyway: Holy sites, broken columns, and prostitutes. <note>original: *putanas*; a term for sex workers, highlighting the irony between Rome’s spiritual status and its street life.</note>

<summary>This page presents a German translation of satirical "triads" mocking the city of Rome. It portrays the papal capital as a place where spiritual items like relics are sold for profit while disease, poverty, and corruption run rampant.</summary>
<keywords>Roman Triads, Satire, Pasquill, Papacy, Indulgences, Ulrich von Hutten, Roman Corruption, Reformation Literature</keywords>

--- Page 414 ---
<meta>This page continues the list of "Roman Triads" from the previous page, translating Ulrich von Hutten’s sharp satirical critique of the city of Rome from Early New High German into English.</meta>

Three things Rome has in the greatest abundance: old towers, poisonous worms, and dilapidated churches.

Three things are not rare in Rome: high prices, bad air, <note>original: *bößer lufft*. This often referred to "mal aria" or the perceived unhealthiness of the Roman climate.</note> and unfaithfulness.

Three things bring everyone to Rome: profit, wonders, and freedom.

# PASQUILLUS THE PSEUDO-THEOLOGIAN.

## PASQUILLUS, GOVERNOR OF THE CITY OF ROME,
## against Luther, formerly an Augustinian.

*Before I attack you, Luther, or refute your paradoxes, I must say a few words in preface, lest I seem to praise and blame the same man at once—which is the mark of a wicked person. I believe there is no place so remote or hidden that the fame of your name has not reached it. I used to hear that the Germans favored you immensely, the French granted you much credit, the Italians praised you with full hands, the Spanish elevated you, the Scots admired you, and the British looked up to you. The Hungarians* <note>original: *Pannones*</note> *babbled nothing else with full cheeks but "Luther" alone. The Bohemians and the Sarmatians* <note>original: *Sarmatas*. A classical term used by Renaissance humanists to refer to the peoples of Poland, Lithuania, and Russia.</note> *believed you had fallen from heaven. I myself—who am not endowed with such singular wisdom as would be fitting for a man of my high rank—even began, imprudently, to love Luther and to proclaim him everywhere as the champion of Christian liberty. But oh, how blind and insane I was to have praised a man who deserves no praise! How much better it would have been to have drawn my pen* <note>original: *calamum*; literally a reed-pen or stylus.</note> *against you then, as I am doing now. However, at that time, business...*

This paradox of yours is divided into two parts; I shall respond to both. If there is to be no fighting against the **Turks** <note>original: *Turcas*; referring to the Ottoman Empire, then the primary military threat to Christendom</note>, under what pretext will **Clement VII** <note>Pope Clement VII (reigned 1523–1534), who faced both the Reformation and the Sack of Rome</note> be able to plunder miserable and blind mortals? In this, however, they differ from them: the Turks do this to those against whom they labor with deadly hatred; the Romans, truly, do it to their dearer and most intimate associates. However, I lived in Rome for a long time; I could never distinguish what "Turkish" thing they had besides that.

My Romans—or rather my "Roman ladies," they are so effeminate—do not cease in the meantime to dream for themselves of noble and ancient Rome, the conqueror of nations, and they marvelously applaud themselves, swollen and haughty with the title of **Roman Citizen**. # DIALOGUE OF MARPHORIUS AND
## Pasquillus. Marph.

Why do you sigh, oh **Pasquillus**? <note>Pasquillus and Marphorius were famous "talking statues" in Rome upon which anonymous satirists posted biting political and religious critiques known as "pasquinades."</note> PAS. You see the **Republic** <note>original: *rempublicam*; referring here to the general state of Christendom or the public welfare</note>: it is going to ruin through the works of both **princes** and **private individuals**. MAR. Is there something in them that you find lacking? PAS. Much, and many things. MAR. If you were **God**, what specifically would you grant to them? PAS. To **CLEMENT** <note>Pope Clement VII (r. 1523–1534)</note>, clemency and piety. To **CHARLES** <note>Holy Roman Emperor Charles V (r. 1519–1556)</note>, magnanimity and diligence. To **FERDINAND** <note>Ferdinand I, Archduke of Austria and brother to Charles V</note>, according to the **Comic's** <note>The Roman playwright Terence; the reference is to a line from his play *Andria*: "Since you cannot do what you want, want what you can do."</note> sentiment: that he should want what he is able to achieve. To **FRANCIS** <note>King Francis I of France (r. 1515–1547)</note>, fortunate judgment and faith <note>original: *fidem*; likely a jab at Francis's reputation for breaking treaties and his alliance with the Ottoman Empire</note>. To **HENRY** <note>King Henry VIII of England (r. 1509–1547)</note>, religion and a sound mind. To the **PORTUGUESE** <note>King John III of Portugal (r. 1521–1557)</note>, as much power as he has arrogance (if indeed this could be provided by me). To the **Purple Senate** <note>The College of Cardinals, named for their distinctive red/purple robes</note>, learning <note>original: *literas*; referring to the *humaniora* or classical scholarship</note> and a **love** <note>original: *venerem*; referring to Venus/sexual conduct</note> that is not perverted. To the **BISHOPS**, I would give the learning they claim to want, but I would take away the pleasures and lordships they actually seek. To the **PRIESTS**, I would give wives, so that they might cast off their concubines. To the **MONKS**, [I would give] concubines, so that they might stop being wives and husbands to one another <note>A sharp satirical attack suggesting that same-sex relationships were common in monasteries, implying they should have female companions instead to end such "marriages."</note>.

# ANOTHER DIALOGUE
## Of the same.

MARPHORIUS. Greetings, **Pasquillus**, what is the matter? You seem sadder to me than you were a little while ago. 

PASQUILLUS. You should know that there is no one for whom good fortunes are so adverse. The joy I recently received from our friendly conversation—when you asked what I would do if I were **God**—is now tainted by a rising distress. 

MARPHORIUS. What is this I hear? 

PASQUILLUS. Friends of venerable authority, of whom I have very many, have informed me that some people were so deeply offended because, while I was bestowing such various **gifts** <note>original: *dotes*; referring to the satirical virtues or "endowments" Pasquillus assigned to kings and popes on the previous page</note>, I did not remember them. Because of this, they threaten such terrible things that I do not dare to set foot out of the house. 

MARPHORIUS. This is exactly why I was coming to you, lest you be unaware. Yesterday, several people approached me to greet and talk with me; they said they had heard of this and even urged me, on account of the very great friendship that exists between us, to warn you: either keep yourself within your own walls, or grant something also to the others who are of most celebrated name. If you are willing to comply with my advice—for I have a well-disposed heart—you will give something to the others as well. Come then, my [Pasquillus...]

Pasquillus, *if you were God, what would you give* to the DUKE OF MILAN? 

PASQUILLUS. *To him I would give a monk’s cowl, so that he might suffer from the same disease as the monks.* 

MARPHORIUS. *I am surprised that monks are afflicted by any disease, since everywhere they seem sleek, plump, and with well-tended skin.* 

PASQUILLUS. *They suffer from hypocrisy and greed. Since* Francesco Sforza <note>original: *Franciscus Fortia*; refers to Francesco II Sforza (1495–1535), the last Duke of Milan of his line, whose reign was marked by the heavy pressures of the Italian Wars</note> *has embraced both, then by the best right a double cowl is owed to him.* 

MARPHORIUS. *What for the* PEOPLE OF MILAN? 

PASQUILLUS. *I would give them a consensus of minds, so that one would not seek out the stupid French, another the shifty Spaniards, and another the raging Germans.* <note>Milan was a constant battlefield where various factions of citizens supported different invading foreign powers during the Italian Wars.</note>

MARPHORIUS. *What for the* DUKE OF SAXONY? 

PASQUILLUS. *Whatever he might wish for! Because he favors the* Gospel <note>original: *Euangelio*; a reference to the Protestant Reformation</note>*, and has always stood as a most fierce defender of Christian liberty.* <note>This likely refers to John Frederick I, Elector of Saxony, a leading protector of Martin Luther and the Schmalkaldic League.</note>

MARPHORIUS. *What are you going to give to the* VENETIANS? 

PASQUILLUS. *Whatever they like: provided they first stripped off their Turkishness, Greekness, and Illyrian nature.* <note>Venice was often mocked by other Italians for its cosmopolitan nature and its pragmatism in trading with the Ottoman Turks and Eastern Christians.</note>

MARPHORIUS. *What would you give to the* DUKE OF SAVOY? 

PASQUILLUS. *Nothing; rather, I would take away his wife, whom I hear is clever and of elegant beauty, while he himself is more deformed than* Thersites <note>In Greek mythology, Thersites was described by Homer as the ugliest and most foul-mouthed soldier in the Greek army at Troy</note>*. For I do not think it is fair for a beautiful woman to sleep with a deformed man.* 

MARPHORIUS. WHAT ABOUT THE DUKE OF MANTUA? 

PASQUILLUS. *I would take away his* Hosschetta <note>original: *Hosschëta*; likely a reference to a mistress or a specific favorite/companion who distracted the Duke</note> *from him: lest his wife be cheated of his beloved embraces...*

# THE GOSPEL OF PASQUILLUS, Once of Rome, now a wanderer.

<note>Pasquillus (or Pasquin) was one of the "talking statues" of Rome where citizens posted anonymous satirical poems and biting critiques of the papacy and government.</note>

->Deceit be with you. And with your companion.<-
<note>original: "Dolus uobiscum. Et comiti tuo." This is a parody of the liturgical greeting "Dominus vobiscum" (The Lord be with you) and its response.</note>

->A reading from the false Gospel, according to the Chest of Gold and Silver.<-
<note>original: "Frequentia falsi Euangelij, secundum Archam Auri & argenti." A mocking imitation of the introduction to a Gospel reading in the Mass.</note>

->Glory to you, O Gold and Silver.<-

AT that time, the greedy POPE said to his **Carpinals**: <note>original: "Carpinalibus." A satirical pun on "Cardinals," deriving from the Latin verb "carpere," meaning to snatch, pluck, or seize greedily.</note> "When the son of man comes to the seat of our Majesty, let the doorkeeper say to him: 'Friend, for what purpose have you come?' And if he passes through, knocking but giving nothing, then with his hands and feet bound, cast him into the outer darkness." <note>This is a dark parody of the Parable of the Wedding Feast in Matthew 22, where the man without a wedding garment is cast out. Here, the "garment" required for entry to the Papal court is money.</note> The **Carpinals** truly said to him, "Master, what must we do to possess money?" He truly replied, "In the law it is written: love gold and silver with all your heart, and with all your soul, and love money as yourselves. Do this, so that you may live. <note>A parody of the "Great Commandment" found in the Gospels (e.g., Luke 10:27), replacing love for God and neighbor with the worship of wealth.</note> For I give this commandment to you, that just as I do, so you also should do." Then there came to the court a certain very poor cleric, who, having been oppressed by his bishop, was a true Israelite <note>original: "uerus Israëlita." A reference to John 1:47, here used ironically to describe a sincere but penniless victim of the church hierarchy.</note>

For I will show him how much he and his country must suffer for my name's sake." 

And Peter went and entered, and kissing his hands, said, "Father Paul, Charles V Augustus <note>The traditional title for the Holy Roman Emperor, "Augustus," emphasizing his claim as the successor to the Roman Caesars.</note> has sent me—he who spoke to you on the road as you were coming—so that you may know him and be filled with a good spirit." And immediately there fell away from him his blindness, his spirit of persecution, and his wicked desires; and rising up, he was filled with sincere love. <note>In this satirical context, "sincere love" represents Paul III’s total political submission to the Emperor's will.</note> And when he had taken food, he was strengthened; and he remained for some days with the supporters of Charles who were in Rome.

## PASQUIL TO DESIDERIUS ERASMUS
## of Rotterdam. Hearty Greetings.

The portrait of Cursius <note>Pietro Corsi, an Italian scholar and poet who engaged in a high-profile literary feud with Erasmus over the "Ciceronian" style of Latin.</note>, requested by you in most urgent letters, and promised by me to you with the greatest generosity—because I, the most dutiful of all men, have not sent it until now, you could justly rebuke my slowness, were it not that the cause of a most just impediment defended me. For while I try to satisfy both myself and you, as well as the excellent painters, because of the constant—that is, natural—turning of Cursius’s limbs and head, you would believe him to be Proteus <note>A shape-shifting sea god from Greek mythology; here, it suggests that Cursius is so fickle or physically restless that he is impossible to capture in a single image.</note>, so much so that more and more often...

...we have been so deceived, that by no skill of craftsmen and by no instrument which we had hoped for, have we been able to aim at and achieve our goal. Therefore, my dear Erasmus, since the situation is such that it is altogether most difficult to promise anything certain about the other man—and especially about our friend Cursius <note>Pietro Corsi (known as Cursius), an Italian poet and scholar who engaged in a famous literary quarrel with Erasmus over the correct style of Latin prose.</note>, since he is always "running" <note>original: "currat." A pun on his name, Cursius, and the Latin verb "currere," to run.</note> both in mind and on his feet—lest you be frustrated in such great desire, I have set aside all difficulties. I have attempted, by myself, to compensate for that very delay with interest by describing a "double Cursius," as it were, to you in this letter. 

And first, I shall begin with his exterior appearance. He exceeds you in height by more or less two feet, with a head that is square rather than oval. His hair is somewhat black and—if he allowed it to grow—would be tightly curled by the nature of Ethiopians <note>original: "Ethiopū natura uibrato." In the 16th century, "Ethiopian" was a general term for Black Africans; the author is describing Corsi’s hair as extremely frizzy or woolly.</note>. He has the face of a bad man, of a somber man, of a terrifying man. Yet, that terrifying quality is only fit for silencing the wailing of children; for men, however, it serves to stir laughter and delight. Elsewhere in our catalog of men of letters, if I remember correctly, we called this kind of face a "lamia" <note>original: "lamiam." A mythical female demon or witch used in folklore to frighten children into obedience.</note>. 

He has small, very goat-like eyes <note>original: "hircissimis." From "hircus" (he-goat). In the pseudo-science of physiognomy, goat-like eyes were thought to indicate a lecherous or shameless character.</note>, walled in by eyelashes which he closes completely whenever he laughs or tries to look intently at something. His eyebrows are large, and his cheeks are rough. His forehead is narrow and furrowed. His jaw is full of wrinkles. His nose is leonine <note>lion-like</note> rather than aquiline <note>eagle-like</note>. He has a large mouth, thin lips, and small, blackish teeth. His brain labors within the narrowness of his temples; his ears are sharp, pointing in a direction contrary to the nature of all others. His chin hangs down slightly. His beard—unless he were to trim it quite often—is bushy and rough, and would occupy his entire face...

...appearing above a short, thin, tortoise-like neck. His voice is not at all unpleasant, though it echoes a certain barbaric Irish tongue <note>original: "Ibernicā... lingua." This likely mocks Corsi's accent or pronunciation by comparing it to a language the author considers "barbaric" or unintelligible.</note>, with an inexplicable native speed in reading or writing. His shoulders, thorax, and chest are compressed, and his arms are quite long; indeed, at dinner parties, according to the learned Collotius <note>Angelo Colocci (1474–1549), a prominent Roman humanist and patron of the arts.</note>, his arms and hands appear even longer. Being "ambidextrous" and "long-handed" <note>A common Latin metaphor for a thief or someone who is grabby.</note>, he pollutes, plunders, and engorges everything on all sides. For this reason, the most gracious Corytius <note>Johann Goritz (c. 1455–1527), a Luxembourgish cleric and patron in Rome, whose nickname "Corytius" was a reference to a character in Virgil.</note> once gave him the nickname "Sponge." 

His feet are both long and wide, which is why he is considered "Platonic"—not because of his philosophical studies (as he himself believes) nor because of his shoulders <note>A pun on the name of the philosopher Plato, which likely derived from the Greek "platys," meaning "broad." Tradition held that Plato was named for his broad shoulders; the author mocks Corsi by saying he is only "broad" in the feet.</note>. As for his member (if I may be pardoned the word), it is enormous, conspicuous, and lecherous. For its sake, certain "nymphs" (for this witty fellow is accustomed to calling his most filthy harlots by that name) compete daily in a rivalry of lust. They pull him about, tear at him, and beat him with sticks—him, the <note>original: "τῶν ἀνάνδρων πορνοβοσχὸν" / "tōn anandrōn pornoboschon."</note> pimp of unmanly men. He has no belly, no buttocks, and finally no body at all—or rather, he is the shadow of a lurid, scrawny, and useless body. 

However, he serves one purpose: with hands outstretched and his testicles exposed, tied to a tall pole, he is remarkably effective at turning away, terrifying, and putting to flight the hands and minds of the wicked and their rash insults from the Maecenatian—I nearly said Coloccian—gardens <note>Maecenas was the famous patron of Virgil and Horace. The "Coloccian gardens" refers to Angelo Colocci's famous estate, a hub for Roman humanists. The author is mocking Corsi by comparing him to a statue of Priapus, the god of fertility, which was used as a grotesque scarecrow in Roman gardens to ward off thieves.</note>. 

As for the "Inner Cursius"—although we lack a window into the human heart—his outward actions are crystal clear to even the most unrefined rustic, let alone to a learned <term>physiognomist</term> <note>original: "Metoposcopo." A practitioner of metoposcopy, the Renaissance "science" of judging a person's character or predicting their future by the lines on their forehead or facial features.</note>.

an undecided, or rather most precarious reputation, he chose to live with prostitutes rather than die—as an invalid (*for so he was accustomed to defend himself*)—under a parched sky at a master’s house. Colonna, Guido, Grimaldus <note>These names refer to prominent Roman families and figures who acted as patrons to humanists; the Colonna family was particularly influential.</note>, and other lords of every rank whom he served in an ungentlemanly manner are themselves witnesses to this. I shall pass over Rodolphus for now, whom no servant serves; he is like a dog barking for bread.

Why is it that Corsi <note>Pietro Corsi (Cursius), the target of this text's mockery.</note> maintains no friendships? Is it because he is deceived by all his friends? Or does he suspect he is being deceived? Or is it because he himself, due to his innate instability, is unable to love anyone steadfastly? Or is it because no vigor of virtue dwells within him? For friendship is born of virtue <note>This is a classic humanist sentiment, famously articulated in Cicero’s "On Friendship" (*De Amicitia*), which argues that true friendship cannot exist without virtue.</note>.

Why do all his friends strive to keep Corsi as their friend? Is it because they fear losing his learning and his most pleasant company? Or is it because everyone avoids taking on the "Corsian Principate"? <note>The author uses "Principatum Cursianum" to likely mock a leadership role or a specific "office" within their social or academic circle that was considered burdensome or ridiculous.</note> For it is recorded in the *Annals of the Roman Academy* <note>The Roman Academy (*Academia Romana*) was an influential group of humanists in Rome, often associated with Pomponio Leto. They were known for adopting classical names and celebrating ancient Roman rituals.</note> that whatever Academician shines with whatever dignity or wisdom—be he serious, self-controlled, or even peevish—if he should be appointed to the position of "Prince," <note>The "Princeps" was the titular head of the Roman Academy.</note> his nature is immediately transformed by some unknown fate, and he reveals himself to be a seeker of pleasure, a wit, and a clown.

Why is it that Corsi is called the "Hermes of Carpentras," <note>original: "Hermes Carpentanus." Hermes was the messenger god, associated with both eloquence and thievery/trickery. Carpentras is a city in Provence where Corsi had ties.</note> and though he has been made a Roman citizen, he nevertheless [has] no...

<meta>catchword: ever [unquam]</meta>

<summary>This page satirizes Pietro Corsi's inability to maintain stable employment or friendships, attributing his failures to a lack of virtue and innate instability. It also references a humorous tradition within the Roman Academy where its leaders supposedly undergo a personality shift toward the ridiculous upon taking office.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the satirical interrogation of Pietro Corsi's character, building on the previous page's discussion of his social instability and his failure to maintain professional or personal relationships. The text uses a rhetorical "question and answer" format common in humanist invective.</meta>

could he ever take on the customs of the city? Or is it because he judges those customs to be the worst, and regrets that he is a citizen? Or is it because he is unable to shed the harshness of his character—that mountain nature? <note>This likely refers to Corsi's origins in the mountainous region of the Apennines; the author suggests his "uncivilized" behavior is an inescapable product of his rustic birthplace.</note> For who can deny what nature has given?

Why is it that Corsi, even when only slightly angry, and without any regard for place, time, or person, opens up all the enclosures of secrets like the most gossiping of men? Is it because he follows a "natural liberty," which he boasts of professing, and would rather lose a friend than a witty remark? <note>original: "mauult perdere amicū quam dictum". This was a common reproach against satirists and wits who prioritized a clever joke over loyalty.</note> Or is it because, out of the perversity of his character and the vileness of his spirit and fortune, he defends himself with whatever vengeance he can? Or is it because mad drunkenness reveals the secret?

Why is it that Corsi appears to be a Madman <term>Maniacus</term> in all his actions? Is it because poets are always contemplating something and always talking to themselves? Or because they seem insane when they recite with some discomposed gesture of the body while people watch in wonder? Or is it because it is difficult to satisfy everyone? Or is it because no great genius exists without some mixture of madness? <note>A reference to the famous classical proverb attributed to Aristotle and Seneca: "nullum magnum ingenium sine mixtura dementiae fuit."</note>

Why is it that in a circle of good men, when Corsi is unknown—whether speaking, silent, or reciting—everyone admires him as a good, prudent, and learned man; but once he is known, they proclaim him evil, impudent, and unlearned? Is it because Corsi alone is a truly good man, while all the others are the worst?

<meta>This page continues the satirical interrogation of Pietro Corsi’s character, following the previous page's discussion of his social failures and volatile nature. The text employs the "Why is it...?" (Propter quid) rhetorical structure to mock Corsi’s public reputation and his intellectual vanity, specifically addressing his recent literary attack on Erasmus.</meta>

...or is it because all things are desired at first sight as if they were good, but once known, they are neglected like childish tricks?

Why is it that Corsi is called by everyone, not Pietro Corsi, but Peter the Fool? <note>original: "Petrus Stultus"</note> Is it because those who envy his learning, by mixing serious matters with jokes and follies, take everything in a bad way? Or is it because Corsi has always been, and always is, insane, and then he seems to have the least wisdom precisely when he seems to himself to have the most? Or is it that "the voice of the people is the voice of God"? <term>vox populi vox dei</term> For the people follow signs.

Why is it that when Corsi has written some bit of ignorance—as he recently did against you, Erasmus—he does not blush to shamelessly publish it immediately, having ignored the advice of good men? <note>In 1532, Pietro Corsi published a defense of Italy against Erasmus, who had criticized Italian Ciceronianism. The author here portrays the publication as a reckless act of ego.</note> Is it because this most boastful man loves his own works too much "without a rival," <note>original: "sine rivali." An allusion to the Roman poet Horace, referring to someone so blinded by self-love that they have no competition because no one else shares their high opinion.</note> and desires at last to spread from the city throughout the whole world? Or is it because, deceived by the appearance of what is right, like that owl of the fables, <note>original: "noctua illa apologica." A reference to Aesop’s fable where the owl describes her ugly chicks to the eagle as the most beautiful creatures in the world.</note> he awards the prize to his own children—that is, to his own compositions? Or is it because, led by greed and envy, he hopes for the greatest profit from them?

Why is it that Corsi thinks whatever is said, seen, or mocked by his friends—whether openly or secretly—is said, seen, or mocked in relation to himself? Is it because he recognizes that they want him to be mad, or because, being the most suspicious man by nature—which is to say, stupidity itself—he fears everything, even things not to be feared, and cannot be on his guard?

*And, wretch that I am, I suspect the truth is under the skin:* <note>original: "Et miser in tunica suspicor esse verum." A quote from the Roman satirist Persius (Satire 1.7). It suggests that despite outward appearances, the truth of a person's character or "illness" lies hidden just beneath their clothes/skin.</note>

The author characterizes Corsi as a man blinded by vanity, suspicious of his friends, and possessed by a "natural" stupidity.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the satirical critique of Pietro Corsi, shifting from the rhetorical "Why?" questions to a mock-philosophical explanation of his stupidity and a closing salutation from Rome. The text maintains the mocking tone established in the previous discussion of Corsi's public reputation.</meta>

Why is it that Corsi does not recognize himself to be a fool? And if he did recognize it, would he then be wise? Or is it because true knowledge of any matter—even of oneself—is not granted to mankind? For the mind follows the nature of its physical organ <note>The author refers to the brain as the "organic member" of the soul, a common Renaissance physiological concept where mental capacity was thought to depend on the physical health and balance of the brain.</note>, and since his is perceptibly corrupted, Pietro Corsi has fallen into the pit of folly. And if he ever seems to be wise, this happens not by nature, but by mere chance; this is evident because, being a fluke, it does not last long but vanishes instantly. Otherwise, one would have to admit that two contrary things <note>original: "duo contraria." In Aristotelian logic, two contraries (such as total wisdom and total folly) cannot exist in the same subject at the exact same time.</note> could exist simultaneously in the same time and place, which is impossible.

This little book says nothing more about Corsi. Therefore, lest I seem to be weaving a long history here, I too shall stop. You, however, should consult your local Luca <note>Likely referring to the famous artist Lucas Cranach the Elder, or perhaps another "Luca" known to the recipient, suggesting that Corsi’s character is so grotesque it requires a master’s hand to illustrate.</note> to see if he can produce a portrait of Corsi for you based on the physical traits and behaviors I have described, since he excels so much at his craft; if he cannot, let this writing serve in its place. Enjoy this until you come to Rome to know the man yourself.

->Farewell, and hold me dear, and<-
->if you desire anything else from here, write and<-
->command me. From the city, the 15th of August, <note>original: "18. Kalenda: septembris." In the Roman calendar, the 18th day before the Kalends of September corresponds to August 15th.</note><-
->in the year<-
->1536.<-
