<meta>This page continues the collection of Roman satires. While the previous page focused on a specific individual, Pietro Corsi, this page transitions to a series of "pasquinades"—anonymous satirical verses traditionally posted on the "Pasquino" statue in Rome. These short, biting epigrams use Biblical parody to mock the Pope and various high-ranking Cardinals of the Roman Curia in the year 1535.</meta>

# ROMAN PASQUILLUS published
# these jests <note>original: "Scommata." A term for a biting or mocking taunt.</note> on the eve of Epiphany,
# posted in Rome in the year
# 1535.

## AGAINST THE POPE

A little while and you will see me, and again a little while and you will not see me, because I go to the Father.
<note>original: "Modicum uidebitis me..." This is a quote from Jesus in John 16:16. In 1535, the Pope was Paul III (Alessandro Farnese). The satire likely mocks the Pope's age or his political evasiveness—implying he is either about to die or is rarely seen doing his duty.</note>

### Against the Cardinal of Siena

*You are the salt of the earth; with what shall it be salted?*
<note>original: "Vos estis sal terræ..." (Matthew 5:13). This refers to Francesco Bandini Piccolomini. The joke suggests that the Cardinal, meant to be the "salt" (wisdom/purity) of the world, has lost his flavor.</note>

### Against the Cardinal of Trani

*My father and my mother are for the worms; where then is my expectation?*
<note>original: "Pater meus & mater mea uermibus..." Paraphrasing Job 17:14-15. This target is Giovanni Domenico de Cupis. The quote mocks his family's mortality or perhaps his own lack of future prospects despite his high office.</note>

### Against the Cardinal of Cesi

*I am the wild vine, and my father is the farmer.*
<note>original: "Ego sum uitis fera..." A parody of John 15:1 ("I am the true vine"). By calling Paolo Emilio Cesi a "wild" or "savage" vine, the satirist portrays him as unrefined, unruly, or illegitimate compared to the "true vine" of Christ.</note>

### Against the Cardinal of Bari

*Now, Barabbas was a robber.*
<note>original: "Erat autem Barrabas latro" (John 18:40). This is a cutting wordplay on the name "Bari" (referring to Girolamo Grimaldi, the Cardinal of Bari). By linking the name of his see to the thief Barabbas released instead of Jesus, the author directly calls the Cardinal a criminal.</note>

### Against Campeggio

*Your children are like olive shoots around your table.*
<note>original: "Filij tui sicut nouellæ oliuarum..." (Psalm 128:3). This is a direct jab at Cardinal Lorenzo Campeggio. Before entering the priesthood, Campeggio had been married and had five children. While legal, the presence of his "olive shoots" (children) was a frequent target for satirists mocking the celibacy of the clergy.</note>

### Against Cardinal Ridolfi

*Lord, let me see.*
<note>original: "Domine fac ut uideam" (Luke 18:41). This refers to Niccolò Ridolfi. Using the plea of the blind man from the Gospel, the satirist suggests that Ridolfi is either physically or spiritually blind.</note>

<meta>This page continues the series of pasquinades—satirical epigrams posted on the Pasquino statue in Rome—dating to the Epiphany season of 1535. While the previous page targeted the Pope and the Cardinals of Siena, Trani, and Cesi, this page continues the list, applying Biblical and liturgical verses to other prominent members of the College of Cardinals to mock their character, physical appearance, or political ambitions.</meta>

## Against Cardinal Salviati
*Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men; grace is poured upon your lips.*
<note>original: "Speciosus forma præ filijs hominum..." from Psalm 45:2. This refers to Giovanni Salviati. The satire likely mocks his vanity or suggests that his influence comes from his appearance and charming speech rather than his merit.</note>

## Against the Cardinal of Santi Quattro
*A certain man was coming.*
<note>original: "Homo quidem ueniebat." A reference to Antonio Pucci, the Cardinal of the titular church of Santi Quattro Coronati. The phrase may allude to his arrival or a specific political move he was making at the time.</note>

## Against Cardinal Cibo
*Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell in unity.*
<note>original: "Ecce quàm bonum & quàm iocundum..." from Psalm 133:1. This targets Innocenzo Cybo. Given the family's reputation for nepotism and power-sharing, the verse sarcastically points to the Cybo family’s tight-knit and self-serving control of ecclesiastical offices.</note>

## Against Cardinal Pisano
*And you are one of them.*
<note>original: "Et tu ex illis es" (Matthew 26:73). Referring to Francesco Pisani. Much like the accusation leveled at Peter in the high priest's courtyard, the satirist identifies Pisani as a member of a specific, perhaps corrupt or conspiratorial, faction.</note>

## Against Cardinal Grimani
*Nason, moreover, begat Salmon.*
<note>original: "Naſon autem genuit salmon." A parody of the genealogy of Christ in Matthew 1:4. This is a pun on Marino Grimani’s physical appearance; "Naso" in Latin refers to a large nose, a feature the Grimani family was famously associated with in Roman satire.</note>

## Against Cardinal Cornaro
*You have satisfied your family, O Lord, with sacred gifts.*
<note>original: "Satiaſti domine familiam tuam..." Adapted from a liturgical prayer. This mocks Francesco Cornaro for using the wealth and "sacred gifts" of the Church to enrich his own family members.</note>

## Against Cardinal Trivulzio
*Behold the King shall come; let us run to meet our Savior.*
<note>original: "Ecce rex ueniet..." An Advent antiphon. Applied to Agostino Trivulzio, a powerful political player, it mocks his regal pretensions or his arrival in Rome as if he were a monarch.</note>

## Against the Cardinal of Mantua
*My tongue is the pen of a ready writer.*
<note>original: "Lingua mea calamus ſcribæ..." from Psalm 45:1. Ercole Gonzaga, the Cardinal of Mantua, was known for his diplomacy and education. The verse may mock his constant letter-writing or his perceived "slick" tongue in negotiations.</note>

## Against Cardinal Cesarini
*Burn our kidneys and our hearts with the fire of the Holy Spirit, O Lord, that we may serve you with a chaste body and please you with a clean heart.*
<note>original: "Vre Igne ſancti ſpiritus..." A standard prayer for clerical chastity. Used against Alessandro Cesarini, it is a biting accusation of his lack of chastity or his involvement in worldly pleasures.</note>

## Against Cardinal de' Medici
*I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered.*
<note>original: "Percutiam paſtorem..." (Matthew 26:31 / Zechariah 13:7). This refers to Ippolito de' Medici. Given that Ippolito died (possibly by poison) in 1535, this "prophecy" reflects the intense political instability following the decline of the Medici influence in Rome after the death of Pope Clement VII.</note>

## Against the Cardinal of Ravenna

*Go and sin no more.*
<note>original: "Vade & noli amplius peccare" (John 8:11). This concludes the satire against Cardinal Grimani from the previous page, perhaps suggesting his previous actions were sinful or that he has been given a second chance he doesn't deserve.</note>

## Against Cardinal de' Gaddi
*Your friends, O God, are exceedingly honored; their rule is exceedingly strengthened.*
<note>original: "Nimis honorati sunt amici tui deus, nimis confortatus est principatus eorum" (Psalm 138:17). This targets Niccolò Gaddi. The verse sarcastically points to the immense wealth and influence of Gaddi’s social circle and family connections in Rome.</note>

## Against Cardinal Grimaldi
*And the servants struck him with the palms of their hands.*
<note>original: "Et ministri alapis ipsum cædebant" (Mark 14:65). Referring to Girolamo Grimaldi. This is a pointed insult, suggesting either that the Cardinal had been physically humiliated or that he was so lowly that even servants could strike him.</note>

## Against the Cardinal of Santa Croce
*But I have prayed for you, that your faith fail not: and you, once you have turned back, strengthen your brothers.*
<note>original: "Ego autem rogaui pro te, ne deficiat fides tua: tu aut̃ aliquando conuersus confirma fratres tuos" (Luke 22:32). This refers to Francisco de los Ángeles Quiñones. As a key negotiator between the Pope and Emperor Charles V, the verse mocks his perceived wavering loyalty or the need for him to "convert" back to the Roman cause.</note>

## Against the Cardinal of Liège
*Like a lion seeking prey, he has devoured souls. A corrupt tree cannot bring forth good fruit.*
<note>original: "Sicut leo quærens prædam, animas deuorauit. Non potest arbor mala fructus bonos facere." A combination of Ezekiel 22:25 and Matthew 7:18. Targetting Erard de La Marck, known for his territorial power; the satirist paints him as a predator whose fundamental nature is "corrupt."</note>

## Against the Bolognese Cardinal
*Friend, how did you get in here without having a wedding garment?*
<note>original: "Amice quomodo huc intrasti, non habens uestẽ nuptialem?" (Matthew 22:12). Likely referring to Cardinal Lorenzo Campeggio, who was associated with Bologna. The "wedding garment" represents worthiness; the joke is that he is an interloper in the sacred college.</note>

## Against Cardinal Doria
*Get behind me, Satan.*
<note>original: "Vade retrò Satana" (Matthew 16:23). A blunt and severe condemnation of Girolamo Doria, casting him as an adversary or tempter.</note>

## Against Cardinal Palmieri
*Could you not watch one hour with me?*
<note>original: "Non potuisti una hora uigilare mecum?" (Matthew 26:40). Targets Andrea Matteo Palmieri. This suggests he was lazy, fell asleep at a crucial moment, or failed to support the Pope during a crisis.</note>

## Against the Cardinal of Germany
*They returned to their own country by another way.*
<note>original: "Per aliam uiam reuersi sunt in regionem suam" (Matthew 2:12). Referring to the German representatives. This alludes to the Magi, but here it mocks the German prelates for bypassing Rome or taking a different political/religious path (referencing the Reformation).</note>

## Against the Cardinals of Spain
*The scribes and the Pharisees have sat on the chair of Moses.*
<note>original: "Super cathedram Moysi sederunt scribæ & pharisæi" (Matthew 23:2). This accuses the Spanish faction in the church of being legalistic hypocrites who demand obedience to laws they themselves do not follow.</note>

## Against the Cardinals of France
*Do you not have houses to eat and drink in?*
<note>original: "Nunquid domi non habetis ad manducandum & bibendum?" (1 Corinthians 11:22). A jab at the French cardinals' reputation for excessive feasting and bringing secular gluttony into the church.</note>

# Praise the Lord, ye children: praise the name of the Lord
<note>original: "Laudate pueri Dominum, laudate nomen Domini" (Psalm 112:1). This heading sets an ironic liturgical tone for the insults that follow.</note>

## Against the College of Cardinals
*Beasts and all cattle of the field, serpents and feathered fowls.*
<note>original: "Bestiæ & uniuersa pecora campi, serpentes & uolucres pennatæ" (Psalm 148:10). This entry characterizes the gathered Cardinals not as holy men, but as a collection of mindless animals and creeping things.</note>

## Against the Emperor
*He shall bind their jaws with bit and bridle.*
<note>original: "In chamo & freno maxillas eorum constringet" (Psalm 31:9). This refers to Holy Roman Emperor Charles V. It suggests his heavy-handed nature in trying to control the unruly princes of Europe and the Church through force.</note>

## Against the King of the Romans
*Silver and gold have I none.*
<note>original: "Argentum & aurum non est mihi" (Acts 3:6). Referring to Ferdinand I, brother of Charles V. This is a sharp jab at Ferdinand's perpetual bankruptcy and his inability to fund his wars against the Ottoman Empire.</note>

## Against the King of France
*Are you he who is to come, or do we look for another?*
<note>original: "Tu es qui uenturus es, an alium expectamus?" (Matthew 11:3). Referring to Francis I. The verse mocks the King’s habit of making grand promises of military intervention or political alliances that he rarely fulfilled.</note>

## Against the Turk
*And they shall be two in one flesh.*
<note>original: "Et erunt duo in carne una" (Genesis 2:24). Referring to Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent. In the context of 1535, this likely mocks the "unholy" alliance between the Catholic King of France and the Muslim Sultan against the Emperor.</note>

## Against the King of England
*And in that day seven women shall take hold of one man,*
<note>original: "Et apprehenderunt septem mulieres uirum unum in die illo" (Isaiah 4:1). A direct mockery of Henry VIII and his scandalous pursuit of multiple wives and annulments following his break from Rome.</note>

## Against the King of Portugal
*My kingdom is not of this world.*
<note>original: "Regnum meum non est de hoc mundo" (John 18:36). Referring to John III. This suggests that the King of Portugal, while wealthy from overseas trade, had little relevance or "kingdom" within the actual political landscape of Europe.</note>

## Against the Duke of Savoy
*Come and behold the works of the Lord, what wonders he has wrought upon the earth.*
<note>original: "Venite & uidete opera domini, qui posuit prodigia super terram" (Psalm 45:9). Referring to Charles III, Duke of Savoy. This is likely sarcastic, referring to the "prodigious" destruction and loss of territory his duchy was suffering at the hands of the French and the Swiss.</note>

## Against the Duchess of Savoy
*The chalice which my father has given me, I must drink it.*
<note>original: "Calicẽ quem dedit mihi pater oportet ut bibã illũ" (John 18:11). Referring to Beatrice of Portugal. It frames her political misfortunes and the loss of her lands as a bitter cup of suffering she is forced to endure.</note>

## Against Don Antonio de Leyva
*They have hands, and they shall not feel; they have feet,*
<note>original: "Manus habent, & non palpabunt, pedes habent" (Psalm 113:7). Antonio de Leyva was a brilliant but infamously gouty Spanish general who had to be carried into battle on a chair because he could not use his hands or feet. The verse mocks his physical disability.</note>

### To Lord Don Fernando.
> This is my beloved son, in whom I am well pleased.
<note>original: "Hic est filius meus dilectus, in quo mihi cõplacuit" (Matthew 3:17). This likely refers to Ferrante (Don Fernando) Gonzaga, a loyal military commander for Emperor Charles V. The verse highlights his status as the Emperor's "favorite" instrument in Italy.</note>

### To the Count of Mirandola
> For you shall eat the labors of your hands; blessed are you, and it shall be well with you.
<note>original: "Labores manuum tuarum quia mandutabis, beatus es et bene tibi erit" (Psalm 128:2). Referring to Galeotto II Pico della Mirandola. The "labors of his hands" is a sarcastic reference to the bloody family feuds and assassinations he used to secure his rule over the small territory of Mirandola.</note>

### To the Archbishop of Milan:
> Verily I say to you, I have not found such great faith in Jerusalem.
<note>original: "Amen dico uobis, non inueni tantam fidem in Hierusalem" (Matthew 8:10). Referring to Giovannangelo Arcimboldi. This is a common satirical jab at Italian prelates, suggesting that "faith" is found everywhere except among the high-ranking clergy in the "Holy City" or their own dioceses.</note>

### To Lord Ieruello of Carpi
> Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom.
<note>original: "Memento mei domine, quãdo ueneris in regnũ tuũ" (Luke 23:42). The quote of the "Good Thief" on the cross. Applying this to a minor noble like Ieruello suggests he is either a criminal awaiting his end or someone desperately hoping for a political promotion that will never come.</note>

### Against the Duke of Urbino
> Be angry, and do not sin.
<note>original: "Irascimi et nollite peccare" (Psalm 4:4). Referring to Francesco Maria I della Rovere. The Duke was notorious for his violent temper; he famously murdered Cardinal Alidosi with his own hands. The verse "be angry but don't sin" is a direct mockery of his inability to control his rage.</note>

### To the Duchess
> Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb.
<note>original: "Benedicta tu in mulieribus et benedictus fructus uentris tui" (Luke 1:42). Referring to Eleonora Gonzaga. In the context of these pasquinades, using the "Hail Mary" often either mocks a Duchess's many children (the "fruit") or ironically comments on her husband's lack of virtues compared to her own.</note>

It highlights the political tensions and personal scandals of the Houses of Sforza, Este, and Della Rovere through sharp, ironic use of the Vulgate Bible.</summary>

> He shall break the bow and shatter the spears, and the shields he shall burn with fire.
<note>original: "Arcum conteret & confringet, arma & scut [scuta] conburet igni" (Psalm 46:9). Ascanio Colonna was a powerful Roman nobleman and military leader. The verse ironically suggests his military might will be neutralized or that his warlike nature is being mocked in the context of Roman power struggles.</note>

> My friends and my neighbors have drawn near.
<note>original: "Amici mei & proximi mei appropinquauerunt" (Psalm 38:11). This likely refers to a member of the influential Cesi family. The verse continues in the Bible with "and stood against me," implying that his social circle or family has turned into a source of trouble or betrayal.</note>

### To Lady Catherine
> I look for the resurrection of the flesh.
<note>original: "Expecto carnis resurrectionem" (from the Nicene Creed). This probably refers to Catherine de' Medici, then Duchess of Orleans. Given the "fleshly" double entendres common in pasquinades, this is likely a ribald joke about her marriage or her hopes for a pregnancy.</note>

### To the Venetians
> We have given our hands to Egypt and to the Assyrians, that we might be satisfied.
<note>original: "Egypto dedimus manus Assirijs, ut satiaremur" (Lamentations 5:6). This mocks the Republic of Venice's famously fluid diplomacy. In their efforts to be "satisfied" (to maintain their trade and territory), they were known for playing the Ottoman Turks (Egypt) against the Holy Roman Empire (Assyrians).</note>

### Against Molza
> How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?
<note>original: "Quomodo cantabimus canticum Domino in terra aliena" (Psalm 137:4). Francesco Maria Molza was a celebrated poet of the era. The verse suggests he is out of place at court, or perhaps mocks his frequent complaints about his personal or financial exile.</note>

### Against Mauro
> Every man is a liar.
<note>original: "Omnis homo mendax" (Psalm 116:11). Referring to Giovanni Mauro d'Arcano, a satirical poet and courtier. In a world of poets and diplomats, calling him a liar is both a common insult and a nod to his profession of "making things up."</note>

> The sinners have built upon my back.

By 1535, he was increasingly isolated and despised; the pasquinade mocks his desperation or perhaps his upcoming political downfall.</note>

# The Great Mystery of Inheritance
<note>original: "Magnum hereditatis miſterium." This title likely refers to a liturgical antiphon, here used ironically to frame the subsequent satires as a series of "revelations."</note>

## To the Duchess

> For he has regarded the lowliness of his handmaiden; for behold, from henceforth all generations shall call me blessed.
<note>original: "Quia reſpexit humilitatē ancillæ ſuæ, ecce enim ex hoc beatum me dicent omnes generationes" (Luke 1:48). These are the words of the Virgin Mary from the *Magnificat*. In this context, it likely mocks a Duchess—perhaps Margaret of Austria, who married Alessandro de' Medici in 1536—suggesting her "humility" is non-existent or her "blessed" status is purely political.</note>

## To the Marquess of Pescara

> That you would deign to lead us to true repentance, we beseech you, hear us.
<note>original: "Ut ad ueram pœnitentiā nos perducere digneris, te rogamus audi nos." A line from the Litany of Saints. It is applied here to the Marquess of Pescara (of the d'Avalos family), perhaps mocking his military severity or a need for penance for his family's shifting allegiances.</note>

## To the Marquess of Guasto

> We run in the fragrance of your ointments; the young maidens have loved you exceedingly.
<note>original: "In odore unguentorum tuorum currimus, adoleſcentulę dilexerunt te nimis" (Song of Solomon 1:3-4). Alfonso d'Avalos, the Marquess of Vasto (Guasto), was a famous imperial general known for his immense vanity, fine clothes, and use of perfumes. The verse mocks his reputation as a "dandy" soldier.</note>

## To Lady Julia Gonzaga

> And rising up, she went into the hill country with haste.
<note>original: "Et ſurgens abijt in montana cum feſtinatione" (Luke 1:39). This is a pointed reference to a famous 1534 event: the beautiful Julia Gonzaga had to flee in her nightgown to escape a kidnapping attempt by the pirate Barbarossa, who wanted to bring her to the Sultan. The "haste" here is literal and comedic.</note>

## To the Spanish Ambassador

> But I, like a deaf man, did not hear.
<note>original: "Ego autem tanquam ſurdus non audiebam" (Psalm 38:13). This mocks the Spanish ambassador's diplomatic tactic of feigning ignorance or refusing to listen to papal demands or complaints.</note>

## To the French Ambassador

> I came not to send peace, but hail.
<note>original: "Non ueni mittere pacem ſed grandinem." A parody of Matthew 10:34 ("not peace but a sword"). By substituting "hail" (grandinem) for "sword," the satirist likely refers to the destructive or "cold" influence of French policy on Italian stability.</note>

## To the Venetian Ambassador

> You have anointed my head with oil.
<note>original: "Impinguasti in oleo caput meum" (Psalm 23:5). This likely refers to the "greasing of palms" or the slick, polished diplomacy for which the Republic of Venice was famous.</note>

## To the Ambassador of Ferrara

> And opening their treasures, they offered gold, frankincense, and myrrh.
<note>original: "Et apertis theſauris ſuis attulerunt aurum, thus & myrrham" (Matthew 2:11). Referring to the gifts of the Magi, this suggests the Este family of Ferrara was buying favor at the papal court with literal treasures.</note>

## To the Ambassador of Urbino

> He who recently replied to the statement that the Duke favored the English: "You lie in your throat; is this how you answer the Pope?"
<note>original: "Is qui nuper reſpondit, ad hoc quod dicebatur Ducem fauere Anglis: Mentiris in collum, Sic reſpondes pontificis?" The phrase "Mentiris in collum" (literally "You lie in the neck") was a formal challenge to one's honor. This records a specific diplomatic spat where the Duke of Urbino's loyalty was questioned regarding the English Reformation or King Henry VIII's divorce.</note>

# Against the Milanese Ambassador
<note>original: "In Oratorem Mediolani." In the 16th century, an "Orator" was a formal term for an ambassador. Milan was a central flashpoint in the wars between France and the Holy Roman Empire; the death of Duke Francesco II Sforza in 1535 left the city in a state of political flux.</note>

> For forty years I was near to this generation, and I said always: These wander in their heart.
<note>original: "Quadraginta annis proximus fui generationi huic, & dixi semper, Hi errant corde" (Psalm 95:10). This suggests a long-standing weariness with the perceived deceit or instability of Milanese diplomacy during the Italian Wars.</note>

## Against the Roman People
<note>original: "In Pop. Rom." (In Populum Romanum).</note>

> Put your sword into its sheath.
<note>original: "Pone gladium in uaginam" (John 18:11). These are the words of Christ to Peter. In this context, it likely refers to the chronic violence and unrest among the Roman citizenry, or perhaps a specific papal decree to disarm the populace.</note>

# To Curzio, the Pope’s Physician
<note>original: "Ad Curtiū Medicū pontificis." Curzio dei Franchi was a physician to Pope Paul III. Satires against doctors were common, often implying that their "cures" were as dangerous as the diseases.</note>

> Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world.
<note>original: "Ecce agnus Dei qui tollis peccata mundi" (John 1:29). This is a highly irreverent use of a central liturgical prayer. Applied to a doctor, it suggests he "takes away" the patients (by killing them) or that he is tasked with cleaning up the physical consequences of the Pope's "sins" or excesses.</note>

## Against the Cardinal's Household
<note>original: "In familiam Card." (In familiam Cardinalium).</note>

> Be sober and keep watch.
<note>original: "Sobrij estote & uigilate" (1 Peter 5:8). This scriptural warning against the devil is turned into a joke about the notoriously debauched, drunken, and negligent behavior of the large retinues that served the Roman Cardinals.</note>

# ON PASQUINO
<note>original: "IN PASQVILLVM." Pasquino (Pasquillus) is the name given to a weathered Hellenistic statue near the Piazza Navona where Romans posted anonymous satirical poems or "pasquinades."</note>

> If I tell you the truth, why do you not believe me?
<note>original: "Si ueritatem dico uobis, quare non creditis mihi?" (John 8:46). Here, the "talking statue" of Pasquino adopts the words of Christ to defend his reputation for telling the bitter, unvarnished truth about Roman society and the corruption of the clergy.</note>

<summary>This page contains a series of satirical epigrams (pasquinades) that use biblical verses to mock the Milanese ambassador, the Roman public, the Pope's physician, and the loose morals of the Cardinals' servants.</summary>

# OF ITALIAN MATTERS
## A Dialogue.

### THE SPEAKERS.

->Mercury. Pasquil.<-

**Mercury.** Greetings to you, O Pasquil!
<note>Pasquil (or Pasquino) is the famous "talking statue" of Rome, a battered Hellenistic fragment upon which citizens posted anonymous satirical poems, known as pasquinades.</note>

**PASQUIL.** And the same greeting to you, my winged **Cyllenian**.
<note>original: "Cylleni." An epithet for Mercury, who was said to be born on Mount Cyllene.</note>

**MERCURY.** May the gods avert such an omen far from my head!

**PASQUIL.** What omen?

**MERCURY.** A "health" similar to yours.
<note>Mercury is joking about Pasquil’s physical state; as a mutilated ancient statue, Pasquil is missing limbs and facial features. To have "health like Pasquil" would be a curse.</note>

**PASQUIL.** Why so?

**MERCURY.** Because, although you are so beautifully decorated today by the Roman people, there is no reason for you to boast of this distinguished finery for long.

**PASQUIL.** Why not?

**MERCURY.** Boys will strip you of it soon enough; and the sun will have scarcely turned its course toward the ocean before you are naked, a mere stump, and mutilated, just as you have always been.
<note>On the feast of St. Mark (April 25), the statue of Pasquin was traditionally dressed up as a mythological or historical figure, and the pedestal was covered in poems. By nightfall, these were often torn down or confiscated.</note>

**PASQUIL.** This is indeed my immortality, and it is what has made me equal to you heavenly beings—or even superior in this one regard: that in these few short hours, I am more formidable to all mortals than the rest of the gods, even if **Jupiter** were to flash his thunderbolts at them today.
<note>Pasquil claims that his satirical "voice" (the poems) is more feared by the powerful men of Rome than divine retribution.</note>

**MERCURY.** By Hercules, that is exactly what I came to see.

**PASQUIL.** I thank you, O

Cerberus: but for those offering gold, did it ultimately profit them to have entered? 
**MERCURY.** Just the same as if they had not entered. 
**PASQUIL.** Ah. 
**MERCURY.** Pluto receives those approaching only with kind words, but afterwards he sends them all back to the judges. 
**PASQUIL.** Who are they? 
**MERCURY.** Those who are moved neither by justice nor softened by prayers. 
**PASQUIL.** Who, then? 
**MERCURY.** **Cobos**, **Granvelle**, and **Mai**.
<note>These are high-ranking officials of Holy Roman Emperor Charles V: Francisco de los Cobos, Nicolas Perrenot de Granvelle, and Miguel Mai. The author is satirically casting these powerful bureaucrats as the heartless judges of the dead.</note> 
**PASQUIL.** Oh, what barbaric names! 
**MERCURY.** Nay, truly hellish; these names alone are sufficiently atrocious to torture wretched men. 
**PASQUIL.** What other punishment do they inflict upon the guilty? 
**MERCURY.** Both the guilty and the innocent are punished with the same exhaustion of endless delay. 
**PASQUIL.** In what way? 
**MERCURY.** The judges withdraw into a hidden inner chamber with the doors closed and guards posted so that no one is allowed to approach. 
**PASQUIL.** It is hard to do business with those who are unwilling. 
**MERCURY.** But harder still with **Cobos**, in whose hands is the supreme power. 
**PASQUIL.** This man seems to be **Chaos**, not **Cobos**. 
<note>original: "chaos uidetur hic, non Couos." A pun on the name of the Imperial secretary and the Greek 'Chaos,' the formless void.</note>
But if this <term>Cocytian</term> mole should ever emerge from the darkness for lunch or dinner, is it not then permitted for everyone to meet him and for each to deliver a brief little speech on his own behalf?
<note>Cocytian refers to Cocytus, the "river of wailing" in the Greek Underworld. Calling the official a "mole" suggests he hides from the public in his office.</note>

...commanded with a loud voice that everyone should go outside, and that none of those present should hope to be heard by **Cobos**, who was already hurrying to lunch—an office and a voice indeed unworthy of such a prince. 

**PASQUIL.** Do not attack Prince Ferdinand <note>Ferdinand I (1503–1564), brother of Charles V and later Holy Roman Emperor.</note> with insults, my Mercury; for he is a faithful lover, a generous man, and a youth of great promise. **MERCURY.** They only hold out humble petitions, which in the Neapolitan tongue they call *memorials* <note>original: "memoriales"; these were formal written petitions or dossiers requesting favors or payment for services.</note>, in which are noted their merits and the sequence of services they have performed for **Caesar** <note>A common title for the Holy Roman Emperor, Charles V.</note>. **PASQUIL.** What then?

**MERCURY.** From there, one hears the groans, complaints, lamentations, and the unspeakable tortures of an infinite number of people.

**PASQUIL.** In what way?

**MERCURY.** By their decrees, they despoil some of their fortunes, and they deny others the right to return to their fatherland; they remove some from magistracies and public offices, while others they drive to the very edge of despair by delaying their rewards. They commit other such acts against all piety and justice. But when these men realize they have been cheated of the justice they have long expected or the reward they have earned—as the human race is by nature fragile and impatient—they cry out and are struck by an incomprehensible grief of soul, especially those...

...who are unable to turn elsewhere, since they have consumed everything they had in this hope, and have slipped from youth into old age.

**PASQUIL.** I pity all of them, but I pity **Caesar** <note>A common title for the Holy Roman Emperor, Charles V.</note> alone even more, for granting so much power to such foolish judges.

**MERCURY.** He does not merely grant it; he plainly obeys them in everything.

**PASQUIL.** O, happy prince!

**MERCURY.** O, most happy, O, most fortunate!

**PASQUIL.** For what reason?

**MERCURY.** Because, no matter how much the councillors <note>original: "consiliarij"; the advisors of the imperial court.</note> strive with perverse minds to throw everything into ruin, fortune nonetheless—by some unhoped-for and incredible, almost divine outcome—turns things out well for Caesar.

**PASQUIL.** You know best, **Son of Atlas** <note>original: "Atlantiades"; a poetic title for Mercury, the grandson of Atlas.</note>, how unstable and fickle fortune is for all people, and especially for kings who seem to place all their trust in it. But tell me, do they also decide upon great matters?

**MERCURY.** So it is; they decide upon the greatest matters, even concerning the administration of the empire of the earth.

**PASQUIL.** I marvel that such grave affairs are conducted according to their whim.

**MERCURY.** Not only theirs, but others' as well.

**PASQUIL.** Such a great burden could not have been sustained by the weak strength of a few men; yet I suppose that many learned and wise men flourish there, whom they might consult, as is fitting for a most powerful prince who hungers for the monarchy of **Europe**.

**MERCURY.** They banish learned and wise men far from their company and their sight, as if they were a pestilential and wicked race of humans. I have heard, O Pasquil, whether...

<summary>Mercury explains that Emperor Charles V is entirely beholden to his foolish advisors, though blind luck continues to save the empire from their poor decisions. He reveals that the court intentionally excludes wise and learned men from the administration.</summary>

--- Page 479 ---
<meta>This page continues the satirical dialogue between Pasquillus and Mercury. The previous page concluded with Mercury explaining that the Imperial court banishes wise men from their sight.</meta>

*...with his own ears, he heard **Granvelle** <note>Nicolas Perrenot de Granvelle (1484–1550), the influential chief advisor to Holy Roman Emperor Charles V.</note>, without a blush and quite openly, say that a learned man cannot live in the court of **Caesar** <note>A title used here for Emperor Charles V.</note>.*

**PASQUILL.** For what reason?

**MERCURY.** He used to say they were not esteemed, and for that reason, they were not fed <note>original: "pasci"; here meaning supported by financial patronage.</note> by Caesar.

**PASQUILL.** Yet the ignorant, the jesters, and the fools are not only fed, but even enriched in Caesar’s court; for that reason, I hear that flocks of them fly there from every direction.

**MERCURY.** They favor such men because they are pleasing to their lord, and because they themselves delight in their witty banter <note>original: "dicacitate"</note> among prostitutes and at banquets.

**PASQUILL.** I understand that this laughable sort of men carries away gifts from that place that would be sufficient to maintain an army.

**MERCURY.** Especially those gifts which **Alfonso d'Avalos** <note>Alfonso d'Avalos (1502–1546), the Marquis del Vasto, a celebrated Italian general for the Empire.</note> recently gave of his own accord to one of them in **Mantua** <note>A city-state in Northern Italy.</note>, of a value scarcely believable, while at his own home, noble men of letters and the fiercest soldiers—whose service he had used in peace and war—were perishing from hunger.

**PASQUILL.** The neglect of good men is a common failing among princes. But we shall speak of this another time; for now, tell me whose counsel the judges follow, as you said.

**MERCURY.** They follow the counsel of Greed, Lust, Ambition, Favor, and Hatred.

**PASQUILL.** They are corrupted by gold, then, like **Simonetta** <note>Likely Giacomo Simonetta (c. 1475–1539), a cardinal and legal expert known for his role in imperial and papal diplomacy.</note>.

Do not believe they fished out that money through the Duke's favor or any reason other than the weariness caused by their own persistence <note>original: "importunitatis tedio"; suggesting they got the money by being annoying rather than through merit</note>. **MERCURY:** What

The dialogue also touches on the opportunistic nature of imperial payouts to German mercenaries and the House of Este.</summary>

...with the treasury worn down and long since exhausted, not even a horse-penny <note>original: "obolum caballinum"; a Neapolitan idiom for a coin of very little value</note>, as they say in Naples, could be paid to him. **MERCURY:** Rightly so then, that old man Pignalosa <note>likely referring to a specific official or treasurer of the time</note>. **PASQUILLUS:** What of him? **MERCURY:** He refused the assignment of funds made in that treasury—funds which he had produced from his own pocket to transport soldiers across the Rhine rivers to Vienna. And because of this, he departed not only unrewarded but actually robbed of his own money. **PASQUILLUS:** And you know, oh **Mercury**, that during that most dangerous undertaking, this old man performed the duty of **Charon** <note>the mythological ferryman who carried souls across the river Styx; here implying he managed the dangerous river transport of the army</note>. **MERCURY:** The memory of **Charon** reminds me, oh **Pasquillus**: I must hasten to **Jupiter** from this Ligurian <note>referring to the region of Genoa and the surrounding coast</note> embassy, and I must row back to those banks as quickly as possible, where souls await me to be transported into that milder **Erebus** <term>the underworld [hærebum]: in Greek mythology, a place of darkness between Earth and Hades</term>. **PASQUILLUS:** But when you have found some leisure, oh **Mercury**, return so that we may talk about these things more at length. **MERCURY:** Expect me after the distribution at Barcelona <note>original: "Barchinonensem"; referring to the Emperor Charles V's court and the distribution of rewards or honors there</note>, and farewell. **PASQUILLUS:** But wait! Put back those writing tablets! Oh, you most fierce one, give back my epigram! Where are you fleeing? He is a thief in his departure, and thus he has testified to the "friendship" of the Spaniards, who always steal something when they leave.

# PASQUILLIC TAUNTS OF THE YEAR A.D. 1537.

## POPE PAUL TO CAESAR.

Whatever great things you did at Bologna with Clement, do also with us here in your homeland.
<note>Pope Paul III refers to the historic 1530 meeting in Bologna where Emperor Charles V (Caesar) and the previous Pope, Clement VII, reached an agreement to settle the power structure of Italy.</note>

### Caesar to Paul.

For no prophet is accepted in his own country.
<note>original: "Nemo enim propheta acceptus est in patria sua"; a quote from the Gospel of Luke 4:24. Charles V is wryly responding to the Pope calling Italy the Emperor's "homeland."</note>

### Paul to Caesar.

Do not doubt; see to it that my grandsons sit—one at the right hand in Florence, the other at the left in Novara—and all things shall be added unto you.
<note>original: "nepotes"; this can mean nephews or grandsons. Paul III was famously devoted to the advancement of his Farnese kin. Here, the author parodies the Gospel of Matthew, where the mother of the sons of Zebedee asks for her sons to sit at Jesus's right and left hands.</note>

### Caesar to Paul.

It is not right to take the children’s bread and give it to the dogs. The voice is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau; yet I will do according to your faith and the necessity of the time.
<note>Charles V counters with more biblical references. He implies the Pope is like Jacob in the Book of Genesis—using the "voice" of a holy man to disguise the grasping "hands" of a hunter.</note>

### Paul to Alessandro Vitelli.

Come out, you unclean spirit, from the citadel of Florence, and give honor and liberty to this people. Look upon the city of Castello, Urbino, and the Duchy of Camerino; all these things I will give to you, if upon leaving you restore that city to us and not to Caesar.
<note>Alessandro Vitelli was a mercenary commander who seized the Florentine fortress after the Duke's assassination. The Pope’s speech begins by mimicking Christ exorcising a demon, but ends by mimicking the Devil tempting Christ in the wilderness by offering him worldly kingdoms.</note>

<meta>catchword: Alexander</meta>

<summary>This page features a series of satirical dialogues ("Pasquinades") using biblical parodies to mock the political negotiations between Pope Paul III and Emperor Charles V over the control of Florence and Novara.</summary>
<keywords>Pasquillus, Pope Paul III, Emperor Charles V, Alessandro Vitelli, Florence, Novara, Satire, Nepotism, Italian Wars</keywords>

## Alessandro to Paul.
<note>Alessandro de' Medici, the murdered Duke of Florence, speaks from the afterlife or as a ghost in this satirical dialogue.</note>

These favors are under dispute; being faithful, I render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s.
<note>original: "reddo quæ ſunt Cæſaris, Cæſari"; a reference to Matthew 22:21. Alessandro remained loyal to Emperor Charles V (Caesar) even in death, refusing the Pope's influence over Florence.</note>

## Paul to Cardinal Cibo.
<note>Pope Paul III addresses Cardinal Innocenzo Cibo, who held the fortress of Florence after the Duke's murder and was a key power broker.</note>

You also are one of them; behold, the legations of Bologna and Ancona are in your hand, if you, having been converted, return to me and to the King.
<note>The Pope is attempting to bribe Cibo with lucrative administrative posts (legations) in exchange for shifting his loyalty from the Emperor to the Papacy and the King of France.</note>

## The Cardinal to Paul.

Let your legations and provisions be your own support; we have no king but Caesar.
<note>original: "non habemus Regem niſi Cæſarem"; a mocking use of the words of the chief priests in John 19:15. Cibo rejects the Pope's bribe, maintaining his Imperial allegiance.</note>

## Paul to the people of Florence.

O senseless and foolish ones, return to your former liberty; there is no good without it.
<note>The Pope appeals to the Republican tradition of Florence, hoping they will reject the Medici dynasty (and by extension, Imperial control) and return to a Republic that he can more easily influence.</note>

## The People of Florence to Paul.

The yoke of Caesar is sweet, and his burden is light; would that it endure forever.
<note>original: "Iugum Cæſaris ſuaue est, & onus ſuum leue"; a parody of Matthew 11:30. The "People" (representing the ruling pro-Medici faction) sarcastically claim they prefer the "yoke" of the Emperor over the "liberty" offered by the Pope.</note>

## Paul to Cosimo de' Medici.
<note>Cosimo I de' Medici, then a young man, was chosen to succeed Alessandro. The Pope opposed his rise.</note>

It is not lawful for you to take the Duchy and your brother's wife, nor to exercise his tyranny.
<note>original: "Non licet tibi..."; a reference to John the Baptist's rebuke of Herod in Mark 6:18. Alessandro's widow was Margaret of Austria, the Emperor's daughter. The Pope argues that Cosimo has no legal right to Alessandro's titles or his widow.</note>

## Cosimo to Paul.

The Lord gave the Duchy, Caesar will give the wife; I will do whatever pleases Caesar.
<note>original: "Dominus dedit... Cæſari placuerit"; a play on Job 1:21. Cosimo asserts his power comes from God and the Emperor, dismissing the Pope's authority.</note>

## The College of Cardinals to 
## the King of France.

How long will you take away our souls? Behold, the whole world...
<note>original: "Quouſq; animas noſtras tollis"; based on John 10:24. The Cardinals are likely complaining about the political instability caused by the rivalry between the French King and the Emperor.</note>

<summary>This page contains a series of satirical "Pasquillades" in which Pope Paul III attempts to exert influence over Florence following Duke Alessandro's death, only to be rebuffed by the Imperial party and the new Duke, Cosimo I.</summary>
<keywords>Pope Paul III, Cosimo de' Medici, Cardinal Cibo, Florence, Imperial-Papal rivalry, Pasquinade, Charles V, political satire</keywords>

--- Page 506 ---
<meta>This page continues the satirical dialogue following the assassination of Alessandro de' Medici in 1537. The previous page featured Pope Paul III and Cardinal Cibo debating the fate of Florence and their loyalty to the Emperor (Caesar).</meta>

<page-num>356</page-num>

Has he gone after Caesar? Are you the one who is to come, or do we look for Suleiman or Barbarossa? Come to deliver us, Lord, King of virtues; if not, we shall perish in the Council.
<note>This passage parodies the Gospel of Matthew 11:3 ("Are you the one who is to come?"). The "Council" refers to the long-delayed Council of Trent, which many high-ranking clergy feared would strip them of their power and wealth. Suleiman the Magnificent and the pirate-admiral Barbarossa represent the Ottoman threat, which some European powers—scandalously—viewed as a potential ally against the Holy Roman Emperor.</note>

### The King to the Cardinals.
<note>Likely Francis I of France, who was a chief rival to the Emperor and often sought to influence the College of Cardinals.</note>

You of little faith, why do you doubt? Suleiman and we will come, and you will be safe.
<note>original: "Modicæ fidei, quare dubitatis?"; a quote from Matthew 14:31. The satire mocks the French King's willingness to ally with the Turks to protect his interests in Italy.</note>

### The College to the Venetians:
<note>The "College" refers to the College of Cardinals. The Republic of Venice was a crucial maritime power that often tried to remain neutral in the struggle between the Pope, France, and the Empire.</note>

And you, be ready for our assistance, for you know neither the day nor the hour.
<note>original: "nō enim scitis diem neq; horam"; a reference to the Parable of the Ten Virgins in Matthew 25:13. The Cardinals are pressuring Venice to be ready for war or political upheaval.</note>

### The Venetians to the same.

Distresses hold us, but our soul is still in our body; we shall not fail.
<note>A reflection of Venice's resilient but precarious position, caught between the Ottoman navy and European land wars.</note>

### The Cardinals to the King of the Romans.
<note>Ferdinand I, the brother of Emperor Charles V, who held the title "King of the Romans" and was the primary defender of the Habsburg interests in Central Europe.</note>

What have we to do with you, our King? Have you come to destroy us? Behold, we leave all our vices for the sake of the Council; what will there be for us?
<note>The Cardinals mockingly use the words of the demons to Jesus in Mark 1:24 ("Have you come to destroy us?") and Peter's question in Matthew 19:27 ("Behold, we have left all... what then shall we have?"). They sarcastically claim that Church reform—the goal of the Council—is a form of destruction.</note>

### The King of the Romans to the Cardinals.

According to your thoughts, you will receive a hundredfold for every one, and perhaps you will lay aside the Cardinal’s hat forever.
<note>original: "Capellum dimittetis." Ferdinand warns that the reform Council might not reward them with spiritual riches, but might instead result in them losing their prestigious positions (represented by the red hat) entirely.</note>

### Paul and the College to the King of the Turks.
<note>Pope Paul III and the Cardinals addressing Sultan Suleiman.</note>

Get behind me, Satan; do not approach us, nor our borders.
<note>original: "Vade retro Sathana"; the famous rebuke of Jesus to Peter/Satan. Despite the satirical hints of alliance earlier, the Pope officially maintains his role as the defender of Christendom against the "infidel."</note>

It highlights the tension between the Papacy, the Holy Roman Empire, France, Venice, and the Ottoman Empire in the mid-16th century.</summary>

## The King of the Turks to the same
<note>The "same" refers to the Cardinals mentioned on the previous page. "King of the Turks" refers to Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent.</note>

I shall descend into Italy, and upon the city of Rome and your house, I shall build my own.
<note>original: "super Rom. urbem & domum uestram ædificabo meam." This is a dark parody of Matthew 16:18, where Christ says, "on this rock I will build my church." Here, the Sultan threatens to replace the Church with his own rule.</note>

## Paul to the College of Cardinals
<note>Pope Paul III (reigned 1534–1549).</note>

This is a hard saying, and who can be saved in Rome?
<note>original: "Durus est hic sermo, Et quis poterit saluus fieri Romæ." The first part quotes John 6:60, and the second parodies Matthew 19:25. The Pope is depicted as despairing over the Ottoman threat.</note>

## The College to Paul

We shall flee to Perugia.
<note>Perugia was a major city within the Papal States and served as a secondary stronghold for the papacy when Rome was under threat.</note>

## The King of France to the King of the Turks
<note>Francis I of France, who famously (and controversially) formed a "Franco-Ottoman alliance" against Holy Roman Emperor Charles V.</note>

Go forth from your land and your kin, and come into Hungary, Sicily, and Naples, the land which I shall show you, flowing with milk and honey; do not fear, for I will be with you. Come in the strength of your arm. Once the war in Flanders is finished, I too shall come; we shall be one flock. You shall take the Eastern part, and you shall leave the Western part to me. Hasten to my aid.
<note>This passage is a dense web of biblical parodies: the call of Abraham (Genesis 12:1), the promise of the Holy Land (Exodus 3:8), and Christ as the Good Shepherd (John 10:16). The satire suggests that the French King is acting as a "false god" to the Sultan, offering him Christian lands in exchange for a partition of the world.</note>

## The King of France to the Venetians

No one can serve two masters.
<note>original: "Nemo potest duobus dominis seruire"; a quote from Matthew 6:24. The King is pressuring Venice to choose between France and the Holy Roman Empire.</note>

## The Venetians to the King

Lord King, we follow from afar; do not uncover our will. We have given our hand to Egypt and the Assyrians.
<note>The phrase "follow from afar" (Matthew 26:58) refers to Peter's hesitation during the Passion. "Giving the hand to Egypt and the Assyrians" (Lamentations 5:6) implies making shameful alliances with pagans for the sake of survival or profit, reflecting Venice's reputation for prioritizing trade with the East over crusading ideals.</note>

## France to the King of the Romans
<note>"France" refers to the French interest or the King. The "King of the Romans" was Ferdinand I, the brother of Emperor Charles V and the ruler of the Habsburg Austrian territories.</note>

Do not touch my anointed ones in the Council, for they are entering into a pact with us.
<note>original: "Noli tangere Christos meos"; a quote from Psalm 105:15. In this context, it refers to the French bishops and representatives at the Council of Trent, whom the King of France protects to maintain his political influence over church reform.</note>

### The King of the Romans to the King of France
<note>The "King of the Romans" refers to Ferdinand I, the brother of Emperor Charles V and the heir to the Holy Roman Empire. He addresses Francis I of France.</note>
*Your own speech has made you manifest; with bit and bridle, I will bind your jaws and the jaws of your allies.*
<note>original: "Loquela tua manifestum te fecit, in chamo & freno, maxillas tuas & illorum constringam." This is a biting blend of Matthew 26:73 (where Peter is recognized by his accent) and Psalm 32:9, treating the French King like an unruly beast that must be restrained.</note>

### The King of France to Italy.
*Rejoice, daughter of Jerusalem: Francis your King and Suleiman of the Turks come to you, riding upon Naples and Sicily.*
<note>original: "Lætare filia Hierusalem, Franciscus Rex tuus & Solyman Turcarum, ueniunt tibi sedentes super Neapolim & Siciliam." A scandalous parody of the prophecy in Zechariah 9:9 regarding Christ's entry into Jerusalem. It mocks the controversial "unholy alliance" between the Christian King of France and the Ottoman Sultan against the Habsburgs.</note>

### Italy to the King.
*A ruinous visitation is upon our necks; visit the Spains instead. The past evils we have endured because of you are enough; therefore, we appeal to Caesar.*
<note>original: "Pernitiosa uisitatio super ceruicibus nostris... ad Cæsarem appellamus." Italy rejects the French-Ottoman "liberation," preferring the rule of the Emperor (Caesar). The phrase "I appeal to Caesar" references St. Paul's legal appeal in Acts 25:11.</note>

### The King of France to Caesar.
*But Caesar [said] nothing.*
<note>original: "Cæsar autem nihil." This likely parodies "Jesus autem tacebat" (But Jesus remained silent) from the Passion narrative, suggesting the Emperor’s stoic or dismissive response to French provocations.</note>

### Caesar to the King of France.
<note>"Caesar" refers to the Holy Roman Emperor, Charles V.</note>
*You are insane; you shall worship the Lord your God, and me alone shall you serve.*
<note>original: "Insanis, Dominum Deum tuum adorabis, & mihi soli seruies." A subversion of Matthew 4:10. Where the Gospel says "Him only shalt thou serve" (referring to God), Charles V is depicted here as demanding that service for himself.</note>

### Caesar to the King of the Turks.
*With great desire I have desired to fight with you before I suffer.*
<note>original: "Desiderio desideraui pugnare uobiscum antequam patiar." A parody of Christ's words at the Last Supper (Luke 22:15: "With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer"). It frames the conflict with the Ottoman Empire as the Emperor's ultimate trial.</note>

### The Same [Caesar].
*Either you or I shall be Caesar.*

### Caesar to the Venetians.
*If you persevere until the end, you shall be saved.*
<note>original: "Si perseuerabitis usq; ad finem, salui eritis." A parody of Matthew 24:13. Charles V urges the Republic of Venice to remain loyal to his cause against the Turks and the French.</note>

We shall be as we were in the beginning, now and always, and for ages of ages. 
<note>original: "Erimus sicut eramus in principio, nunc & semper. Et in secula seculorum." This is a parody of the *Gloria Patri* (Glory be to the Father...), a standard conclusion to many Catholic prayers. Here, it suggests a return to a former political status quo.</note>

## Caesar to Italy
<note>"Caesar" refers to the Holy Roman Emperor, Charles V.</note>

Caesar does not close his bosom to those who return to him in humility.

## Italy to Caesar

A contrite and humbled heart, O Caesar, you will not despise.
<note>original: "Cor contritum & humiliatum Caesar non despicies." A parody of Psalm 51:17, replacing "God" with "Caesar." It depicts Italy's submission to the Emperor's authority after the devastation of the Italian Wars.</note>

## Paul to Caesar
<note>"Paul" refers to Pope Paul III (reigned 1534–1549), who often had a tense relationship with Charles V over the control of the church and Italian territories.</note>

Remember not, Lord, our former iniquities.
<note>original: "Ne memineris domine iniquitatum nostrarum antiquarum." A parody of Psalm 79:8, used in the Litany of Saints. The Pope is cast in the role of a repentant sinner pleading with the Emperor.</note>

## Caesar to Paul

Remember that you are dust, and to dust you shall return; help us, and you shall say: The snare of the <term>Gaul</term> is broken, and we have been delivered.
<note>original: "Memento quia cinis es... Laqueus Galli contritus est." Caesar uses the somber words of the Ash Wednesday liturgy to remind the Pope of his mortality. The second half parodies Psalm 124:7, using a clever pun: "Galli" in Latin means both "the Frenchman" and "the rooster." It celebrates the breaking of French influence over the papacy.</note>

## Paul to Caesar

Set before me a law, O Lord, the way of your justifications.
<note>original: "Legem pone mihi domine uiam iustificationum tuarum." A parody of Psalm 119:33. In this satirical context, the Pope asks the Emperor to dictate the legal and political path he should follow.</note>

# PASQUILL’S DIALOGUE ON THE COUN-
## cil of Mantua.

->A German. Pasquill.<-

GERMAN. *Hey, Pasquill! Where are you rushing to? Why such haste? What are you muttering to yourself?* PASQUILL. *I think nothing of sanity is left in this City. The Pope is raving. The College of Cardinals is insane. The Bishops are suffering from mania. The priests are struck with madness and folly. The Monks need hellebore.* <note>original: "Elleboro egent Monachi." Hellebore was a plant used in classical medicine as a treatment for madness and melancholy.</note> *In short, that whole herd which follows the Pope's command is mad.* GERMAN. *Hey, I say, Pasquill! Do you hear me? Or are you deaf?* PASQUILL. *Who is calling me?* GERMAN. *It is I calling you.* PASQUILL. *Oh, German! Were you present here? I certainly had not seen you.* GERMAN. *I believe it; but why are you so annoyed with yourself? You seem angrier to me than you usually are.* PASQUILL. *I am annoyed. For why should I deny what is most true? It is for the most just reasons; indeed, I am about to depart from here very soon.* GERMAN. *Why is that?* PASQUILL. *Because of the madness of the <term>Curia</term>,* <note>The administrative and governing body of the Roman Catholic Church.</note> *which I could perhaps endure if it were not joined with the greatest malice.* GERMAN. *But I do not think you can ever truly desert Rome. For even if you were to leave with a firm mind, I do not know if this city could do without your freedom and presence—unless, perhaps, you intend to allow the <term>Romanists</term>* <note>A term often used by critics to describe those fiercely loyal to the Pope's political and ecclesiastical authority.</note> *to dare whatever they please hereafter.* PASQUILL. *What? Anything...*

<meta>This page concludes the dialogue between Geron and Pasquill. Having discussed the corruption of the Roman court and the impending Church Council, the characters decide to leave Rome for Germany, where they believe the Reformation has created a more receptive environment for truth.</meta>

<meta>catchword: INTER- (Between/Among)</meta>

The **Romanists** <note>original: "Romanistae"; a term for those who remained loyal to the Pope and the Roman Catholic Church structure during the Reformation.</note> will not cast off their habits, their outrages, or their tyranny, whether a **Synod** <note>original: "Synodus"; a formal council of church leaders called to decide on matters of doctrine or discipline.</note> meets or does not meet. Therefore, let the Germans see to it that they align their lives and conduct with that kind of doctrine which they defend and profess in opposition to the Pope; let them continually implore God for help, and thereafter remain unconcerned about all else. For there is no plan that can prevail against the **Lord** <note>original: "Dominum".</note>. Indeed, the **Papacy** <note>original: "Papatus".</note> has been so weakened—however much those adversaries of yours may hide the fact—that it can scarcely be restored to its former state.

## THE INTERLOCUTORS
<note>original: "INTERLOCVTORES"; the speakers in the dialogue.</note>

### Leo X, Clement VII, and Cardinal Spinola.

**LEO.** Do not afflict yourself any longer, O Clement, since no remedy <note>original: "remedij".</note> remains.

**CLEMENT.** I cannot help but always endure that wretched fortune of mine most bitterly, as often as my majesty comes to mind—a majesty to which the Church has not seen an equal for so many years. I created Ippolito <note>original: "Hippolytum"; refers to Ippolito de' Medici (1511–1535), whom Clement made a Cardinal and who died under suspicious circumstances.</note> a Cardinal, and I ensured that he received an annual income of sixty thousand ducats. I gave my niece <note>Referring to Catherine de' Medici, who married the future King Henry II of France.</note> in a most honorable marriage to the French court. Now fortune is not satisfied that she made me a prisoner of Bourbon <note>original: "Borbonij"; referring to Charles III, Duke of Bourbon, whose imperial troops captured the Pope during the Sack of Rome in 1527.</note>, that Florence was destroyed for my sake, and that Rome was prostituted and became a prey, with both sacred and secular things being plundered; but she also snuffed me out by poison given at Marseille <note>original: "Marsiliae". Clement VII died in 1534; though he died in Rome, this text references a rumor of poisoning related to his trip to Marseille to meet the King of France.</note>. Having dared the same against Ippolito, she even gave Alessandro over to death—who, as you have seen, carries a body full of wounds among the shades of the underworld <note>original: "apud inferos"; the realm of the dead.</note>. Is that not immense cruelty?

**LEO.** You speak the truth, but what can you do where there is no place [for a remedy]...

### THE END.

### TO PASQUILLO, ROMAN PATRICIAN,
### Marforio sends greetings. <note>original: "PASQVILLO PATRITIO Romano, Marphorius. S. D." Pasquino and Marforio are the "talking statues" of Rome. Starting in the 16th century, people would post anonymous satirical poems and biting social commentaries—called "pasquinades"—on these statues. S.D. stands for the Latin "Salutem Dicit," a formal greeting.</note>

*I sent you many other letters by those who were carrying grain to sell in the Campo de’ Fiori* <note>A prominent square and marketplace in Rome.</note>, *and I have seen no letter from you in reply to mine. Consider, my Pasquillo, that you have kept me in no small anxiety, since I was told that the Apostolic Chamber* <term>Apostolic Chamber: The central financial and administrative board of the Papal government.</term> *has ordered and issued a decree that all those who brought grain to Rome, once they have sold it in their own way, are to be thrown into prison. And because of this, since those poor wretches fell into that punishment and were captured, my letters were unable to reach your hands. The current bearer happened by, who is carrying certain letters from Naples to the Pope’s Duchess* <note>Likely referring to Margaret of Austria, the daughter of Emperor Charles V and widow of Alessandro de' Medici, who was a powerful figure in the Roman court.</note> *regarding I know not what matter; he promised me on the word of a gentleman (because he is Spanish) to give you this present letter*

*...into his own hands, rather than going up to the Palace.*
*For this reason, I let you know of a righteous vision here, in the Field of Grief* <note>original: "Campo Dolio," a satirical play on the word *Campidoglio* (the Capitoline Hill in Rome), replacing "idoglio" with "dolio" to imply a place of sorrow or pain (*dolore*).</note>, *this past night, the likes of which has not been seen in these parts without causing great wonder. An Angel appeared to the Pope, the Cardinals, the entire Court, and the Roman People, and among them the following dialogue took place.*

### Angel to the Pope.

*Feed my sheep.* <note>original: "Pasce oves meas." A biblical command from Jesus to Peter (John 21:16), here used to remind the Pope of his pastoral duty to provide for his hungry flock.</note>

### The People.

*Well-ordered charity begins with oneself.* <note>original: "Charitas ordinata incipit à seipso." A common proverb similar to "charity begins at home." In this context, it ironically suggests the Pope is prioritizing his own family's wealth over the public good.</note>

### The Roman People to Paul. <note>Refers to Pope Paul III (Alessandro Farnese), who reigned from 1534 to 1549.</note>

*Ah Lord, have mercy on your people.* <note>original: "Ach Domine misere populo tuo."</note>

### Paul.

*It is not good to take the children's bread and give it to the dogs.* <note>original: "Non est bonum sumere panem filiorum & dare canibus." A reference to Matthew 15:26. The Pope is depicted as viewing the Roman citizens as "dogs" unworthy of the resources (grain) intended for the "children" (likely his own relatives or the Church hierarchy).</note>

### The Angel to Paul.

*Paul, Paul, why do you persecute me?* <note>original: "Paule paule cur me persequeris?" The words spoken by Jesus to Saul (who became the Apostle Paul) on the road to Damascus (Acts 9:4). The Angel suggests the Pope’s actions are an attack on Christ himself.</note>

### Paul.

*I shall not stray from the footsteps of my predecessors.* <note>original: "Vestigia predecessorum meorum non transgrediar." A cynical defense stating he will continue the (implied corrupt) policies of the Popes who came before him.</note>

### The Angel to the People.

*Woe to the people whose prince is a moneylender.* <note>original: "Ve populo cuius princeps est fœnerator." A "fœnerator" is a usurer or someone who profits from high-interest loans. This accuses the Pope of financial exploitation during a time of famine.</note>

### The People to the Angel.

*Send them help from the sanctuary, and protect them out of Zion.* <note>original: "Mitte eis auxiliũ de sãcto, & de sion tuere eos." A liturgical plea for divine protection, adapted from Psalm 20:2.</note>

### Angel to the People.

> I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered. <note>original: "Percutiam Pastorem & dispergentur oues gregis." A citation of Matthew 26:31. When they had come, he announced his desire to reform the Church, encouraging them to give up their many bishoprics and revenues, so that this holy work might begin from the head <note>The "head" refers to the Papal leadership itself.</note>. The Cardinals, thinking they were called for some benefit of their own, felt greatly burdened, and each one responded thus:

->Cardinal Farnese, the Pope's little grandson through his son.<-
<note>Alessandro Farnese the Younger, who was made a cardinal by his grandfather at age 14.</note>

<note>Antonio Pucci, Cardinal-priest of Santi Quattro Coronati.</note>
I do not agree, Holy Father.

->Cardinal Cesarini.<-
<note>Alessandro Cesarini.</note>

<note>Marcello Cervini, later Pope Marcellus II.</note>

<note>Ennio Filonardi, the Bishop of Rieti.</note>

> Where, then, shall we begin? <note>original: "Vnde ergo initium faciemus."</note>

### The People.

> We approach like a lamb. But whichever of you is without sin, let him be the first to cast a stone. <note>original: "Tanquam agnus accedimus. Sed qui uestrum sine peccato est, primus inijciat lapidem." A reference to the Woman Taken in Adultery (John 8:7), where the people challenge the corrupt leaders to judge themselves first.</note>

<meta>This page continues the series of "Sorti" or satirical prophecies attributed to the Roman statue Pasquino for the year 1540. Following the introduction on the previous page, this section lists various cities, regions, and high-ranking officials, assigning each a biblical verse that serves as a biting commentary on their political status, reputation, or perceived vices.</meta>

## Naples.
->Do not give what is holy to dogs <note>original: "Nolite dare sanctum canibus." A quote from Matthew 7:6. In the satirical atmosphere of 1540, this likely refers to the Spanish occupation of Naples, suggesting that the "holy" city is being handed over to "dogs" (a common insult for foreign soldiers or those considered unworthy).</note><-

## Severino.
->From where shall we buy bread, so that these people may eat? <note>original: "Vnde ememus panes ut Manducent hij." A quote from John 6:5. This refers to the Sanseverino family or perhaps Cardinal Antonio Sanseverino; it may mock their dwindling resources or a local famine.</note><-

## Genoa.
->They shall carry you in their hands, lest perhaps you strike [your foot] <note>original: "In manibus portabunt te ne forte offendas." From Psalm 91:12. This is a double-edged joke about the Genoese, who were the primary bankers and financiers of the Holy Roman Empire—the "hands" that carried the financial weight of Europe.</note><-

## Portugal.
->These are the victors and the friends of God <note>original: "Isti sunt triumphatores & amici dei." An antiphon used in the liturgy for Apostles. It likely alludes to Portugal's role in the Age of Discovery and their missions in the East, though Pasquino often used such praise sarcastically to highlight greed masked as piety.</note><-

## Salzburg.
->My cup, which intoxicates me, how excellent it is! <note>original: "Calix meus inebrians quam preclarus est." From Psalm 23:5. This is a jab at the Prince-Archbishops of Salzburg, known for their wealth and perhaps their fondness for the local drink.</note><-

## Mainz.
->Are you not also one of this man's disciples? <note>original: "Nunquid & tu ex discipulis es hominis istius?" From John 18:17. This likely refers to Cardinal Albrecht of Mainz, whose sale of indulgences famously triggered Martin Luther’s protest; the "man" in question could be Luther himself or the Pope.</note><-

## Legate of Avignon.
->Before Abraham was, I am. <note>original: "Ante quam Abram fieret ego sum." From John 8:58. By applying Christ’s claim of divinity to the Papal Legate of Avignon, the text mocks the extreme arrogance and ancient pretensions of the French papal administration.</note><-

## Lorraine.
->He placed him in the paradise of pleasure. <note>original: "Posuit eum in paradisum uoluptatis." From Genesis 2:15. This refers to the House of Lorraine (specifically the Guise family), mocking their immense wealth and the luxurious, "Eden-like" lifestyle they enjoyed at court.</note> <-

## Bourbon.
->I thirst. <note>original: "Sicio" [Sitio]. From John 19:28. These were Christ's words on the cross. Applied to the House of Bourbon, it likely mocks a thirst for power, land, or perhaps a literal reputation for heavy drinking.</note><-

## Tournon.
->A thorn in the flesh was given to me <note>original: "Datus est mihi stimulus Carnis." From 2 Corinthians 12:7. "Iornon" is likely a transcription of [Cardinal de] Tournon. The "thorn in the flesh" could be a pun on his name (Tournon/thorn) or a comment on his notoriously difficult personality.</note><-

## The Venetian.
->His garments were like snow, <note>original: "Vestimenta eius sicut nix." From Matthew 17:2. A reference to the Transfiguration, here used to mock the legendary "purity" or the white-robed formality of the Venetian Republic's officials.</note><-

## Ghinucci.
->And the last shall be first, and the first shall be last. <note>original: "Et erunt nouissimi primi & primi nouissimi." From Matthew 20:16. "Guiri" likely refers to Cardinal Girolamo Ghinucci, a seasoned diplomat whose fortunes often shifted in the complex politics between England, Rome, and the Empire.</note><-

## Bologna

<meta>This page continues the 1540 series of satirical "Sorti" (prophecies or fates) attributed to Pasquino. The previous page concluded with a jab at the Prince-Archbishop of Salzburg's drinking habits. This page continues to assign biblical verses to various European cities and regions, using scripture to mock their political standing, economic reputation, or religious controversies. The catchword at the bottom, "Cæsarino," suggests the next page will begin with a reference to Cardinal Giuliano Cesarini.</meta>

## Bologna.
->I looked on my right hand, and there was no one who knew me. <note>original: "Considerabant à dextris & non erat qui Cognosceret me." From Psalm 142:4. In the context of 1540, this likely refers to Bologna's status as a "second capital" of the Papal States, suggesting a feeling of being overlooked or abandoned by Rome.</note><-

## Parigi.
->Is he angry every day? <note>original: "Nunquid irascitur per singulos dies." From Psalm 7:12. This likely refers to King Francis I of France, whose volatile temper and constant military campaigning against Emperor Charles V were well known.</note><-

## Macon.
->I am the good shepherd. <note>original: "Ego sum pastor bonus." From John 10:11. This may refer to Charles de Hémard de Denonville, the Bishop of Mâcon and a prominent French diplomat in Rome, perhaps mocking his self-perception or his role in ecclesiastical politics.</note><-

## Sabon.
->A faithful and wise servant whom the lord has set over his household. <note>original: "Fidelis seruus & prudens quem Constituit dominus super familiam suam." From Matthew 24:45. "Sabon" likely refers to the Cardinal of Sabina or the city of Savona. The verse is often used for high-ranking prelates; here, it could be either genuine praise or irony regarding their influence over the Pope's "household."</note><-

## Scocia.
->Their sound went out into all the earth. <note>original: "In omnem terram exiuit sonus eorum." From Psalm 19:4. In 1540, Scotland was embroiled in the religious tensions of the Reformation; this may be a sarcastic comment on the "noise" or notoriety the Scots were making in European affairs.</note><-

## Siuiglia.
->Woe to you Pharisees, who tithe mint and dill and every herb, and pass over judgment and the love of God. <note>original: "Ve uobis pharisei qui decimatis mentam anetĩ & omne olus & preteritis iudiū & charitatem dei." From Luke 11:42. A biting criticism of Seville, then the wealthiest port in Spain, suggesting that its religious authorities were obsessed with minor rules and financial gain (tithing) while ignoring true justice.</note><-

## Toleto.
->Trade until I come. <note>original: "Negociamini dum uenio." From Luke 19:13. This refers to the commercial and banking power of Toledo, then the capital of the Spanish Empire, reminding the merchants that their worldly dealings will eventually be judged.</note><-

## Burgos.
->There are some among you who do not believe. <note>original: "Sunt quidam ex uobis qui non credunt." From John 6:64. This might be a pointed reference to the large population of *conversos* (converts from Judaism) in Burgos and the pervasive suspicion of the Spanish Inquisition.</note><-

## Cordona.
->He heaps up riches and does not know for whom he will gather them. <note>original: "Thesaurizat & nescit cui congregabit ea." From Psalm 39:6. A critique of the wealth of Córdoba, suggesting that their accumulation of fortune is ultimately futile or destined for someone else's hands.</note><-

## S. Iacomo.
->The house of Jacob from a barbarous people. <note>original: "Domus Iacob de populo barbaro." From Psalm 114:1. A pun on the name of Santiago (Saint James/Jacob) de Compostela. While it is a holy pilgrimage site, Pasquino cheekily labels the local population or the pilgrims themselves as "barbarous."</note><-

<meta>This page continues the satirical series of "Sorti" (prophetic lots) from 1540. Following the previous page's conclusion regarding Scotland and the catchword reference to Bologna, this section assigns specific biblical verses to major European powers and high-ranking ecclesiastical figures. The tone remains bitingly critical, using the Latin Vulgate to mock the perceived vices, political failures, or characteristic traits of the subjects.</meta>

### Naples.
*Do not give what is holy to dogs.* <note>original: "Nolite dare sanctum canibus." From Matthew 7:6. This likely reflects the tense relationship between the Papacy and Naples, which was under Spanish rule; it suggests that the "holy" city of Rome should not grant favors to those it considers outsiders or "dogs."</note>

### San Severino.
*Where shall we buy bread that these may eat?* <note>original: "Vnde ememus panes ut Manducent hij." From John 6:5. This likely refers to Cardinal Antonio Sanseverino. The verse, which precedes the miracle of the loaves and fishes, may mock the Cardinal's wealth or his responsibility for feeding his large retinue.</note>

### Genoa.
*In their hands they shall bear you up, lest you dash your foot against a stone.* <note>original: "In manibus portabunt te ne forte offendas." From Psalm 91:12. This is a reference to the Genoese as the primary bankers and financiers of the era, suggesting that the Pope or the Emperor is "carried" or supported by Genoese money.</note>

### Portugal.
*These are the conquerors and friends of God.* <note>original: "Isti sunt triumphatores & amici dei." Adapted from the Roman Catholic liturgy for the Common of Apostles. It refers to the Portuguese maritime expansion and their role in spreading Christianity to the "East Indies" and Brazil.</note>

### Salzburg.
*My cup which inebriates me, how excellent it is!* <note>original: "Calix meus inebrians Quam preclarus est." From Psalm 23:5 (Vulgate). A recurring satirical jab at the Prince-Archbishop of Salzburg, implying a reputation for heavy drinking rather than spiritual devotion.</note>

### Mainz.
*Are you also one of this man's disciples?* <note>original: "Nunquid & tu ex discipulijs es hominis istius?" From John 18:17. Mainz was the seat of the Primate of Germany; this question likely alludes to the Archbishop’s proximity to—or failure to stop—the "disciples" of Martin Luther.</note>

### Legate of Avignon.
*Before Abraham was, I am.* <note>original: "Ante quam Abram fieret ego sum." From John 8:58. This verse, where Jesus claims divinity, is used here to mock the supreme arrogance or the ancient, quasi-independent authority claimed by the Papal Legates in Avignon.</note>

### Lorraine.
*He placed him in a paradise of pleasure.* <note>original: "Posuit eum in paradisum uoluptatis." From Genesis 2:15. This refers to Cardinal Jean de Lorraine, a man famous for his immense wealth, love of art, and legendary indulgence in worldly luxuries.</note>

### Bourbon.
*I thirst.* <note>original: "Sicio." From John 19:28. Referring to Cardinal Charles de Bourbon, this could be a critique of his "thirst" for power or a simpler joke about his fondness for wine.</note>

### Tournon.
*There was given to me a sting of the flesh.* <note>original: "Datus est mihi stimulus Carnis." From 2 Corinthians 12:7. Assigned to Cardinal François de Tournon, a key advisor to the French King, this might refer to a specific physical malady or a moral failing well-known to contemporary readers.</note>

### The Venetian.
*His garments were as snow.* <note>original: "Vestimenta eius sicut nix." From Matthew 17:2. This describes the Transfiguration. Applied to Venice, it likely mocks the Republic's outward appearance of "pure" neutrality while it engaged in complex, often cold-blooded diplomacy.</note>

### Gheri.
*And the last shall be first, and the first shall be last.* <note>original: "Et erunt nouissimi primi & primi nouissimi." From Matthew 20:16. Likely referring to Cosimo Gheri, the young Bishop of Fano, or another member of the Gheri family, suggesting a sudden rise to prominence or a future fall from grace.</note>
