<meta>This page continues the "Sorti" or prophetic lots, a satirical series likely dating to the early 1540s. Following the previous page's commentary on Naples, Genoa, and Salzburg, this section applies specific Latin biblical verses to various European cities and dioceses. In this era of intense political maneuvering between the Holy Roman Empire, France, and the Papacy, these "lots" served as a form of coded political commentary, using the authority of the Vulgate Bible to mock the greed, hypocrisy, or misfortune of high-ranking officials and regions.</meta>

### Bologna.
*I looked on my right hand and saw, and there was no man that would know me.* <note>original: "Considerabant à dextris & non erat qui Cognosceret me." From Psalm 142:4. This likely alludes to Bologna's status as a secondary city within the Papal States, feeling overlooked by the central government in Rome or abandoned during political shifts.</note>

### Paris.
*Is God angry every day?* <note>original: "Nunquid irascitur per singulos dies." From Psalm 7:11 (Vulgate). This is a pointed reference to the near-constant state of warfare maintained by King Francis I of France, suggesting his temperament or the state of his kingdom is one of perpetual conflict.</note>

### Mâcon.
*I am the good shepherd.* <note>original: "Ego sum pastor bonus." From John 10:11. This likely refers to Charles de Hémard de Denonville, the Cardinal of Mâcon. Since he spent much of his time acting as a diplomat in Rome rather than tending his diocese, the use of this verse is deeply ironic.</note>

### Savona.
*A faithful and wise servant, whom his lord has appointed over his family.* <note>original: "Fidelis seruus & prudens quem Constituit dominus super familiam suam." From Matthew 24:45. This verse was commonly used in the liturgy for confessors and bishops; here it likely evaluates a specific local administrator or the city's loyalty to its ruling power.</note>

### Scotland.
*Their sound has gone forth into all the earth.* <note>original: "In omnem terram exiuit sonus eorum." From Psalm 19:4. While originally referring to the Apostles, in this satirical context it may mock the far-reaching reputation of Scottish soldiers of fortune or the international spread of Scotland's internal religious and political struggles.</note>

### Seville.
*Woe to you, Pharisees, who pay tithes on mint and rue and every herb, but disregard justice and the love of God.* <note>original: "Ve uobis pharisei qui decimatis mentam aneti & omne olus & preteritis iudium & charitatem dei." From Luke 11:42. A harsh critique of the wealthy ecclesiastical center of Seville, suggesting that the clergy there are more concerned with collecting small taxes and following rigid rules than with true Christian charity.</note>

### Toledo.
*Trade with these until I come.* <note>original: "Negociamini dum uenio." From Luke 19:13. Toledo was the seat of the wealthiest archbishopric in Spain. This verse mocks the commercial and financial preoccupations of the Spanish high clergy.</note>

### Burgos.
*There are some among you who do not believe.* <note>original: "Sunt quidam ex uobis qui non credunt." From John 6:64. This is a biting reference to the large population of "New Christians" (converts from Judaism) in Burgos, reflecting the era's suspicion and the activities of the Spanish Inquisition.</note>

### Cordoba.
*He stores up treasure and does not know for whom he gathers it.* <note>original: "Thesaurizat & nescit cui congregabit ea." From Psalm 39:6. Another jab at the immense wealth of the Spanish sees, suggesting that their accumulated riches will eventually be seized or wasted by others.</note>

### Santiago.
*The house of Jacob from a barbarous people.* <note>original: "Domus Iacob de populo barbaro." From Psalm 114:1. A pun on the name "Iacomo" (James/Jacob). It refers to the famous pilgrimage site of Santiago de Compostela, perhaps mocking the rough nature of the pilgrims or the local Galician population.</note>

<meta>This page continues the satirical "Sorti" (prophetic lots), shifting the focus from geographical regions to specific high-ranking members of the Roman Curia. These individuals, primarily Cardinals, are assigned biblical verses that either mock their personal character, comment on their political ambitions, or reflect their public reputations during the mid-16th century. The tone ranges from sincere praise to biting irony, particularly regarding the austere and often-feared Gian Pietro Carafa (Chieti).</meta>

## Cesarini.
These are they who, living, planted the Church in the flesh. <note>original: "Hi sunt qui uiuentes in Carnem planttauerun [plantaverunt] ecclesiam." This is a variation of a liturgical phrase usually referring to the Apostles planting the Church with their blood. Assigned to Cardinal Alessandro Cesarini, it may satirically suggest that his contributions to the Church were more worldly or physical than spiritual.</note>

## Del Monte.
Blessed are you who hunger now, for you shall be filled. <note>original: "Beati qui nunc esuritis quia saturabimini." From Luke 6:21. Assigned to Giovanni Maria Ciocchi del Monte (the future Pope Julius III), this may allude to his known love of fine food and luxury, or his ambition for higher office.</note>

## Giacobazzi.
Are you then the Son of God? <note>original: "Ergo Filius dei es tu." From Luke 22:70. Assigned to Cardinal Domenico Giacobazzi, this question—originally posed to Jesus by the Sanhedrin—is used here to mock a sense of self-importance or a high-handed manner.</note>

## Chieti.
Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly are ravening wolves. <note>original: "Attendite a falsis prophetis qui ueniunt ad uos in uestimentis ouium intrinsecus autem sunt lupi rapaces." From Matthew 7:15. This is a sharp attack on Gian Pietro Carafa, the Bishop of Chieti and future Pope Paul IV. Carafa was the founder of the Theatines and a leader of the Roman Inquisition; while he projected an image of holy austerity, his contemporaries often viewed him as a dangerous and aggressive zealot.</note>

## Grimani.
O Lord, rebuke me not in your fury, nor chastise me in your wrath. <note>original: "Domine ne in furore tuo arguas me, neque in ira tua Corripias me." From Psalm 6:1. Assigned to Cardinal Marino Grimani, this suggests a man in a state of political or personal disgrace, pleading for mercy from either God or the Pope.</note>

## Cornaro.
Today you shall be with me in paradise. <note>original: "Hodie mecum eris in paradiso." From Luke 23:43. The words spoken by Jesus to the "Good Thief" on the cross. For Cardinal Francesco Cornaro, this might imply a late-life repentance or a mocking suggestion that he is barely escaping divine judgment.</note>

## Contarini.
That man was simple and upright, and fearing God, and avoiding evil. <note>original: "Erat uir ille simplex & rectus ac timens deum & Recedens à Malo." From Job 1:1. Unlike many of the other entries, this verse for Cardinal Gasparo Contarini is likely sincere. Contarini was widely respected as a man of genuine integrity and a leading voice for moderate reform within the Church.</note>

## Brindisi.
Has not God made foolish the wisdom of this world? <note>original: "Nonne stultam fecit deus sapientiam huius mundi." From 1 Corinthians 1:20. Assigned to Girolamo Aleandro, the Archbishop of Brindisi. Aleandro was a famed humanist scholar and diplomat; the verse ironically suggests that for all his worldly learning, he has missed the point of true spiritual wisdom.</note>

## Pisani.
Remember not the sins of my youth and my ignorance. <note>original: "Delicta Iuuentutis Mee & Ignorantias meas ne memineris." From Psalm 25:7 (Vulgate 24:7). Cardinal Francesco Pisani was known for his vast wealth and the many ecclesiastical offices he accumulated while still quite young; the verse points to a reputation for youthful excesses or greed.</note>

<meta>This page continues the satirical series of "Sorti" (prophetic lots or fortunes) applied to prominent members of the Roman Curia. Each high-ranking official is assigned a biblical verse that serves as a witty, often biting, commentary on their character, career, or current political situation. The previous page ended with a harsh critique of Cardinal Carafa (Chieti); this page continues through the roster of influential Cardinals and bishops during the mid-16th century.</meta>

## Bembo.

->I will sing to the Lord a new song.<-
<note>original: "Cantabo Domino canticum nouum." From Psalm 96:1. This is assigned to Pietro Bembo, the famous humanist, poet, and scholar who revolutionized Italian literature. The "new song" likely refers to his immense influence on modern poetry and his status as a man of letters rather than a traditional theologian.</note>

## San Quattro.

->Do not think that I will accuse you<-
->before the Father.<-
<note>original: "Nolite putare quia ego acusaturus sum uos apud patrem." From John 5:45. This refers to Cardinal Lorenzo Pucci, titled "San Quattro" after his titular church. As he held high offices related to justice and the granting of favors (the Penitentiary), the verse suggests his power to either condemn or show mercy.</note>

## Salviati.

->For he did not wish to walk in Judea because<-
->the Jews sought to kill him.<-
<note>original: "Non enim uolebat in Iudeam Ambulare quia querebant eum Iudei interficere." From John 7:1. Cardinal Giovanni Salviati was a perpetual candidate for the papacy who faced intense opposition from the Imperial faction. The verse likely alludes to his political maneuverings and the "hostile territory" he had to navigate in Rome.</note>

## Ridolfi.

->Do not weep; the girl is not dead but asleep.<-
<note>original: "Nolite flere non est mortua puella sed dormit." From Luke 8:52. Cardinal Niccolò Ridolfi was a prominent patron of the arts. This verse might mock a failed political ambition or a temporary loss of influence, suggesting that his prospects are merely "resting" rather than finished.</note>

## Grimaldi.

->Lord, you delivered five talents to me; behold,<-
->I have gained five more.<-
<note>original: "Domine quinque talenta tradidisti Mihi, ecce alia quinque super lucratus sum." From Matthew 25:20. Girolamo Grimaldi was known for his administrative and financial skills. The verse highlights his reputation for increasing wealth or successfully managing the Church's resources.</note>

## Cybo.

->Crucify him, crucify him!<-
<note>original: "Crucifige crucifige eum." From Luke 23:21. Assigned to Cardinal Innocenzo Cybo, this shockingly harsh verse reflects his reputation as a ruthless political figure or perhaps the intense animosity he inspired in his rivals.</note>

## Gaddi.

->May another take his office.<-
<note>original: "Episcopatum eius accipiet alter." From Acts 1:20, originally referring to the replacement of Judas Iscariot. This is a direct jab at Cardinal Niccolò Gaddi, suggesting either that he is unfit for his position or that others are eagerly waiting for him to lose it.</note>

## Ravenna.

->You have appointed his bounds that could not<-
->be passed.<-
<note>original: "Constituisti terminos eius qui præteriri non poterant." From Job 14:5. This refers to Benedetto Accolti, the Archbishop of Ravenna. Accolti was famously imprisoned by Pope Paul III in 1535; the "bounds" here likely refer to his arrest and the literal walls of his prison.</note>

## Veroli.

->For I am the least of the apostles, who am not<-
->worthy to be called an apostle.<-
<note>original: "Ego enim sum minimus apostolorum qui non sum dignus uocari apostolus." From 1 Corinthians 15:9. Assigned to Ennio Filonardi, Bishop of Veroli. This could be a mockery of a perceived lack of status or a satirical take on his public displays of humility.</note>

## Doria.

->For your voice is sweet and your face is beautiful.<-
<note>original: "Vox enim tua dulcis & facies tua decora." From the Song of Solomon 2:14. Cardinal Girolamo Doria was noted for his noble lineage and perhaps his physical appearance or courtly charm, making this romantic verse a playful comment on his persona.</note>

<meta>This page continues the satirical "Sorti" (fortunes) of the Roman Curia. Having finished with Ridolfi on the previous page, the text now moves through a list of prominent mid-16th-century Cardinals, using biblical citations to comment on their reputations, their relative youth, or their proximity to the Pope.</meta>

## Sadoleto.
->*Beloved of God and men,*<-
<note>original: "Dilectus deo & hominibus." From Ecclesiasticus 45:1. This refers to Jacopo Sadoleto, a celebrated humanist, diplomat, and reformer. Unlike many of his peers, Sadoleto was widely respected for his genuine piety and learning, making this "fortune" a rare sincere compliment.</note>

## Trivulzio.
->*What I have written, I have written.*<-
<note>original: "Quod scripsi scripsi." From John 19:22. These are the words of Pontius Pilate. For Cardinal Agostino Trivulzio, a major player in the political intrigues between France and the Papacy, it likely suggests a stubborn or irrevocable political stance.</note>

## Carpi.
->*For he was the one who would betray him, though he was one of the twelve.*<-
<note>original: "Hic enim erat traditurus eum cum esset unus ex duodecim." From John 6:71. This is a devastating satire of Cardinal Rodolfo Pio da Carpi. By casting him as Judas Iscariot, the text marks him as a traitor within the inner circle of the College of Cardinals.</note>

## Mantua.
->*I have become like a solitary sparrow on the roof.*<-
<note>original: "Factus sum sicut passer solitarius in tecto." From Psalm 102:7. This refers to Ercole Gonzaga, the Cardinal of Mantua. It may refer to his periods of political isolation or his independent streak that often put him at odds with the Roman mainstream.</note>

## Ferrara.
->*You yourself are my King and my God.*<-
<note>original: "Tu es ipse Rex meus & deus meus." From Psalm 44:4. Cardinal Ippolito d’Este of Ferrara was famous for his staggering wealth and the magnificence of the Villa d'Este. The verse likely mocks his devotion to worldly princes or his own kingly ambitions.</note>

## Farnese.
->*I do nothing of myself, but as my father taught me, I speak these things.*<-
<note>original: "A me ipso facio nihil sed sicut docuit me pater hoc loquor." From John 8:28. A very sharp joke aimed at Cardinal Alessandro Farnese "the younger." As the grandson of Pope Paul III, his entire career was seen as an extension of his grandfather's (his "father's") will and nepotism.</note>

## Santa Fiora.
->*A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another.*<-
<note>original: "Mandatum nouum do uobis ut diligatis uos Inuicem." From John 13:34. This refers to Guido Ascanio Sforza di Santa Fiora. As another young "cardinal-nephew" of the Pope, the call to "love one another" might be a sarcastic comment on the tight-knit and self-serving nature of the papal family factions.</note>

## Sermonetta.
->*The child however grew and was strengthened in spirit, and he was in the deserts of Judea until the day of his manifestation to Israel.*<-
<note>original: "Puer autem crescebat & confortabatur spiritu & erat in desertis Iudeæ usque ad diem ascensionis suæ ad Israël." Adapted from Luke 1:80. Cardinal Niccolò Caetani di Sermoneta was created a cardinal at the age of fourteen; the verse mocks his extreme youth and his "growth" into a position of power.</note>

## Sanello.
->*Let the children come to me and do not forbid them; for of such is the kingdom of heaven.*<-
<note>original: "Sinite pueros uenire ad me & nolite uetare eos talium est enim regnum celorum." From Matthew 19:14. This continues the theme of the "boy cardinals" (fanciulli) who populated the Curia during this era of rampant nepotism.</note>

## Borgia.
<note>The page ends with the name of Cardinal Ennio Filonardi (associated with the Borgia faction or titular legacy), but the corresponding verse is missing or continued on the next page.</note>

<meta>This page continues the satirical "Sorti" (fortunes) of the Roman Curia, specifically focusing on the College of Cardinals and high-ranking prelates during the mid-16th century. ->Let us pray for our people.<-
<note>original: "Oremus pro populo nostro." This is a standard liturgical invitation to prayer, here used as a header for the list of "fortunes" that follows.</note>

### Guevara.
<note>The text reads "Geuenra," likely a misspelling of Guevara, referring to Iñigo Ávalos de Aragón, often called the Cardinal of Guevara.</note>

->You believe in God.<-
<note>original: "Credis in deum." From John 14:1. In this satirical context, it might imply a simple or perhaps questionable faith.</note>

### Orleans.
<note>Refers to Jean du Bellay, the Cardinal of Orleans, a powerful French diplomat and poet.</note>

->Intercede for their devout fasting.<-
<note>original: "Intercede pro deuoto Ieiunio eorum." This is adapted from a liturgical prayer. It likely mocks the French Cardinal's reputation for luxury, contrasting it with the "devout fasting" of others.</note>

### Salerno.
<note>Refers to the Cardinal of Salerno, likely Federico Fregoso or Girolamo Seripando.</note>

->For your obedience has become known in every place; therefore I rejoice over you.<-
<note>original: "Vestra enim obedientia diuulgata est in omni loco, gaudeo igitur uobis." From Romans 16:19. A compliment toward his loyalty to the Roman see.</note>

### Gambara.
<note>Refers to Cardinal Uberto Gambara, a prominent papal diplomat.</note>

->I have greatly desired to eat this Passover with you.<-
<note>original: "Desiderio desideraui hoc pascha manducare vobiscum." From Luke 22:15. These are Christ's words at the Last Supper; applied to Gambara, it might poke fun at his eagerness for social or political gatherings.</note>

### Rimini.
<note>Refers to the Cardinal of Rimini, Francesco Parisani.</note>

->These are they who were not defiled with women, for they are virgins, and they follow the Lamb wherever he goes.<-
<note>original: "Hi sunt qui cum mulieribus non sunt coinquinati uirginij enim sunt & sequuntur agnum quocunque ierit." From Revelation 14:4. Given the satirical nature of this manuscript, this is likely a sarcastic remark regarding the Cardinal's actual chastity.</note>

### Parisio.
<note>Refers to Cardinal Pierpaolo Parisio, a renowned jurist.</note>

->What shall I do? I am not strong enough to dig; I am ashamed to beg.<-
<note>original: "Quid faciam? fodere non ualeo mendicare erubesco?" From Luke 16:3. This is the speech of the "Unjust Steward" in the parable. Using it for Parisio suggests he was viewed as a shrewd, perhaps self-serving, administrator.</note>

### Guidiccioni.
<note>Refers to Cardinal Bartolomeo Guidiccioni, one of the original members of the commission that approved the Jesuit order.</note>

->Dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return.<-
<note>original: "Puluis es & in puluerem Reuerteris." From Genesis 3:19. A somber reminder of mortality, perhaps reflecting Guidiccioni’s age or his stern, ascetic reputation.</note>

### Brother Dionysius.
<note>Refers to Dionisio Laurerio, known as "Fra Dionisio" because he was a member of the Servite Order. He was a prominent theologian and Cardinal.</note>

->That which was, remained; and that which was not, he assumed.<-
<note>original: "Id quod fuit permansit & quod non erat assumpsit." A phrase from a liturgical antiphon for the Feast of the Circumcision regarding the nature of Christ. Applied here, it might joke about his transition from a humble friar to a prince of the Church.</note>

### Marcello.
<note>Refers to Marcello Cervini, who later became Pope Marcellus II. He was known for his integrity and high standards of reform.</note>

->Show us the Father, and it is enough for us.<-
<note>original: "Ostende nobis patrem & sufficiat nobis." From John 14:8. This likely refers to Cervini's role as a trusted advisor and "right hand" to the Pope (the Holy Father).</note>

<meta>This page continues the satirical "Sorti" (fortunes) attributed to various high-ranking European figures and members of the Roman Curia. Each individual or group is paired with a biblical verse that acts as a commentary on their character, political standing, or current reputation.</meta>

### College of Cardinals
<note>Refers to the group of high-ranking clergy who advise the Pope and elect his successor. At this time, the College was often criticized for its size and international political factions.</note>

> I saw a great multitude, which no one could number, from all nations and tribes and peoples and tongues.
<note>original: "vidi turbam magnam quam dinumerare nemo poterat ex omnibus gentibus & tribubus & populis & linguis." From Revelation 7:9. This likely mocks the excessive size and diverse, often conflicting, national interests within the College.</note>

### Bishop of Verona
<note>Refers to Gian Matteo Giberti (1495–1543), a prominent reformer and diplomat who eventually withdrew from the papal court to focus on his diocese.</note>

> There was no room for him in the inn.
<note>original: "Non erat ei locus in diuersorio." From Luke 2:7. In this context, it may suggest that Giberti, known for his reforming zeal, found no place or welcome in the corrupt Roman court.</note>

## THE EMPEROR
<note>Refers to Holy Roman Emperor Charles V (r. 1519–1556), the most powerful monarch in Europe at the time.</note>

> Passing through the midst of them, he went his way.
<note>original: "Transiens per medium illorum ibat." From Luke 4:30. This refers to the Emperor’s constant travels across his vast territories and his ability to navigate through political enemies.</note>

### The Prince of Spain
<note>Refers to the future Philip II of Spain, son of Charles V.</note>

> Hail, King of the Jews.
<note>original: "Aue Rex Iudeorum." From Matthew 27:29. This is a biting reference to the Spanish crown's obsession with "purity of blood" and the Inquisition's pursuit of "Conversos" (Jewish converts to Christianity).</note>

### Constable of Castile
<note>The Constable was one of the highest military and administrative offices in Spain, held at this time by the Velasco family.</note>

> We found this man subverting our nation and forbidding tribute to be given to Caesar.
<note>original: "Hunc inuenimus subuertentẽ gentem nostram & prohibentem tributa dari Cæsari." From Luke 23:2. This verse, originally an accusation against Jesus, is used here to imply political subversion or financial corruption by the Spanish official.</note>

### Cobos
<note>Refers to Francisco de los Cobos y Molina, the powerful Secretary of State to Emperor Charles V.</note>

> You are a Samaritan, and you have a demon.
<note>original: "Sammaritanus es, & demonium habes." From John 8:48. This is a severe insult, painting the influential secretary as an outsider or someone possessed by malicious ambition.</note>

### Don Luigi da Villa
<note>Refers to Don Luis de Ávila y Zúñiga, a Spanish loyalist, commander, and historian close to Charles V.</note>

> The King has loved me and introduced me into his chamber.
<note>original: "Dilexit me Rex & introduxit in cubiculum suum." Adapted from the Song of Solomon 1:4. This mocks the intimate favor and access Don Luis enjoyed with the Emperor.</note>

### King of France
<note>The text reads "Re' xxia," a likely shorthand for "Re di Francia," referring to Francis I (r. 1515–1547).</note>

> Behold, he who will betray me is now near.
<note>original: "Ecce iam prope est qui me tradet." From Matthew 26:46. This refers to the perceived untrustworthiness of the French King in his shifting alliances against the Emperor and the Pope.</note>

### The Queen
<note>Likely referring to Eleanor of Austria, Queen of France and sister of Charles V, or perhaps Catherine de' Medici.</note>

> The queen stood at your right hand in clothing of gold, surrounded by variety.
<note>original: "Astitit regina a dextris tuis in uestitu deaurato Circundat a uarietate." From Psalm 45:9. A standard description of royal majesty and the diverse splendor of the court.</note>

### The Dauphin
<note>Refers to the heir to the French throne, the future Henry II.</note>

> I will make your enemies a footstool for your feet.
<note>original: "Ponam inimicos tuos scabellum pedum tuorũ." From Psalm 110:1. A prophecy of future military triumph over his rivals.</note>

<meta>This page continues the satirical "Sorti" (fortunes), shifting focus from the Roman Curia and the Emperor to the French royal family and other European monarchs. These biblical associations often contain double meanings regarding fertility, political legitimacy, or personal reputation.</meta>

## The Dauphine
<note>Refers to Catherine de' Medici (1519–1589), wife of the heir to the French throne. At this time, her difficulty in conceiving an heir was a matter of intense international scrutiny.</note>

> She shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel; he shall eat butter and honey.
<note>original: "Concipiet & pariet filium & uocabitur nomē eius emanuel, butirum & mel comedet." From Isaiah 7:14-15. This is a pointed reference to the hope for a male heir to the Valois dynasty.</note>

## Orléans
<note>Refers to Henry, Duke of Orléans (1519–1559), the second son of Francis I of France, who later became King Henry II.</note>

> Tell us if you are the one who is to reign among the people of Israel.
<note>original: "Nuncia nobis si tu es ipse qui Regnatur us es in populo Israël." Adapted from Matthew 11:3. This likely alludes to his position in the line of succession or his growing political influence.</note>

## Madame Marguerite
<note>Refers to Marguerite de France (1523–1574), daughter of King Francis I, or possibly his sister, Marguerite de Navarre. Given the wedding theme, it likely refers to the diplomatic negotiations for her marriage.</note>

> The wedding indeed is ready, but those who were invited were not worthy.
<note>original: "Nuptie quidem paratæ sunt sed qui fuerāt uocati non fuerunt Digni." From Matthew 22:8. This suggests a history of failed marriage alliances or political snubs.</note>

## The Constable
<note>Refers to Anne de Montmorency (1493–1567), Grand Constable of France and a powerful military and political leader.</note>

> Blessed are the peacemakers.
<note>original: "Beati pacifici." From Matthew 5:9. This is likely ironic, given Montmorency's role as a military commander, or refers to his efforts to negotiate peace between France and the Empire.</note>

## The King of Navarre
<note>Refers to Henry II of Navarre (1503–1555), whose kingdom had been largely annexed by Spain.</note>

> Remember me when you come into your kingdom.
<note>original: "Memento mei cum ueneris in regnum tuum." From Luke 23:42. A poignant reference to his lost lands and his desire to reclaim his sovereign territory.</note>

## The Queen of Navarre
<note>Refers to Marguerite de Navarre (1492–1549), sister of Francis I, a celebrated author and patron of religious reformers.</note>

> Every day he was teaching in the temple.
<note>original: "Erat quotidie docens in templo." From Luke 19:47. This alludes to her deep intellectual engagement with theology and her protection of reform-minded scholars.</note>

## The King of the Romans
<note>Refers to Ferdinand I (1503–1564), brother of Charles V and heir to the Holy Roman Empire.</note>

> Forgive us our debts.
<note>original: "Dimitte nobis debita nostra." From the Lord's Prayer (Matthew 6:12). Likely a satirical jab at the financial struggles and heavy debts incurred by the Habsburgs to fund their wars.</note>

## The Queen
<note>Refers to Eleanor of Austria (1498–1558), Queen of France and sister of Emperor Charles V.</note>

> Your wife shall be as a fruitful vine by the sides of your house.
<note>original: "Vxor tua sicut uitis abundans in lateribus domus tuæ." From Psalm 128:3. This verse traditionally celebrates family and fertility, often used here to comment on her role in the French court.</note>

## The Queen of Hungary
<note>Refers to Mary of Hungary (1505–1558), sister of Charles V and Governor of the Netherlands, known for her formidable leadership.</note>

> Though a host should encamp against me, my heart shall not fear.
<note>original: "Et si consistant aduersum me Castra non timebit cor meum." From Psalm 27:3. A tribute to her reputation as a strong, resilient ruler who faced frequent military threats.</note>

## The Duchess of Milan
<note>Refers to Christina of Denmark (1521–1590), the young widow of the Duke of Milan, famously portrayed by Holbein when Henry VIII sought her hand.</note>

> We acknowledge your preserved and laudable virginity.
<note>original: "Cōferuatā agnouimus tuā laudabilē uirginitatē." A phrase from liturgical texts (similar to sequences for the Virgin Mary). Here, it likely comments on her status as a young, sought-after widow whose "purity" was a valuable political asset.</note>

<meta>This page continues the satirical "fortunes," expanding the scope from the French court to the major power players of 16th-century Europe. The author continues to use Latin liturgical and biblical phrases to mock or comment on the political reputations, wealth, and misfortunes of various rulers.</meta>

## King of Portugal
<note>Likely referring to John III of Portugal (r. 1521–1557). During this era, Portugal grew immensely wealthy through its monopoly on the spice trade from the East Indies.</note>

> Oh, the depth of the riches!
<note>original: "O altitudo diuiciarum." From Romans 11:33. A direct reference to the legendary wealth flowing into Lisbon.</note>

## King of Scotland
<note>Refers to James V (r. 1513–1542). This verse suggests a state of mourning or political distress, perhaps related to the constant tensions with England.</note>

> I have forgotten to eat my bread.
<note>original: "Oblitus sum comedere panem meum." From Psalm 102:4. In a satirical context, this implies a ruler consumed by anxiety or misery.</note>

## King of England
<note>Refers to Henry VIII (r. 1509–1547). This is a biting satirical choice given Henry's infamous series of marriages and his break with the Catholic Church over his divorce from Catherine of Aragon.</note>

> There was a wedding in Cana of Galilee.
<note>original: "Facte sunt nuptiæ in Cana Galilee." From John 2:1. The "wedding" theme is a clear jab at Henry's marital history.</note>

## Duke of Guelders
<note>Refers to Charles of Egmond (1467–1538), who spent his life in a bitter struggle to maintain the independence of Guelders (in the modern-day Netherlands) against the Habsburgs.</note>

> On that day, Herod and Pilate became friends.
<note>original: "In illa die facti sunt amici herodes & pilatus." From Luke 23:12. This likely refers to a cynical or unexpected political alliance made between former enemies.</note>

## The Turk
<note>Refers to Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent (r. 1520–1566), the primary threat to Christian Europe. The humor here lies in applying a Christian liturgical prayer to the "infidel" Sultan.</note>

> We beseech thee that thou wouldst deign to grant peace and true harmony to Christian kings and princes.
<note>original: "Ut regibus & principibus christianis pacem & ueram concordiam donare digneris te rogamus." This is a standard petition from the Litany of the Saints, usually addressed to God. Here, it ironically suggests that only the Sultan’s actions (or restraint) could force the bickering Christian monarchs into unity.</note>

## Exiles of the Kingdom (Hear us)
<note>Refers to the *fuorusciti*—political exiles, specifically those from the Kingdom of Naples who lived in Rome or France and plotted to regain their lands.</note>

> Hail, our hope, to you we exiles cry out.
<note>original: "Spes nostra salue ad te clamamus exules." A parody of the *Salve Regina* ("Hail Holy Queen"), a common prayer. It emphasizes the desperation of those living in political banishment.</note>

## The Voivode
<note>Refers to John Zápolya (1487–1540), the Voivode of Transylvania and a claimant to the Hungarian throne, who was often caught between the Holy Roman Empire and the Ottomans.</note>

> Salvation from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate you.
<note>original: "Salutem ex inimicis nostris & de manu omnia um qui oderunt uos." From the *Benedictus* (Luke 1:71), a prayer for deliverance from enemies, reflecting Zápolya's precarious military position.</note>

## King of Poland
<note>Refers to Sigismund I the Old (r. 1506–1548). Poland was often characterized as the "bulwark" of Christendom against the East.</note>

> I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail.
<note>original: "Rogaui pro te ne dificiat fides tua." From Luke 22:32. This may refer to the religious tensions of the Reformation or Poland's role as a Catholic stronghold.</note>

## King of Tunis
<note>Refers to Mulay Hassan, the ruler of Tunis who was reinstated by Emperor Charles V in 1535 after the conquest of Tunis, making him a client-king of the Christians.</note>

> You are no friend of Caesar.
<note>original: "Non es amicus Cæsaris." From John 19:12. "Caesar" here refers to the Holy Roman Emperor, Charles V. The verse suggests a lack of loyalty or a tenuous alliance.</note>

## Barbarossa
<note>Hayreddin Barbarossa (c. 1478–1546), the famed privateer and Admiral of the Ottoman Fleet who terrorized the Mediterranean.</note>

> He said, "It is I."
<note>original: "Dixit ego sum." From John 18:5. In this context, it evokes the terror inspired by Barbarossa's name alone when his fleet appeared on the horizon.</note>

## Andrea Doria
<note>The Genoese admiral (1466–1560) who famously switched his allegiance from France to Emperor Charles V, changing the course of the Italian Wars.</note>

> And they turned back.
<note>original: "Et abierunt Retrorsum." From John 18:6. This is a clever double entendre referring to his tactical maneuvers at sea and his political "turning back" on his former allies.</note>

## Duke of Savoy
<note>Charles III, Duke of Savoy (r. 1504–1553). His lands were largely occupied and partitioned by the French and the Swiss during this period.</note>

<meta>catchword: They divided</meta>
<note>original catchword: "Diuiserunt." This likely completes the verse from Psalm 22:18: "They divided my garments among them," a poignant reference to the Duke's loss of territory.</note>

These associations mock Henry VIII's marriages, the Sultan's threat to Europe, and the political instability of figures like the Duke of Savoy and Andrea Doria.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the sequence of satirical "fortunes" for European political powers. The previous page ended with an entry for the Ottoman Sultan ("The Turk"). Based on the structure, the first biblical verse on this page serves as the "fortune" for the Sultan, before moving into the major Italian noble houses and the Republic of Venice.</meta>

They divided my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots.
<note>original: "Diuiserunt sibi uestimenta mea & super uestem meam miserunt sortem." From Psalm 22:18. In this context, it likely refers to European powers plotting to divide the territories of the Ottoman Empire—or perhaps the Sultan doing the same to Europe.</note>

### The Marquis of Saluzzo
<note>Likely referring to the final years of the independent Marquisate of Saluzzo, which was a pawn in the wars between France and the Holy Roman Empire.</note>

He went out and wept bitterly.
<note>original: "Exiuit foras & fleuit amare." From Matthew 26:75, describing Saint Peter's regret. This refers to the loss of independence or the political betrayal suffered by the Marquisate.</note>

### The Venetians
<note>The Republic of Venice, the "Serenissima," was a dominant maritime power, though often isolated diplomatically.</note>

But the boat was in the middle of the sea, tossed by the waves, for the wind was against it.
<note>original: "Nauicula autem in medio mari iactabatur fluctibus, erat enim contrarius uentus." From Matthew 14:24. A fitting metaphor for a maritime republic navigating the "stormy" alliances of the Italian Wars.</note>

### Duke of Ferrara
<note>Likely Ercole II d'Este (r. 1534–1559), whose reign was defined by navigating the tensions between France and the Papacy.</note>

This poor man cried out, and the Lord heard him, and saved him from all his troubles.
<note>original: "Iste pauper clamauit & dominus exaudiuit eũ & de omnibus tribulationibus suis saluauit eum." From Psalm 34:6.</note>

### The Duchess
<note>Probably Renée of France, Duchess of Ferrara, known for her controversial religious leanings and her isolation from the court.</note>

On my bed at night I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him but I did not find him.
<note>original: "In lectulo meo per noctes quesiui quem diligit anima mea quesiui illũ & non inueni." From Song of Solomon 3:1.</note>

### Duke of Mantua
<note>Likely Federico II Gonzaga (r. 1519–1540). The Gonzaga family was deeply entangled in both Imperial and Papal politics.</note>

I absolve you from every sentence of <term>greater or lesser excommunication</term>, if you have incurred any.
<note>original: "Absoluo te ab omni sententia excommunicationis maioris uel minoris si quam incurristi." This is the formal formula for sacramental absolution. A "greater" excommunication completely cut one off from the Christian community, while a "lesser" one only barred the person from receiving the sacraments.</note>

### The Duchess
<note>Likely Margaret Palaeologina, Duchess of Mantua.</note>

My inheritance is excellent to me.
<note>original: "Hereditas mea preclara est mihi." From Psalm 16:6. Margaret brought the strategic territory of Montferrat to the Mantuan inheritance.</note>

### Duke of Urbino
<note>Likely Francesco Maria I della Rovere, whose career was marked by losing and regaining his duchy.</note>

Neither for me nor for you.
<note>original: "Nec mihi nec tibi." From 1 Kings 3:26, the Judgement of Solomon. This suggests a stalemate or a territory that neither claimant can truly possess.</note>

### Duchess of Urbino
<note>Eleonora Gonzaga, Duchess of Urbino.</note>

Our inheritance has been turned over to strangers, and our houses to foreigners.
<note>original: "Hereditas nostra conuersa est ad alienos & domus nostre ad extraneos." From Lamentations 5:2. This refers to the periods when the Della Rovere family was exiled and their lands seized by the Medici or the Papacy.</note>

### The Widowed Duchess
<note>Likely a reference to a prominent widow of the era, such as Christina of Denmark (widow of the Duke of Milan) or perhaps a general personification of the many noblewomen widowed by the Italian Wars.</note>

My sorrow is always in my sight.
<note>original: "Dolor meus in conspectu meo semper." From Psalm 38:17.</note>

<meta>This page continues a series of satirical "fortunes" or prophetic mottos for Italian political figures and states, following the previous page's focus on the Duke of Ferrara and his Duchess. The text now moves to the powerful Medici family in Florence, the Sienese Republic, and the Farnese family (the Duke of Castro, Ottavio, and the influential women of that house).</meta>

### The Duke of Florence
<note>Referring to Cosimo I de’ Medici (r. 1537–1574), who transformed Florence from a fragile republic into a stable hereditary duchy. This verse suggests a divine or imperial decree that his rule should remain undisturbed.</note>
> I will that he remain so until I come.
<note>original: "Sic eum uolo manere donec ueniam." From John 21:22. In the Gospel, Jesus speaks of the apostle John; here, it implies the Duke’s power is fixed and enduring.</note>

### The Castellans of Florence
<note>The "Castellani" were the commanders or guards of the city's fortresses, particularly the Fortezza da Basso, which was a symbol of both imperial protection and Medici control over the citizens.</note>
> We have no king but Caesar.
<note>original: "Non habemus Regem nisi Caesarem." From John 19:15. This satirizes the garrison’s loyalty to the Holy Roman Emperor, Charles V, rather than to the old Florentine ideals of liberty.</note>

### The Florentine Republic
<note>The Republic had effectively ended with the return of the Medici and the siege of 1530. By the time this was written, the Republic was a "dead" political entity.</note>
> Grant them eternal rest, O Lord.
<note>original: "Requiem aeternam dona eis Domine." From the Introit of the Latin Requiem Mass. This is a biting political joke: the Republic is dead and buried.</note>

### The Exiles
<note>The *fuorusciti* were the anti-Medici political exiles who fled Florence. Many were wealthy merchants and intellectuals who tried, and failed, to overthrow Cosimo I at the Battle of Montemurlo in 1537.</note>
> Lord, forgive them, for they know not what they do.
<note>original: "Domine ignosce illis quia nesciunt quid faciūt." From Luke 23:34, the words of Christ on the cross. This portrays the exiles as either tragic martyrs or perhaps mocks their political incompetence.</note>

### Lorenzino de’ Medici
<note>Lorenzo di Pierfrancesco de' Medici, nicknamed "Lorenzino" or "Lorenzaccio," who famously assassinated his cousin, Duke Alessandro de' Medici, in 1537.</note>
> This is the heir; come, let us kill him.
<note>original: "Hic est haeres uenite occidamus eum." From Matthew 21:38, the Parable of the Wicked Tenants. This is a literal reference to Lorenzino’s plot to eliminate the head of the Medici family.</note>

### The Sienese
<note>The Republic of Siena was known for internal factionalism and its long-standing rivalry with Florence. It would eventually lose its independence to Cosimo I in 1555.</note>
> O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you?
<note>original: "O Insensati galate quis uos fascinauit." From Galatians 3:1. This mocks the Sienese for their perceived political madness or for being "bewitched" into a conflict they could not win.</note>

### The Duke of Castro
<note>Pier Luigi Farnese (1503–1547), the illegitimate son of Pope Paul III. He was granted the Duchy of Castro and later Parma and Piacenza. He was a deeply controversial and often hated figure.</note>
> Let us break their bonds asunder.
<note>original: "Dirumpamus uincula eorum." From Psalm 2:3. This refers to the Duke’s attempts to break the power of the local nobility or perhaps his desire to break free from imperial control.</note>

### The Duchess
<note>Likely Gerolama Orsini, wife of Pier Luigi Farnese, though the quote is a standard Marian liturgical phrase.</note>
> After childbirth, you remained an inviolate virgin.
<note>original: "Post partum uirgo inuiolata permansisti." From the Marian Liturgy. Used here, it likely serves as a sarcastic comment on the Duchess’s reputation or her relationship with her husband.</note>

### Madame
<note>Margaret of Austria (1522–1586), the illegitimate daughter of Emperor Charles V. She was the widow of Alessandro de' Medici and later married Ottavio Farnese.</note>
> Woman, why are you weeping?
<note>original: "Mulier quid ploras." From John 20:15. This likely refers to her difficult position as a political widow caught between the interests of the Emperor and the Farnese family.</note>

### Lord Ottavio
<note>Ottavio Farnese (1524–1586), Duke of Parma and Piacenza, and husband of Margaret of Austria.</note>
> But what I have, I give to you.
<note>original: "Quod autem habeo hoc tibi do." From Acts 3:6. The words of St. Peter to a lame man. In this context, it may refer to Ottavio’s reliance on his father or the Pope for his titles and lands.</note>

### Lady Costanza
<note>Costanza Farnese (1500–1545), the influential daughter of Pope Paul III. She was known for wielding significant power at the papal court on behalf of her children.</note>
> Lord, command that these two sons of mine may sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your kingdom.
<note>original: "Domine dic ut sedeant hij duo filij mei unus ad dextram & unus ad sinistram in Regno tuo." From Matthew 20:21. A perfect description of Costanza’s nepotism in securing high positions (like the cardinalate) for her sons, Guido Ascanio and Alessandro Sforza.</note>

### Lady Vittoria
<note>Vittoria Farnese (1519–1602), daughter of Pier Luigi Farnese. She eventually married Guidobaldo II della Rovere, Duke of Urbino.</note>
> Come, bride of Christ, receive the crown which the [Lord...]
<note>original: "Veni sponsa christi accipe coronam quam tibi [dominus...]" From the Common of Virgins in the Liturgy of the Hours. This likely refers to her prestigious marriage prospects.</note>

...the Lord has prepared.
<note>original: "dominus preparauit." This is the conclusion of a sentence from the previous page, likely referring to the fate of the Florentine exiles.</note>

### Lord Girolamo Orsini
<note>Girolamo Orsini (d. 1540s) was a member of the powerful Orsini clan and lord of Bracciano. The Orsini were traditional rivals of the Colonna family.</note>
*Even until the night, my conscience has rebuked me.*
<note>original: "Vsq; ad noctem increpuerunt me renes mei." From Psalm 16:7. In early modern thought, the "reins" (kidneys) were seen as the seat of the conscience or hidden emotions.</note>

### The Wife of Lord Girolamo
<note>Referencing Francesca Sforza di Santa Fiora. This quote suggests a state of overwhelming distress or drowning in sorrow.</note>
*The waters have entered even unto my soul.*
<note>original: "Intrauerunt aquæ usque animam meam." From Psalm 69:1.</note>

### The Abbot of Farfa
<note>The Abbey of Farfa was one of the wealthiest and most influential Benedictine houses in Italy, often held by members of the Orsini family. The use of this verse for a powerful prelate may be a sarcastic comment on his proximity to power.</note>
*This is that disciple who reclined upon the breast of the Lord.*
<note>original: "Hic est discipulus ille qui supra pectus domini Recubuit." From John 21:24/13:23, referring to the "Beloved Disciple."</note>

### The Hunchback of Sermoneta
<note>Likely referring to a member of the Caetani family, who held the Duchy of Sermoneta. The choice of the Pharisee's prayer is a biting satirical joke, playing on the man's physical deformity to suggest his "uniqueness" is not a virtue.</note>
*God, I give thanks to you because I am not like other men.*
<note>original: "Deus ago tibi gratias quia non sum sicut Ceteri homines." From the Parable of the Pharisee and the Publican, Luke 18:11.</note>

### Lord Ascanio Colonna
<note>Ascanio Colonna (1500–1557) was a powerful Roman nobleman and Grand Constable of Naples. He famously rebelled against Pope Paul III during the "Salt War."</note>
*Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me? It is hard for you to kick against the goad.*
<note>original: "Saule saule, Quid me persequeris durum est tibi contra stimulum calcitrare." From Acts 9:4. This suggests Ascanio is a rebel or a persecutor of the Church who is fighting a losing battle.</note>

### Doña Juana
<note>Giovanna d'Aragona (1502–1575), wife of Ascanio Colonna and a famous beauty and patron of the arts. She was of royal Spanish-Neapolitan blood.</note>
*Man ate the bread of angels.*
<note>original: "Panem angelicum manducauit homo." From Psalm 78:25. This likely refers to her high status or perhaps her renowned celestial beauty.</note>

### The Vice-Roy of Naples
<note>Don Pedro de Toledo, the iron-fisted Spanish governor of Naples (r. 1532–1553). This motto captures the deep-seated resentment the Neapolitan people felt toward their Spanish ruler.</note>
*This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me.*
<note>original: "Populus hic me labijs honorat Cor autem eorum longe est à me." From Matthew 15:8.</note>

### Lord Don Ferrante
<note>Ferrante Gonzaga (1507–1557), a brilliant military commander and Governor of Milan, brother to the Duke of Mantua.</note>
*He shall rain snares upon sinners.*
<note>original: "Pluet super peccatores laqueos." From Psalm 11:6. This characterizes Ferrante as a stern judge or a dangerous military opponent.</note>

### The Princess, his wife
<note>Isabella di Capua (d. 1559), Princess of Molfetta and wife of Ferrante Gonzaga. The verse describes the relief of a mother after childbirth.</note>
*She no longer remembers the anguish because of the joy that a man is born into the world.*
<note>original: "Iam non meminit pressuræ propter gaudium quia natus est homo in mundum." From John 16:21.</note>

## Marquis of Vasto
<note>Alfonso d'Avalos (1502–1546), Marquis of Vasto and Pescara, was a preeminent Neapolitan military commander for Emperor Charles V and later the Governor of Milan.</note>

->*He gathered the wheat into his granary.*<-
<note>original: "Congregauit triticum in horreum suum." From Matthew 3:12. This may refer to the Marquis's success in provisioning the imperial armies or his great personal wealth and accumulation of titles.</note>

## The Marchioness, his wife
<note>Maria d'Aragona (1503–1568), wife of Alfonso d'Avalos. She was a central figure in Neapolitan cultural life and a patron of the arts.</note>

->*Since she stands behind our wall, looking*<-
->*through the lattices.*<-
<note>original: "Cum ipsa stat post parietem nostram respiciens per cancellos." From the Song of Solomon 2:9. This poetic verse likely alludes to her beauty or her life within the courtly domestic sphere while her husband was away at war.</note>

## Milan
<note>The Duchy of Milan was a major point of contention between the French and the Spanish-Habsburgs. This verse critiques the city's relationship with its rulers.</note>

->*They sent an embassy after him, saying, "We will*<-
->*not have this man reign over us."*<-
<note>original: "Miserunt legationem post illum dicentes uolumus hunc Regnare supra nos." From Luke 19:14. This is a biting political commentary on the resistance or dissatisfaction of the Milanese toward their foreign governors.</note>

## Marchioness of Pescara
<note>Vittoria Colonna (1492–1457), perhaps the most famous woman of the Italian Renaissance, a celebrated poet and a leader of the "Spirituali" religious reform movement.</note>

->*Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about*<-
->*many things; one thing is necessary,*<-
<note>original: "Marta marta solicita es & occuparis erga plurima unum est necessarium." From Luke 10:41-42. This is a clever play on Vittoria's public life: despite her fame for religious contemplation (the "Mary" role), she was constantly entangled in the political and reformist "business" (the "Martha" role) of her era.</note>

## Friar Bernardo Scapunic-
## cino
<note>Likely a reference to a specific monk or preacher known in these court circles, possibly a diminutive or nickname.</note>

->*It is not good for man to be alone; let us make*<-
->*him a helper fit for him.*<-
<note>original: "Non est bonum hominem esse solum faciamus ei adiutorium simile sui." From Genesis 2:18. Applying the verse regarding the creation of Eve to a friar is a standard satirical trope of the period, poking fun at the perceived lack of celibacy among the clergy.</note>

## Prince of Sulmona
<note>The title "Prince of Sulmona" (here transcribed as "Salmone") was held by the Lannoy family, starting with Charles de Lannoy, the commander who captured the French king at the Battle of Pavia.</note>

->*He shall leave father and mother and shall cleave*<-
->*to his wife.*<-
<note>original: "Relinquet patrem & matrem & adherebit uxori suæ." From Genesis 2:24. This could be a literal reference to a notable marriage or a humorous observation on the Prince's domesticity.</note>

## The Princess

->*And he saw that it was good.*<-
<note>original: "Et uidit quod esset bonum." From the creation story in Genesis 1. This is a common courtly compliment to a lady’s virtue or appearance.</note>

## Lady Giulia
<note>Giulia Gonzaga (1513–1566), Countess of Fondi. She was legendary for her beauty—so much so that the pirate Barbarossa tried to kidnap her for the Sultan—and she was a key figure in religious reform circles.</note>

->*How admirable is your name in all the*<-
->*earth.*<-
<note>original: "Quam admirabile est nomen tuum in uniuersa terra." From Psalm 8:1. A fitting tribute to a woman whose reputation for beauty and intellect was known throughout Europe.</note>

## Lady Camilla di Novellara
<note>Camilla Gonzaga (1500–1585), of the Novellara branch of the family, known for her prominence in the courts of northern Italy.</note>

->*His face shone like the sun.*<-
<note>original: "Resplenduit facies eius sicut sol." From Matthew 17:2, describing the Transfiguration of Jesus. Here, the masculine pronoun of the Latin is applied to a woman to praise her radiant beauty.</note>

## Signora Ginevra Malatesta
<note>Ginevra Malatesta was a member of the illustrious Malatesta family of Rimini; this verse may refer to her personal tribulations or the waning power of her house.</note>

## Countess of Maschera
<note>The "Contessa di Maschera" likely refers to a member of the Mascheroni family or perhaps a satirical title (maschera meaning mask).</note>

*“Why do you trouble this woman? For she has wrought a good work.”*
<note>original: "Quid molesti estis huic mulieri bonum enim opus operata est." From Matthew 26:10. In the Gospel, Jesus says this to defend a woman who anointed him with expensive oil; here it suggests the Countess is being unfairly criticized for her actions.</note>

## Marchioness of Massa
<note>Ricciarda Malaspina (1497–1553) was the sovereign Marchioness of Massa and Carrara. She was known for her intense legal and political battles, even against her own children.</note>

*“My bone cleaves to my skin and to my flesh, and there are left only the lips around my teeth.”*
<note>original: "Pelli mee consumpsis carnibus ad hescit os meū & derelicta sunt tantummodo labia circa dentes meos." From Job 19:20. This stark image of physical decay or extreme suffering may mock her aging or her notorious hardships.</note>

## Marquis of Aguilar
<note>Juan de Silva y Rivera, Marquis of Aguilar de Campoo, served as the Spanish Ambassador to Rome for Emperor Charles V during the 1540s.</note>

*“Arise, make haste, my love, my dove, my beautiful one.”*
<note>original: "Surge propera amica mea columba mea formosa mea." From the Song of Solomon 2:10. This romantic verse is likely a satirical commentary on the Marquis's courtly manners or perhaps an illicit dalliance.</note>

## The Valenzuela
<note>Likely a reference to a Spanish courtier or official named Valenzuela, a common name in the Imperial administration.</note>

*“He sought an opportunity to betray him.”*
<note>original: "Opportunitatem querebat ut eum traderet." From Matthew 26:16. This verse associates the figure with Judas Iscariot, accusing him of treachery or political backstabbing.</note>

## Ambassador of France
<note>During this period, the French ambassadors (such as Georges d'Armagnac or Jean de Morvillier) were constantly maneuvering against Spanish interests in Italy.</note>

*“Be valiant in war and fight with the old serpent, and you shall receive an eternal kingdom.”*
<note>original: "Estote fortes in bello & pugnate cum antiquo serpente & accipietis Regnum eternum." From a Catholic responsory based on Hebrews 11:34 and Revelation. It frames the French political struggle as a holy or epic crusade.</note>

## Morlue
<note>Likely Jean de Morvillier (1506–1577), a French diplomat and Bishop of Orléans, who was active in Italian diplomacy.</note>

*“There arose a dispute among them, as to which of them should be seen as the greatest.”*
<note>original: "Facta est contentio inter eos quis eorum uideretur esse maior." From Luke 22:24. This mocks the pride and procedural squabbles regarding rank and precedence among the diplomats.</note>

## Ambassador of Portugal
<note>Cristóvão de Sousa Falcão was one of the Portuguese envoys in this era, often concerned with trade and religious jurisdiction.</note>

*“To what purpose is this waste?”*
<note>original: "Vt quid perdicio haec." From Matthew 26:8. This likely critiques the perceived extravagance or the high cost of the Portuguese embassy's activities.</note>

## Ambassador of Venice
<note>The Venetian ambassadors were famous for their detailed reports (*relazioni*) and their vast network of informants.</note>

*“The very hairs of your head are all numbered.”*
<note>original: "Vestri capilli capitis omnes numerati sunt." From Matthew 10:30. A witty reference to the Venetian reputation for obsessive surveillance and knowing everyone's secrets.</note>

<meta>This page continues the satirical catalog of high-ranking officials, diplomats, and clergy associated with the Roman Curia in the mid-16th century. Like the previous page, it assigns a specific biblical verse to each person, often with a biting or ironic subtext regarding their character or political situation.</meta>

### Ambassador of Ferrara
<note>The Ambassador of the Duchy of Ferrara, representing the House of Este. The Este family was famous for its diplomatic maneuvers and the lavishness of its gifts to the Papacy.</note>
*“We have come with gifts to adore him.”*
<note>original: "Venimus cum muneribus adorare eum." Derived from Matthew 2:2, describing the Magi. In a diplomatic context, this suggests the bribery or "gift-giving" required to maintain favor in Rome.</note>

### Ambassador of Urbino
<note>Representing the Duchy of Urbino, governed by the Della Rovere family. Their relationship with the Papacy was often fraught with tension over territory.</note>
*“He takes away mortal things who gives celestial kingdoms.”*
<note>original: "Eripit mortalia qui Regna dat Celeſtia." A line from the hymn *Crudelis Herodes* by Sedulius. It implies that while the Pope (the giver of "celestial kingdoms") may take away earthly lands, he offers spiritual ones in return—a sarcastic comment on Papal land-grabs.</note>

### Archbishop Colonna
<note>Likely referring to a member of the powerful Colonna clan, such as Cardinal Pompeo Colonna or a relative. The family was frequently at war with the Popes.</note>
*“Trouble me not; the door is now shut, and my children are with me in bed.”*
<note>original: "Noli mihi moleſtus eſſe iam clauſum eſt oſtium & pueri mei mecum ſunt in cubili." From Luke 11:7. This suggests the Colonna family's refusal to help others or their isolationist and defensive stance within their Roman palaces.</note>

### Archbishop of Benevento
<note>Giovanni della Casa (1503–1556) held this title. While famous for his book on manners, *Galateo*, his career was marked by ambition and controversy.</note>
*“He offered him money, saying: Give me also this power.”*
<note>original: "Obtulit ei pecuniam dicens, date mihi hanc poteſtatem." From Acts 8:18. This is an accusation of Simony—the sin of attempting to buy spiritual power or church offices with money.</note>

### Bishop of Bologna
<note>Bologna was the second most important city in the Papal States. Its bishopric was a prestigious and often politically sensitive position.</note>
*“We are become orphans without a father.”*
<note>original: "Pupilli facti ſumus abſque patre." From Lamentations 5:3. This may refer to a period of "Sede Vacante" (a vacant see) or a feeling that the city had been abandoned by its protector.</note>

### Sebastian da Cona, by grace Bishop of Segni
<note>Sebastianus de Gona (or da Cona) served as Bishop of Segni from 1541 to 1548. This entry is particularly insulting.</note>
*“The reproach of men and the outcast of the people.”*
<note>original: "Opprobrium hominum & obiectio plebis." From Psalm 22:6. This verse describes the suffering Christ, but here it is used to mock the Bishop as a man universally despised.</note>

### Paolo Giovio
<note>The manuscript writes "Gaionico Iouio," likely a corruption of "Paolo Giovio" (1483–1552), the famous historian and Bishop of Nocera. He was known for his sharp tongue and sometimes dubious historical accuracy.</note>
*“He himself bore our sins in his body.”*
<note>original: "Peccata noſtra ipſe pertulit in corpore ſuo." From 1 Peter 2:24. Applied to Giovio, this may mock his personal vices or his role in chronicling the "sins" of others in his histories.</note>

### Sinolfo Petrucci
<note>A member of the Sienese Petrucci family and a clerk of the Apostolic Camera, Sinolfo was a well-known figure in Roman financial circles.</note>
*“For they knew him in the breaking [of bread].”*
<note>original: "Cognouerunt enim in fractione." From Luke 24:35. This is likely a pun on the word "fractione" (breaking), perhaps referring to the "breaking" of a contract, the splitting of profits, or his eventual financial ruin.</note>

### Durante
<note>Likely Durante Duranti (1507–1558), who was a trusted favorite of Pope Paul III and eventually became a Cardinal.</note>
*“By the grace of God I am what I am.”*
<note>original: "Gratia dei ſum id quod ſum." From 1 Corinthians 15:10. While a statement of humility for St. Paul, here it likely mocks Duranti’s rapid rise to power, implying he had little merit of his own.</note>

### Latino Giovenale
<note>Latino Giovenale Manetti (1486–1553) was a Roman diplomat and the "Commissary of Antiquities." He was responsible for many urban renovations in Rome.</note>
*“I will destroy this temple and in three days [rebuild it].”*
<note>original: "Deſtruam templum hoc & triduo." From Mark 14:58. This refers to his reputation for demolishing ancient ruins or old buildings to make way for new Papal projects.</note>

### Bishop of Spain
<note>This likely refers to the Spanish Ambassador to the Vatican or a high-ranking Spanish prelate residing in Rome.</note>
*“Amen I say to thee, thou shalt not go out from thence till thou repay [the last farthing].”*
<note>original: "Amen dico tibi non exies inde Donec reddas." From Matthew 5:26. A reference to debt or perhaps a political stalemate where the Spanish interest was "held hostage" by financial or diplomatic obligations.</note>

<note>original: "nouiſsimum quadrantem." This is the conclusion of a verse from the previous page, likely Matthew 5:26: "Truly, I say to you, you will never get out until you have paid the last penny."</note>

## Benvenuto
<note>Likely Benvenuto Cellini (1500–1571), the famous goldsmith and sculptor known for his violent temper and frequent brushes with the law.</note>
“Which of the two do you want me to release to you?” And they said, “Barabbas.”
<note>original: "Quem uultis uobis dimitti de duobus ? illi dixerunt barrabam." From Matthew 27:21. By comparing the subject to Barabbas, the criminal chosen for release over Jesus, the author implies the subject is a notorious rogue or villain.</note>

## Ambrogione
<note>Likely referring to Ambrogio Recalcati, a powerful secretary to Pope Paul III who eventually fell from grace.</note>
“By now he stinks, for he has been there four days.”
<note>original: "Iam fetet quia triduanus est." From John 11:39, regarding the death of Lazarus. In this context, it suggests the subject is morally corrupt or that his reputation is "dead" and decaying.</note>

## Varchi of Pescia
<note>Benedetto Varchi (1503–1565), a famous humanist, historian, and poet from Pescia. He was a prominent figure in the literary academies of the time.</note>
“He grew fat, he grew thick, he was covered with fatness.”
<note>original: "Incraſsatus impinguatus dilatatus." Derived from Deuteronomy 32:15. This is a jab at Varchi's physical weight or perhaps his perceived intellectual complacency after finding patronage.</note>

## Giovanni della Casa
<note>Giovanni della Casa (1503–1556), an archbishop and poet best known for his treatise on etiquette, *Il Galateo*. He served as a papal nuncio.</note>
“He wrote, saying, ‘John is his name,’ and they all wondered.”
<note>original: "Scripsit dicens Ioannes est nomen & admirati sunt omnes." From Luke 1:63, concerning the naming of John the Baptist. This is a literal pun on his name (Giovanni/John) and perhaps a comment on his fame as a writer.</note>

## "Dried Meat"
<note>Italian: "Il Carne secca." This was likely a nickname for a thin, gaunt, or perhaps stingy individual in the papal court.</note>
“That disciple was known to the high priest.”
<note>original: "Discipulus ille erat notus pontifici." From John 18:15. This suggests the individual is an "insider" or a spy within the Vatican who has special access to the Pope.</note>

## Ubaldino
<note>Likely Roberto Ubaldini or another member of the noble Florentine Ubaldini family active in Rome.</note>
“Have I been with you all this time, and you still do not know me?”
<note>original: "Tanto tempore uobiscum ſum & non cognouiſtis me." From John 14:9. This might mock the subject's self-importance or his failure to make a lasting impression despite being a long-time fixture at court.</note>

## Molza
<note>Francesco Maria Molza (1489–1544), a celebrated poet of the Renaissance. He was notorious for his scandalous lifestyle and for contracting syphilis.</note>
“We have been saved by means of wood.”
<note>original: "Propter lignum salui facti ſumus." While this traditionally refers to the wood of the Cross (Wisdom 14:7), here it is a crude joke. Molza was known to have used "guaiacum" (known as "holy wood" or *lignum vitae*) as a treatment for the "French disease" (syphilis).</note>

## Cesano
<note>Gabriele Cesano (1490–1568), a bishop and diplomat who was part of the inner circle of the Medici and later the French court.</note>
“Am I a Jew?”
<note>original: "Nunquid iudeus ſum ego." From John 18:35, spoken by Pontius Pilate. This could be a joke about his lineage, his loyalty, or his attempt to distance himself from a controversial decision.</note>

## Claudio Tolomei
<note>Claudio Tolomei (1492–1556), an influential philologist and bishop who attempted to reform Italian spelling and verse.</note>
“This is a hard saying; who can listen to it?”
<note>original: "Durus est hic ſermo & quis poteſt eum audire." From John 6:60. This mocks Tolomei's dense, academic style of writing or his difficult linguistic theories.</note>

## Pier Giunchi
<note>A lesser-known figure, likely a courtier or minor official in the Roman circle.</note>
“Her many sins are forgiven, for she loved much.”
<note>original: "Remittuntur ei peccata multa, quoniam dilexit multum." From Luke 7:47, regarding the woman who anointed Jesus' feet. Applying this feminine verse to a man was a common satirical way to insult his masculinity or mock a history of sexual promiscuity.</note>

<meta>This page continues the satirical catalog of Roman figures and institutions, using the format of a pasquinade—a traditional form of Roman satire where mocking verses are posted on a statue. The previous page ended with a verse concerning the "last penny," and the catchword for this page is "Sepulchrum" (Tomb), though the text begins immediately with the list of targets.</meta>

# For Petro Nullini
<note>This is likely a pun on the name Pietro and the Latin "nullus," meaning "nobody" or "nothing."</note>
->*Whoever exalts himself shall be humbled.*<-
<note>original: "Qui se exaltat humiliabitur." From Matthew 23:12. This mocks the subject's vanity or social climbing.</note>

# For Julio Porcaro
<note>Giulio Porcari was a member of a prominent Roman family; the name "Porcaro" literally translates to "swineherd," providing an easy target for satire.</note>
->*I will return to my house from which I came.*<-
<note>original: "Reuertar in domum meam unde exiui." From Matthew 12:44, spoken by an unclean spirit. It implies the subject is a demon or a persistent nuisance.</note>

# For the Conservators of Rome
<note>The "Conservatori" were the high-ranking municipal magistrates of the city, responsible for civil administration.</note>
->*Why do you stand here idle all day?*<-
<note>original: "Quid statis tota die ociosi." From Matthew 20:6. This is a jab at the perceived laziness or uselessness of the city’s civic leaders.</note>

# For the Governor of Rome
<note>The Governor was the chief judicial and police official in the city, typically a prelate.</note>
->*With him was a great crowd with swords and clubs.*<-
<note>original: "Cum eo turba multa cum gladijs & fustibus." From Matthew 26:47, describing the mob that came to arrest Jesus. It likens the Governor's guards to a band of thugs.</note>

# For Rome
->*Simon Peter, do you love me? Feed my sheep.*<-
<note>original: "Simon petre diligis me pasce oues meas." From John 21:17. In a satirical context, this highlights the gap between the Papacy's pastoral duty to care for the faithful and its actual political or financial interests.</note>

# For the Rota
<note>The Roman Rota is the highest ecclesiastical court of the Catholic Church.</note>
->*They devour my people as they eat bread.*<-
<note>original: "Deuorant plebem meam sicut escam panis." From Psalm 14:4. This accuses the legal system of being predatory and "consuming" the common people through fees and corruption.</note>

# For the College of Bishops
->*There was a herd of many swine there.*<-
<note>original: "Erat ibi grex porcorum multorum." From Matthew 8:30, regarding the Gerasene swine into which demons were cast. A biting comparison of high-ranking clergy to a pack of pigs.</note>

# For the Priests
->*There is no one who does good, not even one.*<-
<note>original: "Non est qui faciat bonum non est usque ad unum." From Psalm 14:3. A blanket condemnation of the morality of the Roman priesthood.</note>

# For the Friars
->*Love your wives.*<-
<note>original: "Diligite uxores uestras." From Ephesians 5:25. Since friars take a vow of celibacy, this mocks their frequent and well-known violations of that vow.</note>

# For the Nuns
->*Be subject to your husbands.*<-
<note>original: "Estote subdite uiris uestris." From Ephesians 5:22. Similar to the jab at the friars, this implies that the nuns are not living as chaste "brides of Christ" but have secret lovers.</note>

# For the Soldiers
->*They gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ.*<-
<note>original: "Conuenerunt in unum ad uersum Dominum & ad uersum Christum eius." From Psalm 2:2. This suggests that the mercenary forces in Rome are effectively enemies of the faith they are meant to protect.</note>

# For the Courtiers

Their belly is an open sepulcher.
<note>original: "Sepulchrum patens est uenter eorum." A variation of Psalm 5:9. In this satirical context, it likely accuses the subjects of gluttony, greed, or consuming the wealth of others.</note>

## For the Caroli Families.
<note>Italian: "Famiglie di Caroli." This likely refers to the partisans or family of Emperor Charles V (Carlo), or perhaps a specific Roman noble house like the Caroli.</note>

->I have compassion on this crowd.<-
<note>original: "Misereor super turbam hanc." From Matthew 15:32. Here it mocks the large, perhaps unruly or desperate, following of these families.</note>

## For the Kings of the Church.
<note>Italian: "Re' de la chiesia." This is a biting reference to the Popes or high-ranking Cardinals who lived with the wealth and power of secular monarchs.</note>

->As it was in the beginning, and now, and always, and for ever and ever, amen.<-
<note>original: "Sicut erat in principio..." This is the "Gloria Patri," a standard prayer. The satirist uses it here to suggest that the corruption or worldly nature of the Church hierarchy is eternal and unchanging.</note>

## For the Council.
<note>Italian: "Concilio." Likely referring to the ongoing or anticipated church councils intended to address the Reformation (such as the Council of Trent). The satire suggests the Council is ineffective or non-existent.</note>

->He is risen, he is not here; behold the place where they laid him.<-
<note>original: "Surrexit non est hic..." From Mark 16:6, describing the empty tomb of Christ. By applying this to the Council, the author implies that the meeting is "dead" or that nothing of substance can be found where it is supposed to be.</note>

## The Meeting and the Kissing
### Between the Emperor and the King.
<note>Italian: "Labbocamento e uasamento Del Inperatore el ue [re]." This refers to the diplomatic summits between the great rivals Emperor Charles V and King Francis I of France. The "kiss of peace" was a formal protocol that rarely reflected true friendship.</note>

->O wonderful exchange.<-
<note>original: "O ad mirabile commercium." A liturgical antiphon. In this context, it sarcastically describes the cynical political trade-offs and "buying and selling" of territories between the two monarchs.</note>

## The Restitution of Milan.
<note>Italian: "La restitution di millano." The Duchy of Milan was a central prize in the Italian Wars, frequently changing hands between French and Imperial forces.</note>

->It shall not be forgiven him, neither in this world, nor in the world to come.<-
<note>original: "Non remittitur ei in hoc seculo neq; in alio." From Matthew 12:32, regarding the "unforgivable sin." The satirist jokes that the loss of Milan is a permanent state that will never be reversed.</note>

## Italy.

->Her people groan and seek bread.<-
<note>original: "Populus eius gemens & querens panem." From Lamentations 1:11. This reflects the genuine suffering, famine, and economic ruin brought upon the Italian peninsula by constant warfare.</note>

## France.

->Wash yourselves and be clean.<-
<note>original: "Lauamini & mundi estote." From Isaiah 1:16. This may be an allusion to the perceived moral or religious "stains" of the French court, or a jab at their alliances.</note>

## Germany.
<note>Italian: "Lamagna," an archaic term for *La Magna* (Allemagna).</note>

->Behold, your King comes to you, peaceful, sitting upon a donkey.<-
<note>original: "Ecce Rex tuus uenit tibi pacificus sedens super asinum." From Matthew 21:5, describing Jesus' entry into Jerusalem. This is a satirical mockery of the Emperor's entry into German lands, perhaps contrasting his military power with a false image of peace.</note>

## Spain.

->O faithless and perverse generation.<-
<note>original: "O generatio incredula & peruersa." From Matthew 17:17. A common Roman insult toward the Spanish, who were often viewed with suspicion regarding the sincerity of their faith (due to the history of the Inquisition and "New Christians").</note>

## Brother Baccio.
<note>Italian: "Fra Baccio." This likely refers to Baccio Valori, a powerful and controversial Florentine politician and soldier who often acted on behalf of the Medici popes.</note>

->God has chosen the foolish things of the world.<-
<note>original: "Quæ stulta sunt mundi elegit Deus." From 1 Corinthians 1:27. A typical "Pasquinade" insult, suggesting the subject is a fool who has been inexplicably elevated by divine (or papal) whim.</note>

### Marforio.

# THE VERGILIAN LOTS *collected by Pasquin.*
<term>Vergilian Lots|Known as "Sortes Vergilianae," this was a classical form of divination where one would open a volume of Virgil's poetry at random to find a verse that predicted the future. Here, Pasquin uses the practice to find "prophecies" that insult the Pope.</term>

## The Pope to whom the defection of *England* happened unexpectedly.
<note>This refers to the English Reformation and Henry VIII’s break from the Roman Catholic Church, which was a staggering loss of power and revenue for the Papacy.</note>

Neither the prophet Helenus, though he warned me of many horrors, predicted these sorrows for me.
<note>original: "Nec uates Helenus..." From Virgil’s Aeneid, Book 3, lines 712–713. In the epic, Helenus is a seer; here, the verse suggests that even the best prophets could not have foreseen the "horror" of losing England.</note>

### The Pope hated by both Germans and Italians.

For whom there is no place anywhere among the Greeks, and furthermore, the Trojans themselves are hostile.
<note>original: "Cui neq; apud Danaos..." From the Aeneid, Book 2, lines 67–72. In this political lampoon, the Greeks and Trojans represent the Germans (associated with the Protestant Reformation) and the Italians (subject to the Pope’s local rule), both of whom are depicted as being at odds with the Pontiff.</note>

### The Pope who was insignificant before his primacy was claimed.

Not yet did Troy and the citadels of Pergamum stand; he lived in the lowest valleys.
<note>original: "Nondum ilium..." From the Aeneid, Book 3, lines 109–110. This verse mocks the humble or perhaps lowly origins of a Pope before he attained the heights of the "citadel" of the Vatican.</note>

--- Page 555 ---
<meta>This page continues the "Vergilian Lots" (Sortes Vergilianae) begun on the previous page. These are satirical applications of Virgil’s classical poetry to the contemporary religious and political crisis of the Reformation. Each heading describes a specific grievance or situation, followed by a verse from the *Aeneid* repurposed as a prophecy or commentary on the Papacy.</meta>

## The Pope grieving that he did not crush Luther at the beginning.

*And Troy would now stand, and you, high citadel of Priam, would remain.*
<note>original: "Troiaque nunc stares priamique arx alta maneres." From Virgil’s Aeneid, Book 2, line 56. This suggests that if the Pope had suppressed Martin Luther immediately, the "citadel" of the Roman Church would still be secure.</note>

## The Pope made great from nothing.

*Sent from small Cures and a poor land into a great empire.*
<note>original: "Curibus paruis & paupere terra Missus in imperium magnum." From Virgil’s Aeneid, Book 6, lines 811–812. Cures was a humble Sabine town; the verse mocks the Pope’s rise from modest origins to vast worldly power.</note>

## To those who want the Pope to preside over the Council.

*Do you place the ill-omened monster in the sacred citadel?*
<note>original: "An monstrum infelix sacrata sistitis arce?" From Virgil’s Aeneid, Book 2, line 245, referring to the Trojan Horse. Here, the "monster" is the Pope, and the "sacred citadel" is the Church Council.</note>

## The doctrine of the Protestants.

*Let pure descendants remain in this religious practice.*
<note>original: "Hæc casti maneant in religione nepotes." From Virgil’s Aeneid, Book 3, line 409. This implies the Protestant movement is a return to a "pure" or uncorrupted form of worship.</note>

## The Sophist Theologians.

*They defile everything with their filthy touch.*
<note>original: "Contractuque omnia fœdant Inmundo." From Virgil’s Aeneid, Book 3, lines 227–228. Originally describing the Harpies, this verse is used here to accuse Catholic scholastic theologians of corrupting divine truth with their arguments.</note>

## The Pope despising the predictions of his own ruin.

*If the Phrygians boast of any divine responses on their behalf, I too have my own fates to counter them.*
<note>original: "Si qua phryges pro se iactant responsa deorum Sunt & mea contra fata mihi." From Virgil’s Aeneid, Book 9, lines 134–136. The "Phrygians" represent the Protestants; the Pope is depicted as arrogantly asserting his own divine right to rule against them.</note>

## The Nations oppressed by the Pope's Tyranny.

*All confess they know what the fortune of the people brings, but they hesitate to speak.*
<note>original: "Cuncti se scire fatentur. Quid fortuna ferat populi, sed dicere mussant." From Virgil’s Aeneid, Book 11, lines 344–345. This describes a state of fear where the public recognizes the Church's decline but is too intimidated by Papal authority to speak out.</note>

## The Fall of the Papacy.

*These things do not come about by human resources or by the mastery of art.*
<note>original: "Non hæc humanis opibus non arte Magistra. Proueniunt." From Virgil’s Aeneid, Book 12, lines 427–428. This suggests that the collapse of Papal power is a result of divine intervention rather than mere human politics.</note>
