I saw there new shapes of hoods being prepared, new and horrible rites which our ages have not yet seen, but which are reserved for the conquering of the Gospel. For never could faith be more conveniently assaulted than by superstitions.

**M.** Can the reputation for holiness really do so much among everyone?

**P.** You see examples of this everywhere. Do you not remember when the **Franciscan** <note>The religious order founded by St. Francis of Assisi in the 13th century, known for their vows of poverty</note> order first began to grow, how those "good fathers" so enticed all mortals with their reputation for holiness in those beginnings, that those who did not have a monastery of Saint **Francis** in their city or small town thought themselves unhappy? Indeed, so great was the foolish persuasion of men regarding these **Seraphics** <note>original: *Zeraphicis*; a title for the Franciscans, referring to the "Seraphic" vision of St. Francis</note>, that they thought putting on their garments, or imitating their color, was effective against quartan fevers <note>A form of malaria where paroxysms occur every fourth day</note> and other ailments. Indeed, it was even believed that to be buried in their hoods <term>cuculla: a monk's hood or cowl, often believed in this period to have protective spiritual powers if worn at death</term> was to hasten straight to heaven. 

This went so far that our friend **Longolius** <note>Christophe de Longueil (1488–1522), a famous humanist scholar who was obsessed with pure Ciceronian Latin</note>, having set aside the name of "Roman Citizen" for which he had pleaded so fiercely, wished to be carried to his grave as a **Franciscan** rather than be buried under a title so proud and (as he once thought) auspicious. The same madness possessed **Alberto, Prince of Carpi** <note>Alberto III Pio (1475–1531), a nobleman and diplomat who, despite a life of politics, joined the Franciscan order on his deathbed</note>. And why say more?

**Pasquillus:** But is this "hoping for better things"—to believe that someone is perpetually in **purgatory**? Why do they not rather hope that he is in heaven? These sacrifices, by their annual repetition, show clearly enough that they are never sufficient. Or do you not think that this endless repetition of masses has led many today to believe that there is no **redemption** from purgatory at all?

**Marphorius:** This discourse pleases me. But since you have happened upon the mention of purgatory, and you confessed above that no one returns from the dead, I ask you to tell me: have you seen purgatory?

Furthermore, before I even had these logical arguments, the painters themselves often made me doubt this fire. Moreover, I knew that this fire was more commonly in use among those **Northerners** <note>original: "septentrionales", referring to the people of Northern Europe, particularly Germans</note> who, so they would not arrive before **God** cold, needed a bit of reheating. <meta>This page continues the satirical dialogue between the statues Marphorius and Pasquillus. Having previously argued that Purgatory is a theological invention rather than a biblical reality, Pasquillus now offers a mock-scientific and mythological explanation for why the "fire" of Purgatory has seemingly lost its power in the modern era.</meta>

...instantly reveal it to the depths. And that seems to have been the **purgatorial fire** <note>original: "ignis purgatorius"</note> of the ancients. But this other fire, so terrible that it compels the whole world to tremble today—I do not know by what stroke of fortune it was extinguished, even though it was already most prepared for burning. 

**M.** O, if only you were speaking the truth. But did you hear this from anyone? 

**P.** Recently, while returning from **Geneva** and passing through **Upper Rhaetia** <note>A region in the Alps, roughly modern-day eastern Switzerland</note>, I heard this from my host. 

**M.** Tell the story. 

**P.** Do you not remember that year when such great floods were predicted everywhere by the **Astrologers**? 

**M.** I remember: it was the year **twenty-four** <note>1524; a year of widespread panic in Europe due to astrological predictions of a second Great Flood</note>. 

**P.** That very one. Do you also remember how at that time many prayers were made to the **Most High**, so that He might turn away such dire prognostications? 

**M.** I remember; it was prayed for and feared by everyone. 

**P.** Quite right. At that time, God, taking pity on us, commanded **Neptune** <note>The Roman god of the sea, used here to represent the floodwaters</note> to lead the waters elsewhere. Since Neptune could not lead all that massive filth <note>original: "colluuiē"</note> wherever he wished, he diverted a large part of it down into **purgatory**. Because of that event, this fire suffered such damage that it never burned purely again. **M.** If the difference is that which exists between things that are made up or painted and those that are real, then the difference is certainly great.

**M.** Oh, what a nuisance! But what was that queen called? 

**P.** She was called the Blessed Virgin. 

**M.** But where was Christ? 

**P.** I did not see him: but having been ordered to leave the council, I saw a little boy playing with some spirits <note>original: *Genijs*; guardian spirits or minor deities, often depicted in Renaissance art as winged children or "putti"</note> in front of the palace. When I asked my guide about him, he said it was Christ playing there, who had committed everything to his mother. 

**M.** O wonderful heaven, where Christ is perpetually a child! 

**P.** When the play of this boy had delighted me for a little while, I went off to see the rest of the citadel. **M.** Were they all full? 

**P.** Some were stuffed with wax candles <note>original: *ceris*; literally "waxes," likely referring to the massive quantities of votive candles used in Catholic worship</note>,

<meta>This page continues the satirical dialogue between Marforio and Pasquille. ...the heaven of the Moon, we came to the **heaven of Mercury** <note>In the traditional Ptolemaic system, Mercury is the second planet/sphere, associated with eloquence, commerce, and trickery</note>: in which I found a certain man, who was bound between two poles by a cord drawn through his middle, so that he hung as if in the center, not touching the ground with his feet. 

**M.** What was the man’s appearance? 

**P.** On his head he had two **stag horns**; from his feet hung a small bag with many gold pieces, and he himself was being perpetually rotated. But when the breeze died down for a moment, he would slide back down onto his feet by the weight of the bag. By this means, the wretched man was perpetually tumbled back and forth. **M.** Who did your **Spirit** <note>original: *Genius*; the guide through the heavens</note> say he was? 

**P.** I will whisper it in your ear. 

**M.** Woe is me! Such a great man? 

**P.** So it is, **Marforio**. 

**M.** But why was he tortured in this manner?

**M.** I grieve for the fate of such a witty man. 

**P.** He had that vice, but otherwise he was a **great man** <note>original: *uir magus*; literally "a magic man," implying a person of extraordinary or almost supernatural talent and learning</note>. 

**M.**

Proceed to the rest. **P.** Having left the **heaven of Mercury** <note>The second sphere in the ancient geocentric model of the universe</note> behind, we ascended through the remaining heavens: where, in the middle of our journey, I saw that everything was arranged in a wondrous order by the most just God, and that everything runs in its course as He first commanded, flowing into the earth according to the design of such a good **Craftsman** <note>original: *artificis*; a common Renaissance term for God as the Divine Architect</note> and according to the needs of humanity. <meta>This page continues the dialogue between the characters Marforio and Pasquille. The previous page ended mid-sentence discussing Christ as the true high priest according to the order of Melchizedek. This page picks up with the implications of our relationship to Christ as brothers and the finality of his sacrifice, directly attacking the Roman Catholic practice of the Mass.</meta>

<page-num>524</page-num>

*If we are brothers of Christ, we are children of God, for Christ is the Son of God. Truly, that he called us brothers is clear from the Psalm, where Christ says, "I will declare your name to my brothers."* <note>original Latin: *Annūciabo nomen tuum fratribus meis*; a reference to Psalm 22:22, which is quoted in the New Testament to show Christ’s humanity.</note> *This same Christ is the perpetual sacrifice before God, the perpetual Aaron* <note>the biblical first High Priest of Israel, used here as a title for Christ's priestly role</note>*, the perpetual priest, who offered himself once (for all time) for our salvation, presenting a sacrifice that is* <term>unchanging</term> <note>original Greek: *ἀπαράβατον* (aparabaton); in a legal or religious sense, this means a priesthood or sacrifice that does not pass to a successor and cannot be set aside.</note> *that is, it cannot be repeated. Why then do we have need of so many* <term>petty sacrificers</term> <note>original Latin: *sacrificulis*; a derogatory term used by Reformers to mock priests who claimed to "sacrifice" Christ again during the Mass.</note>*, and why will we not finally dismiss* <note>The author uses a pun here: *missas faciemus* can mean "we will dismiss/send away," but *missas* also means "the Masses." He is suggesting they "dismiss the Masses."</note> *so many Masses?*

**P.** *Such is the nature of the world, always contrary to Christ. For while it constantly repeats sacrifices, it does nothing other than demonstrate that Christ’s sacrifice was imperfect. For if it were perfect and sufficient, what need would there be for such great repetition?*

**M.** *But I have heard that the Mass is nothing other than a commemoration.*

**P.** *I wish it were only that; then we would not have so many "Mass-mongers"* <note>original: *missastas*</note> *and petty sacrificers. But today they sacrifice, Marforio, for the sins of the living, and what is more, for the dead; and this is their chief source of profit. Therefore, see what an injury is done to Christ: whom we know performed the sacrifice once for all time, and it will endure forever; it needs no repetition, but only a commemoration.*

**M.** *Now I understand. I wish our Italians knew this; they would not be so foolish and superstitious regarding these scoundrels* <note>original: *nebulones*; a term for worthless or deceptive people.</note>.

**P.** *Be of good cheer; not all of Italy is foolish. [God] has retained for himself...*

<vocab>Christ, sacrifice, Aaron, priest, Mass, Marforio, Italians, commemoration</vocab>

<summary>In this dialogue, Pasquille argues that because Christ’s sacrifice was perfect and happened "once for all," the repeated sacrifices of the Roman Catholic Mass are unnecessary and even insulting to Christ. He critiques the priesthood as a profit-driven enterprise and expresses hope that the Italian people will eventually reject these superstitions.</summary>

<keywords>Protestant Reformation, sacrifice of Christ, critique of the Mass, priesthood, Italian religious thought, anti-clericalism, Marforio and Pasquille</keywords>

The Lord [reserved] seven thousand men, who did not bow their knees before Baal. <note>A reference to 1 Kings 19:18, often used by reformers to argue that a "true church" of believers exists even when the visible church seems corrupt.</note> **M.** Therefore Christ governs all things, and has entrusted nothing to the saints? **P.** Nothing. For He alone prepares a place for the saints; they, however, are at rest, concerned with none of these things that are being done among us. There is one will among them all: that Christ be praised and that He reign through all things. This is what the divine Virgin asks, this is what Saint Peter asks, as do the confessors and the martyrs. <note>The text uses the honorifics *diua* and *diuus*, classical Latin terms for "divine" or "saintly," reflecting the Renaissance humanist style of the dialogue.</note> **M.** Was there no diverse worship [of these individuals] here? **P.** None. There was one wedding garment for all, which was marked with the title of charity. There was one mind for all, one heart, one will; there was no ambition for <term>filthy lucre</term> <note>original Latin: *sordidi quæstus*; refers to gain made through shameful or greedy means, a common critique of the sale of indulgences or church offices.</note>. Do you not know the Lord said in the Gospel that the Antichrist would overturn faith with miracles? And this is by the permission of God, so that those who do not believe may be confirmed in the snare. Do you not know that once seven spirits went out from God’s sight, who had sworn they would be lying spirits in the mouths of the prophets of Ahab? <note>1 Kings 22:21-22.</note> Furthermore, it is known that Satan puts on the form [of an angel of light...] <note>The sentence continues on the next page; the catchword *angeli* indicates the quote is from 2 Corinthians 11:14.</note>

<summary>Pasquille argues that true saints in heaven do not desire earthly worship or power, as they are focused solely on Christ's glory. He asserts that the cult of the saints and the complex church hierarchy are actually deceptions orchestrated by unclean spirits and the Antichrist.</summary>

*...angels of light. And since there are so many deceptions, and the gullibility of Christians has always been great, it is no wonder if so many trifles have been accepted. Do you think the good Paul, who foresaw these things, cried out so many times for no reason that we should test the spirits to see if they are from God?* <note>Pasquille refers to 1 John 4:1, here attributed to Paul’s general warnings against spiritual deception, a common theme in Reformist critiques of medieval miracles.</note> *How often do you read that the Divine Virgin appeared and demanded from foolish men that temples and monasteries be built for her? Do you think that most humble handmaid—who, because of her humility, holds the first place in the body of the Church and the Bride of Christ, and who loves her Groom intimately—would ever have desired that which she knew belonged to the Groom alone? For to whom, except to the gods alone, were temples built even by the most foolish pagans? Why did she not rather desire in those apparitions that the Gospel be soundly preached? That the vineyard of Christ be well-cultivated? That drunken dogs, unable to bark, should not be in charge?* <note>Isaiah 56:10 describes "dumb dogs that cannot bark," a biblical metaphor frequently used by critics of the Renaissance Church to describe lazy or uneducated clergy who failed to preach.</note> *On the contrary, from what we see, she* <note>Pasquille is likely referring to the institutionalized "image" of Mary used by the Church to justify its power.</note> *is the one who has put such pigs in charge of the pens.*

**M.** *The more I hear you speaking, Pasquille, the more and more the truth is revealed to me. I wish you could be made Pope just once, and proclaim these things to the whole world; for these lessons are no less learned than they are necessary.*

**P.** *Do not wish this for me, Marforio. Why would you want a rough stone* <note>Pasquille is literally a weathered, ancient statue (a "rough stone") in Rome upon which critics posted satirical verses.</note> *to administer anything in such a <term>flesh-obsessed Rome</term>?* <note>original Latin: *carnulenta Roma*; implying a city preoccupied with worldly pleasures, corruption, and the "flesh" rather than the spirit.</note> *You know I do not suit their taste.*

**M.** *I wonder that, in such a hunger for the word of God, no one demands anything from you.*

**P.** *Because in this state of need, I am despised,*

<meta>catchword: little</meta>

<summary>Pasquille argues that the Virgin Mary would never demand the construction of temples for herself, as such worship belongs only to God, and he critiques the corruption of the Roman Church. He explains to Marforio that his blunt truth-telling makes him unfit for the Papacy in a city devoted to carnal interests.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between the statues Pasquille and Marforio. Pasquille is describing his vision of the true, heavenly Church, contrasting its Christ-centered unity with the corruption and idolatry of the Roman Church discussed on the previous page.</meta>

<page-num>327</page-num>
<sig>R 2</sig>

It matters little to me: I would rather be despised than vomited out. <note>A reference to Revelation 3:16, where God threatens to spit out the "lukewarm" who are neither hot nor cold.</note>
**M.** Do you have nothing else to say about this heaven? **P.** I have already said that there are almost all things there which it is not permitted for a man to speak, even if he had a thousand mouths. What I saw is contained in this summary: There, Christ, the head of all, is the bridegroom of the Church. The Church is composed of various members constituting one unity, for whom access to God the Father is open only through the bridegroom. There is no ambition here, nor care for these temporal <term>temporal: things belonging to the physical world or time, as opposed to the eternal</term> things; there is a single effort of all, that the Father may be praised through Jesus forever and ever, Amen. Upon him they desire all glory, all praise, and all honor to be heaped. No one seeks their own interests, but only those of the bridegroom. You would have said that all had forgotten this world and are truly otherworldly. Indeed, all things are administered by Christ, who prays for us, who intercedes continually, whose sacrifice is always present before the Father, who daily sends to the elect his own unique Spirit, shared with the Father, and rules his Church through him. Here there are no demigods, nor any men like Sejanus <note>Lucius Aelius Sejanus was the notoriously corrupt and ambitious advisor to the Roman Emperor Tiberius. Pasquille uses him here as a symbol for corrupt papal favorites or "power behind the throne" figures.</note>; he alone is King and Lord, the Alpha and Omega <note>original: "α & ω"</note> of all things, and the head of all saints, of all piety, all sincerity, and true religion. Here there are no informers regarding earthly matters. He himself is the light of the world, and he sees all things: to him be praise forever. No one persuades him of anything, for he is the Truth. Whatever happens without him is error, for he himself is the Way.

<summary>Pasquille describes a vision of the true Church in heaven, which is characterized by a direct relationship with Christ and a total absence of earthly ambition or corrupt advisors.</summary>

--- Page 672 ---
<meta>This page continues the dialogue between the famous "talking statues" of Rome, Pasquille (Pasquino) and Marforio. Having just described a vision of the true heavenly Church, Pasquille now explains Christ’s role as the sole mediator, contrasting this with the popular religious practices of the day.</meta>

<page-num>528</page-num>

Upon him all things stand and fall. For he is the life of all, and through him alone the Father hears us: for whatever you ask in my name (says the Gospel) he will do it. <note>original: "in nomine meo... hoc faciet" — a reference to John 14:13.</note> This alone is certain: that prayer is made through him, for the Father, who cannot lie, made his promise through him. He promised nothing to those who ask in the name of others. Indeed, he is angry that they think any saint could be more merciful than Christ, better, more attentive, or more acceptable to the Father. For if we wish to have an advocate, *who is more merciful than Christ? Who is better? Who is more acceptable to God?*

**M.** I see the whole error: it is because we judge heavenly things by our own human nature. For we think in this way: that the divine Virgin is of a much more gentle nature than Christ, whom we imagine to be a grim judge and a tyrant. This is an error arising solely from the difference of sex, because we think women are somewhat milder than men.

**M.** That might be forgiven, were it not for the fact that they have even snatched the sovereignty away from Christ and given it to his mother—as if Christ, who is the wisdom of the Father, were now completely delirious!

**P.** I am glad, Marforio, that from a subtle <term>Canonist: an expert in Canon Law, the internal legal system of the Catholic Church</term> you have been made a simple <term>Evangelist: here meaning one who adheres strictly to the teachings of the Gospels</term>.

**M.** I owe this to you, Pasquille, for you have rescued me from such thick mists. But is this the end of the story?

**P.** Nothing else remains, except that after a long gaze, I unwillingly returned by the same path I had come to my crypt <note>The "crypt" or "pit" refers to the physical location of the statue in Rome.</note>; there I gave great thanks to the angel, who had shown me all these things in good faith.

<summary>Pasquille and Marforio conclude their dialogue by affirming Christ as the sole mediator between God and humanity, critiquing the contemporary elevation of the Virgin Mary and saints over Christ, and ending Pasquille's visionary journey.</summary>

He <note>Referring to the guide or spirit from the previous vision.</note> promised the same assistance to me if I wished to visit the lower regions, saying I would see many things there worth reporting. For this service I thanked him, but deferred it to another time.

**M.** Wisely done. For you know what the poet <note>Virgil, in the *Aeneid*, Book VI.</note> once sang:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*But to retrace one's steps, and escape to the upper air,*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*This is the task, this is the toil.*
<note>original: "Sed reuocare gradũ, superasq́; euadere ad auras. Hoc opus, hic labor est."</note>

**PAS.** That is true. But it matters a great deal if one makes the journey with a favorable **Mercury**. <note>The Roman messenger god who also served as the "Psychopomp," the guide who leads souls to the underworld.</note>

**M.** My dear Pasquille, for such a pleasant conversation I owe you more than I have ever owed anyone. I do not wish to question you any further at this time, as the dawn is drawing forth, and the watchmen stationed here demonstrate by their first <term>pandiculations: the act of stretching and yawning upon waking</term> that they have overcome their sleep. I would not want this meeting of ours to be known to anyone, since the truth that is sought here with you is now hated by all. Therefore, may you fare well; and if ever a vision of the underworld is offered to you, I ask that you be willing to remember me.

**P.** I shall do so gladly. In the meantime, farewell to you too, Marforio; continue to be sincere and a Christian.

**M.** It shall be so.

->THE END.<-

# THE TAUNTS OF
## Pasquille against the Germans. Published
### In the year 1542.
### In the month of November.

->Pasquille.<-
<note>Pasquille (or Pasquino) refers to a famous ancient statue in Rome where citizens would secretly post anonymous satirical poems and biting political critiques, known as "pasquinades."</note>

I am the voice of one crying out in the wilderness: prepare the way of the Lord.
<note>original: "Ego uox clamantis in deserto, parate uiam domini." A quote from John 1:23; Pasquille casts himself as a prophet warning of coming judgment.</note>

### The Holy Roman Empire.

*They have mouths and shall not speak; they have eyes and shall not see; they have ears and shall not hear; they have noses and shall not smell; they have hands and shall not touch; they have feet and shall not walk.*
<note>original: "Os habent & non loquentur..." etc. This quote from Psalm 115, originally describing lifeless idols, is used here to mock the Empire as a paralyzed and ineffective institution.</note>

### The Emperor.
<note>In 1542, this was Charles V, who was struggling to manage the rise of Protestantism and the threat of the Ottoman Empire.</note>

*Every kingdom divided against itself shall be brought to desolation. I have not come to bring peace, but a sword.*
<note>original: "Omne regnum diuifum... Non ueni ut mitterem pacem, fed gladium." Combined quotes from Matthew 12:25 and 10:34, highlighting the civil and religious strife of the era.</note>

### The Estates of the Holy Roman Empire.

*Put your sword back into its place. For all those who take up the sword shall perish by the sword.*
<note>original: "Conuerte gladium tuum in locum fuum..." A quote from Matthew 26:52, the warning given to Peter in Gethsemane, here suggesting the folly of the warring German princes.</note>

### The Prince Palatine 
### of the Rhine, Elector.
<note>The Elector Palatine was one of the most powerful princes in Germany, responsible for choosing the Emperor.</note>

*Peace be with you.*
<note>original: "Pax uobis." A traditional greeting from John 20:19, perhaps used here ironically regarding the Elector's attempts to mediate or his desire for neutrality.</note>

# The Supreme Captain of the Empire in the Hungarian war.
<note>In 1542, the "Supreme Captain" (Generalissimo) of the Imperial army was Joachim II Hector, Elector of Brandenburg. His campaign to retake Buda was a widely mocked failure.</note>
*I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered.*
<note>original: "Percutiam pastorem & dispergentur oues gregis." A quote from Matthew 26:31. Here it suggests that the failure of the leadership caused the imperial army to dissolve in chaos.</note>

## Soldiers, the army of the Empire in Hungary.
*They returned to their own country by another way.*
<note>original: "Per aliam uiam reuersi sunt in regionem suam." A quote from Matthew 2:12 regarding the Magi. In this context, it mocks the soldiers for retreating or deserting the campaign.</note>

## Buda.
<note>Buda (part of modern Budapest) was the capital of the Kingdom of Hungary, captured by the Ottoman Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent in 1541.</note>
*My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?*
<note>original: "Deus meus, Deus meus, ut me dereliquisti." The cry of Christ on the cross (Matthew 27:46), used here to represent the city of Buda feeling abandoned by the Holy Roman Empire's failed relief efforts.</note>

## The Town of Pest.
<note>Pest sits across the Danube from Buda; it was also a focal point of the 1542 siege.</note>
*Your burnt offerings are not accepted, and your sacrifices have not pleased me.*
<note>original: "Holocaustomata uestra non sunt accepta, & uictimæ uestræ non placuerunt mihi." From Jeremiah 6:20. This implies that the military efforts and lives lost at Pest were a waste and found no favor with God or the people.</note>

## The Kingdom of Hungary.
*Are you the one who is to come, or should we look for another?*
<note>original: "Tu es ille qui uenturus est, an alterū expectamus." From Matthew 11:3. Hungary asks if the Holy Roman Empire is truly its savior or if they must look elsewhere for protection from the Turks.</note>

## The King of the Romans.
<note>In 1542, the <term>King of the Romans</term>—the title for the heir-apparent to the Empire—was Ferdinand I, brother of Emperor Charles V. He was directly responsible for the defense of the Austrian and Hungarian lands.</note>
*Silver and gold I have none, but what I have, I give to you.*
<note>original: "Argentum & aurum non est mihi, quod autem habeo hoc tibi do." From Acts 3:6. This mocks Ferdinand’s chronic lack of funds to pay his troops or fund the war.</note>

## The Imperial Cities.
*Opening their treasures, they offered him gifts: gold, and frankincense, and myrrh.*
<note>original: "Apertis thesauris suis obtulerunt illi munera, Aurū, & thus & Mircham." From Matthew 2:11. A sarcastic reference to the "Free Imperial Cities" being forced to provide the wealth and resources to fund the Emperor's wars.</note>

## The Princes of the Empire.
*Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy, and where thieves break in and steal.*
<note>original: "Ne reponatis uobis thesauros in terra, ubi erugo & tinea corrumpit, & ubi fures perfodiunt ac furantur." From Matthew 6:19. This suggests the German Princes are being greedy or hoarding wealth while the Empire’s borders are falling.</note>

# TAUNTS OF PAS-
# quil against the Germans. Published
## In the Year 1542.
### In the Month of November.

## Pasquil.
<note>Pasquil (or Pasquino) refers to a famous "talking statue" in Rome where people posted anonymous satirical poems or "pasquinades" mocking the authorities.</note>

> *I am the voice of one crying out in the wilderness: prepare the way of the Lord.*
<note>original: "Ego uox clamantis in deserto, parate uiam domini." A quote from John 1:23. Pasquil presents himself as a lonely truth-teller in a desert of political corruption.</note>

## The Roman Empire.
<note>Referring to the Holy Roman Empire of the German Nation.</note>

> *They have mouths and will not speak; they have eyes and will not see; they have ears and will not hear; they have noses and will not smell; they have hands and will not touch; they have feet and will not walk.*
<note>original: "Os habent & non loquentur..." from Psalm 115. The satirist compares the Empire to a useless pagan idol—ornate and massive, but completely incapable of acting or responding to the crises of the day.</note>

## The Emperor.
<note>At this time, the Emperor was Charles V, who was struggling to manage the Reformation in Germany and the Ottoman threat simultaneously.</note>

> *Every kingdom divided against itself shall be brought to desolation.*
<note>original: "Omne regnum diuifum aduerfus fefe, desolabitur." From Matthew 12:25. This refers to the religious and political fractures between Catholic and Protestant territories.</note>
> *I have not come to bring peace, but a sword.*
<note>original: "Non ueni ut mitterem pacem, sed gladium." From Matthew 10:34. This likely mocks the Emperor's constant state of warfare.</note>

## The Estates of the Roman Empire.
<note>The "Status Imperii" refers to the Imperial Diet, the assembly of princes and representatives who governed the Empire with the Emperor.</note>

> *Put your sword back in its place. For all who take the sword shall perish by the sword.*
<note>original: "Conuerte gladium tuum in locum fuum..." From Matthew 26:52. This serves as a warning to the German princes about the dangers of civil and religious war.</note>

## The Prince Palatine of the Rhine, Elector.
<note>The Elector Palatine at this time was Ludwig V (until 1544). He was known for trying to maintain a middle ground and keep peace during the religious conflicts.</note>

> *Peace be with you.*
<note>original: "Pax uobis." From John 20:19. In this satirical context, it likely mocks the Elector's perceived passivity or his role as a mediator who achieves little.</note>

## The Imperial Chamber, or the Treasurers

> *“How much do you owe my lord?” He said: “A hundred measures of oil.” And he said to him: “Take your bond, and sit down quickly and write eighty.”*
<note>original: "Quantum debes domino meo... accipe cautionem tuam & scribe octoginta." A quote from the Parable of the Unjust Steward in Luke 16:5-7. By applying this to the Imperial treasurers, the satirist suggests they are engaged in embezzlement or fraudulent accounting of the Empire's funds.</note>

## The Regents of the Imperial Estates

> *“And I say to you: make friends for yourselves from the mammon of unrighteousness, so that when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings.”*
<note>original: "Ego dico uobis : facite uobis amicos ex mammona iniusto..." From Luke 16:9. This implies that the regents (the administrative body governing in the Emperor's absence) are more concerned with securing their own future through bribes and ill-gotten wealth than with the common good.</note>

## The Diet of Nuremberg

> *“To be spat upon and scourged; and on the third day he will rise again.”*
<note>original: "Ad conspuendum & flagellandum, & tertia die resurget." From Luke 18:32-33. The Diet of 1542 was a contentious meeting where the Estates were pressured to provide funds for the Turkish war; the satirist views the assembly as a place of suffering or humiliation that nonetheless keeps "resurrecting" or reconvening.</note>

## The Schmalkaldic Confederates
<note>The Schmalkaldic League was a defensive alliance of Lutheran princes and cities within the Holy Roman Empire.</note>

> *“I say to you: Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you cannot enter the kingdom of heaven.”*
<note>original: "Dico uobis: Nisi abundauerit uestra iustitia..." From Matthew 5:20. The satirist mocks the Protestant princes, suggesting that for all their talk of religious reform and "righteousness," they are just as legalistic or hypocritical as those they oppose.</note>

## The Confederates of the Opposing Side
<note>This refers to the Catholic League, the princes loyal to the Pope and the Emperor who opposed the Protestants.</note>

> *“No one can serve two masters. For either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will cling to the one and neglect the other. You cannot serve God and mammon.”*
<note>original: "Nemo potest duobus dominis seruire... Non potestis deo seruire & mammonæ." From Matthew 6:24. This suggests that the Catholic princes are torn between their religious duties and their greed or political ambitions.</note>

## The Imperial Chamber Court
<term>Imperial Chamber Court<gloss>The *Reichskammergericht*, the highest judicial body in the Holy Roman Empire.</gloss></term>

> *“The scribes and Pharisees sit in the seat of Moses: Therefore, all things whatsoever they bid you observe, observe and do; but do not do according to their works.”*
<note>original: "In cathedra Mosi sedent scribe et pharisæi..." From Matthew 23:2-3. This is a sharp critique of the Imperial judges, implying they hold legitimate authority but are personally corrupt and do not practice the justice they preach.</note>

## Brabant & Flanders
<note>Brabant and Flanders were the heart of the Habsburg Netherlands. In the early 1540s, these territories were heavily taxed and suffered from the ongoing wars between Emperor Charles V and Francis I of France.</note>

> When distress comes, they will seek peace and there shall be none. Trouble upon trouble shall come, and rumor upon rumor.
<note>original: "Anguſtia ſuperueniente requirent pacem... Et rumor ſuper rumorem erit." From Ezekiel 7:25-26. This reflects the constant state of anxiety and the failed peace treaties that characterized the region during the Italian War of 1542–1546.</note>

### The Brabantine Court

> From the north all evil shall break forth upon all the inhabitants of the land. For behold, I will call together all the kindreds of the kingdoms of the north; and they shall come, and every one shall set his throne at the entrance of the gate.
<note>original: "Ab aquilone pandetur omne malum... ponent unuſquiſq; ſolium ſuum in introitu portæ." From Jeremiah 1:14-15. This "evil from the north" likely refers to the threat posed by the Duke of Cleves and his allies to the Habsburg administration in Brussels.</note>

### The Duke of Cleves & Jülich
<note>William "the Rich," Duke of Jülich-Cleves-Berg, was a major rival to Emperor Charles V. His claim to the Duchy of Guelders led to a significant military conflict that threatened the stability of the Empire's northwestern territories.</note>

> Behold, the day of the Lord shall come, cruel, and full of indignation, and of wrath, and of fury, to lay the land desolate.
<note>original: "Ecce dies domini ueniet crudelis... ad ponendam terram in ſolitudinem." From Isaiah 13:9. This choice of verse suggests the impending military devastation of the Duke's lands by Imperial forces.</note>

### Henry, Duke of Brunswick
<note>Henry V (the Younger) of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel was a staunch Catholic defender. In 1542, he was driven into exile and his lands were occupied by the Protestant Schmalkaldic League. The satirist uses his "voice" to recite a psalm of lamentation.</note>

> My strength is weakened through poverty. I have become a great reproach among all my enemies, and especially to my neighbors, and a fear to my acquaintances. They that saw me fled from me, and I am forgotten, as one who is dead. I have become like a vessel that is destroyed; for I have heard the insults of many who dwell round about. While they assembled together against me, they consulted to take away my life.
<note>original: "Infirmata eſt in paupertate uirtus mea... accipere animam meam conſiliati ſunt." From Psalm 31:10-13 (Vulgate Psalm 30:11-14). The passage perfectly mirrors Henry's sudden fall from power to the status of an impoverished exile.</note>

### The Bishop of Bremen
<note>Christoph of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel, brother to Duke Henry, served as the Prince-Archbishop of Bremen. Like his brother, he faced significant opposition from the rising Protestant tide in Northern Germany.</note>

<note>Albert of Brandenburg was the Elector and Archbishop of Mainz. He was a primary target of the early Reformation due to his role in the sale of indulgences.</note>

### The Council of Trent to be Celebrated
<note>The Council of Trent (1545–1563) was the Catholic Church's formal response to the Reformation. At the time of this writing, it was the subject of intense political maneuvering.</note>

### Pasquillus
<note>A "Pasquillus" (or Pasquinade) is a form of anonymous political satire. The name comes from "Pasquino," a statue in Rome where people would post biting lampoons and verses. Here, the author adopts this persona to deliver a final, sharp jab at the political establishment.</note>

*If I tell the truth, why do you not believe me?*
<note>original: "Si ueritatem dico, quare uos non creditis mihi." From John 8:46. By ending the manuscript with this question from Jesus, the author frames his political comparisons not as mere insults, but as uncomfortable truths that the authorities refuse to acknowledge.</note>

# Description of the Binding

**Material:** Dark green **Morocco leather** <term>Morocco leather: a high-quality, durable goatskin leather characterized by a distinct pebbled grain; often used for luxury bookbinding</term>.

**Decoration:**
*   **Front Cover:** Features an elaborate border and four large, ornate corner pieces applied through **gold-tooling** <term>gold-tooling: the process of pressing gold leaf into leather with heated brass stamps</term>.
*   **Style:** The delicate floral and leaf-like scrollwork is executed in the **Rococo style** <note>a highly ornamental and asymmetrical style of decoration popular in 18th-century Europe</note>.

**Spine:**
*   **Structure:** The spine features **raised bands** <note>horizontal ridges across the spine covering the cords used to sew the book's sections together</note>.
*   **Ornamentation:** The compartments between the bands are decorated with gold-tooled **fleurons** <term>fleuron: a flower-shaped typographic or binding ornament</term>.
